The Court affirmed the dismissal as to the county. The holding was limited to these statutes and this party alignment; other statutory language or alignments could produce a different answer.
sections.Reasoning:
The plaintiff relied on Gibbs's common-nucleus-of-operative-fact test and on ancillary jurisdiction, noting that one discharge produced both sets of claims and that a combined trial would avoid duplication. The Court reviewed both doctrines. The pendent-claim cases involved nonfederal claims connected to a proper federal dispute between parties already before the court; the ancillary cases included claims to property or funds under federal control. Those examples showed additional-party jurisdiction exists in some settings, not that it exists whenever claims share facts.

The decisive distinction was statutory. Gibbs involved state claims against a defendant already properly present on a substantial federal claim. Here the plaintiff sought to add a different defendant solely through a state-law claim. Article III's scope and the convenience of a joint trial could not answer whether Congress had authorized that extension, since federal courts have limited jurisdiction and their statutory grants must be examined. Section 1343(3) covered civil actions authorized to redress specified deprivations, and section 1983, the relevant cause of action, excluded counties. The jurisdictional grant should not be read to bring back that excluded defendant merely because state law imposed a related obligation.

The inquiry is therefore twofold: Article III must permit the jurisdiction, and Congress must not have expressly or implicitly negated it. The Court left diversity jurisdiction over municipal corporations undisturbed and observed, without deciding, that exclusive federal jurisdiction over a claim against the United States could strengthen the case for joinder.

Justice Brennan, dissenting, would have applied Gibbs to related parties, treating convenience and fairness as matters of discretion and not power. He disputed the inference that Congress had forbidden such jurisdiction and stressed the purpose of providing a federal forum for civil rights. A casebook editorial note observes that Monell later held municipalities to be covered persons under section 1983.

CP-ATLAS-AMCHEM.rule: A class certified only for settlement must still satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b), apart from trial manageability; the fairness of the settlement under Rule 23(e) cannot substitute for predominance of common questions and adequate representation of conflicting groups within the class.

sections.Parties: Twenty former asbestos manufacturers belonging to the Center for Claims Resolution (CCR) were the defendants in the settlement class action and joined the plaintiffs in presenting the settlement and the certification motion. Nine lead plaintiffs and their families purported to represent a class of persons exposed to the defendants' asbestos, or related to exposed persons, who had not already sued a CCR defendant. Objectors challenged the certification and the settlement, arguing that the compensation was inadequate and that the same lawyers and representatives could not fairly bargain for groups with conflicting needs.
sections.Procedural History:
After the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation transferred pending federal asbestos cases to the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and broader negotiations failed, the parties on January 15, 1993 simultaneously filed a complaint, an answer, a proposed settlement and a certification motion. Judge Weiner conditionally certified a Rule 23(b)(3) opt-out class and appointed class counsel. Judge Reed conducted the fairness proceedings. The district court found the settlement fair, the notice adequate and certification appropriate, rejected the claimed conflicts, declined to create subclasses, and enjoined class members' separate suits.

The Third Circuit vacated the certification and the injunction, concluding that Rule 23's prerequisites were unmet. The Supreme Court reviewed the proper role of settlement in certification and, on June 25, 1997, affirmed the Third Circuit's judgment, leaving the class decertified.
sections.Material Facts:
Asbestos exposure can produce disease after decades of latency, and asbestos litigation had produced large backlogs and high costs. CCR approached lawyers who represented thousands of existing "inventory" plaintiffs. Those lawyers negotiated an administrative system for people whose claims had not yet been filed, with whom they had no attorney-client relationship, while CCR separately settled the inventory cases, including one agreement exceeding $200 million. The parties never intended a trial.

More than half the named plaintiffs alleged existing physical injuries; the others alleged exposure without manifested disease. Each represented the whole class, and there were no subclasses. The complaint asserted a range of state-law claims.

The settlement set compensation for mesothelioma, lung cancer, other specified cancers and nonmalignant conditions, with ordinary mesothelioma payments from $20,000 to $200,000. Annual caps limited the number of claims paid in each category, and payments were not adjusted for inflation. Loss of consortium, exposure-only emotional distress, enhanced risk, medical monitoring and pleural plaques without impairment received no separate compensation. Most members would be bound indefinitely, while defendants could withdraw after ten years. Members had an initial three-month period to opt out.
sections.Issue: Can a class action proposed only for settlement be certified under Rule 23(b)(3) when the class would not satisfy the rule's predominance and adequacy-of-representation requirements, on the ground that the global settlement is fair? What role does the fact of settlement play in the certification inquiry?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1997, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg for six Justices (6-2, Justice O'Connor not participating), held that settlement is relevant to certification but does not replace Rule 23's requirements. A court need not ask whether a trial would be manageable, but the other requirements of Rule 23(a) and (b) remain fully applicable and can demand heightened attention; Rule 23(e) fairness review is additional to them. This class failed predominance and lacked adequate representation. The Court affirmed the Third Circuit while correcting its statement that settlement is irrelevant. It did not categorically bar mass-tort or settlement classes, and it did not decide the objectors' jurisdictional or notice challenges.
sections.Reasoning:
Because no trial was proposed, manageability under Rule 23(b)(3)(D) dropped out. But a settlement court lacks the usual chance to adjust the class as litigation develops, so the remaining safeguards matter more. Under the Rules Enabling Act, courts must apply the rule as adopted and may not invent a fairness-only standard; certification on an overall impression of a good bargain would also strip class counsel of the leverage that a viable litigated action provides.

Predominance was not shown. Commonality under Rule 23(a)(2) is less demanding than predominance under Rule 23(b)(3). Shared exposure and a common interest in a fair settlement could not predominate over individual questions: members encountered different products, exposure routes and durations, and had different smoking histories, medical conditions and governing state law. Some were ill and others might never be. If a shared interest in settling sufficed, the requirement would be empty in every settlement case.

Representation was inadequate. Currently injured members wanted generous immediate payments, while exposure-only members needed durable future funding, inflation protection and meaningful later options. Named plaintiffs with diverse conditions did not cure the conflict when each bargained for the whole class. Adequacy required structural assurance that the different groups' interests had been represented in the negotiations. The Court made no finding of collusion or misconduct by counsel.

The Court treated certification as logically antecedent to the Article III and amount-in-controversy objections and did not decide them. It noted the difficulty of notifying people unaware of their exposure but did not hold the notice plan unconstitutional.

Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Stevens, agreed that settlement matters to certification but would have vacated and remanded for the lower courts to apply that principle, deferring more to the district court's extensive findings. He did not pronounce the settlement fair.

CP-ATLAS-AMERICAN-WELL.rule: A suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action, so a state-law claim for injury to business does not arise under the patent laws merely because a defense may require deciding patent validity or infringement.

sections.Parties: American Well Works Co., the plaintiff, alleged that it owned, manufactured and sold a pump and sued for damage to its business. The defendants, with Layne & Bowler Co. named in the caption, were alleged to have falsely and maliciously accused the pump of infringing their patent. American Well Works wanted the removed case sent back to state court; in the Supreme Court it challenged the federal district court's dismissal of its action.
sections.Procedural History:
The action began in state court and was removed to federal court. American Well Works moved to remand. Instead, the federal District Court dismissed the action, reasoning that the claim arose under the patent laws, that the state court therefore had no jurisdiction over it, and that consequently the federal court receiving the removed action also lacked jurisdiction.

A proper certificate brought the jurisdictional question directly to the Supreme Court. The Court, on May 22, 1916, reversed the District Court's dismissal. It was not reviewing any merits judgment on patent infringement.
sections.Material Facts:
American Well Works alleged that it owned, manufactured and sold a pump for which it held or sought a patent. It claimed that the defendants falsely and maliciously told customers that the pump and its components infringed the defendants' patent, brought suits against users of the pump without probable cause, and threatened suits against anyone using it. According to the pleading, these statements and threats injured the manufacturer's business. It alleged $50,000 in actual damage and asked for the same amount in punitive damages.

These were allegations and demands only. There had been no finding that the statements were false, that any patent was infringed, or that any loss had occurred.
sections.Issue: Does a claim for injury to business caused by statements that the plaintiff's product infringes a patent, and by threats of infringement suits, arise under the patent laws merely because a defense to it may require deciding patent validity or infringement?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1916, in an opinion by Justice Holmes with Justice McKenna dissenting, held that it does not. The suit arose under the state law that created the cause of action. Jurisdiction depended on the plaintiff's declaration, and the patent questions were not necessary elements of the plaintiff's affirmative case; the possible need to examine patents in a justification or defense did not make this a suit under the patent laws. The Court reversed the dismissal without deciding whether the statements were false, whether any patent was infringed, or whether damages were owed.
sections.Reasoning:
Holmes identified the alleged injury as lost business caused by language tending to persuade the public to stop dealing with the plaintiff, whether by persuasion, threats or falsehood. The plaintiff's case required a business capable of being damaged and actionable conduct producing that damage. Whether the business rested on patents was immaterial to that inquiry.

Justifications belonged to the defense. A competitor might justify persuasion by competition, good faith or reasonable grounds, and a statement of fact might be defended as true. American Well Works did not have to prove the validity or infringement of the defendants' patent, or the validity of its own, as an element of its claim. A statement that its pump infringed could be true even if it held a patent of its own.

The source of the alleged wrong therefore answered the jurisdictional question. State law determined whether conduct injuring the business was actionable and what justifications were available, as Holmes illustrated by the variation among states in the treatment of truth and malicious statements. If the state abolished such actions, the patent laws would not independently preserve this cause of action. The possible federal content of a defense did not create the affirmative claim.

Justice McKenna dissented on the ground that the case involved a direct and substantial controversy under the patent laws; the report gives that view in a single statement without further analysis.

The casebook uses the case to introduce Holmes's creation formula, and its surrounding discussion cautions that the formula is more useful for inclusion than for exclusion. The opinion resolves this state business-injury suit and does not itself examine every later category of state-law claim containing an embedded federal question.

CP-ATLAS-ANDERSON-LIBERTY.rule: On summary judgment the judge asks whether the evidence, viewed favorably to the nonmovant, could support a reasonable jury verdict under the substantive burden of proof that will apply at trial, including the clear-and-convincing standard for actual malice.

sections.Parties: Liberty Lobby, Inc., a nonprofit corporation describing itself as a citizens' lobby, and Willis Carto, its founder and treasurer, were the libel plaintiffs. The defendants were publisher Jack Anderson, Bill Adkins, the corporate president and chief executive, and Investigator Publishing Co. The plaintiffs sued over allegedly false and derogatory statements in a publication, The Investigator; the defendants sought summary judgment on the ground that actual malice could not be proved.
sections.Procedural History:
Liberty Lobby and Carto sued in the federal district court in the District of Columbia under diversity jurisdiction. After discovery, the defendants moved for summary judgment. The district court treated the plaintiffs as limited-purpose public figures and granted the motion, reasoning that the author's research and reliance on numerous sources precluded actual malice.

The D.C. Circuit affirmed as to 21 of the challenged items but reversed as to nine. It held that the clear-and-convincing standard should not be applied at summary judgment, and asked only whether a jury could find the statements false, defamatory and malicious. The Supreme Court reviewed that legal standard and, on June 25, 1986, vacated the D.C. Circuit's decision and remanded for application of the correct standard.
sections.Material Facts:
The October 1981 issue of The Investigator published two longer articles about Carto and Francis Yockey, introduced by a shorter article about an alleged neo-Nazi underground. The articles portrayed Liberty Lobby and Carto as neo-Nazi, anti-Semitic, racist and Fascist. The plaintiffs alleged that 28 statements and two illustrations were false and derogatory.

In support of summary judgment, Charles Bermant, the employee who wrote the two longer articles, submitted an affidavit describing substantial research, numerous sources and his continuing belief in the articles' accuracy, with an appendix identifying sources for the challenged statements. Anderson's shorter introduction relied exclusively on Bermant's information.

The plaintiffs pointed to alleged inaccuracies and to sources they considered patently unreliable, arguing that the defendants had inadequately verified the articles. They also offered evidence that editor William McGaw had described the articles to Adkins before publication as terrible and ridiculous. The plaintiffs did not challenge their public-figure status on appeal, so they had to prove actual malice, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of the truth, by clear and convincing evidence.
sections.Issue: In a public-figure libel action, must the heightened burden of proving actual malice by clear and convincing evidence at trial be taken into account when the court decides whether there is a genuine issue of material fact on a motion for summary judgment?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States, in 1986, in an opinion by Justice White for a 6-3 majority (joined by Justices Marshall, Blackmun, Powell, Stevens and O'Connor), held that it must. The judge asks whether the evidence could support a reasonable jury finding for the nonmovant under the applicable burden of proof, here whether a reasonable jury could find actual malice by clear and convincing evidence, while leaving credibility and legitimate competing inferences to the jury. The Court vacated and remanded without itself deciding whether the publishers were entitled to summary judgment on every disputed statement. Justice Brennan dissented, and Justice Rehnquist dissented joined by Chief Justice Burger.
sections.Reasoning:
A factual dispute defeats summary judgment only if it is material and genuine. Substantive law identifies which facts are material: those whose resolution could affect the outcome. A dispute is genuine if the evidence would permit a reasonable jury to return a verdict for the nonmoving party. The judge does not weigh the evidence or decide who is telling the truth, but a bare allegation, a merely colorable showing or a scintilla of evidence is not enough.

White tied the inquiry to the directed verdict under Rule 50: the question in both is whether reasonable jurors could disagree or whether only one conclusion is legally permissible. One cannot identify a reasonable verdict without knowing what must be proved, so evidence adequate under a preponderance standard is not necessarily adequate under a clear-and-convincing one, just as a criminal judge assessing sufficiency asks about proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The nonmovant's evidence is still to be believed and all justifiable inferences drawn in its favor, and a judge may deny summary judgment where a full trial seems the better course.

The Court rejected a categorical exception for state-of-mind issues. A plaintiff needs affirmative evidence; the mere possibility that a jury will disbelieve the defendant's denial is ordinarily not enough, provided there has been a full opportunity for discovery. The Court assumed the movant's initial burden was met and did not decide that question.

Justice Brennan, dissenting, thought the majority changed summary-judgment law and that its directions to consider the quality and quantity of evidence could not be reconciled with the ban on weighing, risking trial on paper and encroachment on the jury. Justice Rehnquist, joined by Chief Justice Burger, saw an added procedural requirement, faulted the majority for not applying its standard to the record, and questioned the criminal analogy.

CP-ATLAS-ARNSTEIN.rule: Under the Second Circuit's approach in 1946, summary judgment is improper where there is the slightest doubt as to the facts, particularly where the outcome turns on the credibility of a witness whom the jury has not seen testify.

sections.Parties: Composer Ira B. Arnstein was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sued Cole Porter, the defendant and appellee, for musical copyright infringement, seeking damages and demanding a jury, on the contention that Porter had obtained access to and copied his compositions. Porter denied access and copying, obtained summary judgment, and also challenged Arnstein's copyright ownership, the inclusion of uncopyrighted material and song titles, and the allegedly vexatious nature of the suit.
sections.Procedural History:
Arnstein sued in federal district court and demanded a jury. Both parties were deposed, and recordings of the disputed music were submitted. The district judge found portions of Arnstein's account implausible, accepted Porter's denial, and granted summary judgment for Porter.

Arnstein appealed to the Second Circuit, which itself listened to the recordings. On February 11, 1946, a divided panel modified the judgment in part and otherwise reversed and remanded. Claims on two uncopyrighted works and two titles were converted into dismissals for lack of jurisdiction; the remaining adverse judgment was reversed for further proceedings. The result required a trial opportunity and was not a finding that Porter copied or infringed.
sections.Material Facts:
Arnstein contended that Porter had access to his compositions and copied them. Porter denied both. Arnstein's account included assertions, including some involving intermediaries or "stooges," that the district judge found implausible.

The record contained more than those assertions. More than a million copies of one Arnstein composition had been sold, and other pieces had been sold, distributed to radio stations, bandleaders or publishers, or publicly performed. The appellate court, listening to the recordings, found some similarity between the works: not enough by itself to infer copying, but enough to be probative if access were established.

Arnstein had brought previous unsuccessful suits. His claims included the uncopyrighted "Twilight Waltz" and "Duet" from "Song of David," and the titles "What Is Love" and "Night and Day." For "A Mother's Prayer," he had assigned the copyright but alleged an oral agreement that it would revert on the assignee's death, which had occurred.
sections.Issue: Was summary judgment proper in a copyright infringement action where the defendant denied access and copying, the district judge disbelieved the plaintiff on the depositions, and the record contained circumstantial evidence of access and some similarity between the works?
sections.Holding: The Second Circuit, in 1946, in an opinion by Judge Jerome Frank joined by Judge Learned Hand, with Judge Clark dissenting (2-1), held that summary judgment was improper. Applying the circuit's then-expressed caution against summary judgment where there is even the slightest factual doubt, the majority concluded that the wide circulation of Arnstein's works and the unresolved credibility of Porter's denial presented a genuine issue for a jury. The court ordered the claims on the uncopyrighted works and the titles dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, allowed the claim on "A Mother's Prayer" to proceed, and otherwise reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority separated two questions. Copying may be shown by admission or by circumstantial evidence, usually access plus sufficient similarity; without other proof of access, the similarities must be striking enough to exclude independent creation, and expert analysis may help. Unlawful appropriation is a second question: whether the defendant took enough of what appeals to ordinary listeners, a matter on which expert taste does not control. Here the similarity was insufficient alone to prove copying but would be probative if access were shown, and the court could not say it was too trivial to support appropriation.

The district judge had resolved credibility on depositions without hearing the parties. However unlikely parts of Arnstein's story were, a jury that rejected Porter's denial could infer access from the circulation of the works. Arnstein's deposition of Porter did not exhaust the value of trial: live cross-examination might draw admissions and let the jury observe demeanor. The majority did not bar all summary judgments in copyright cases, giving examples where documentary proof or an unmistakable lack of similarity would make trial futile.

A title is not copyrightable, and the nonfederal claims could not be joined. On "A Mother's Prayer," no one in the assignee's chain of title was before the court, so the parol-evidence rule did not bar proof of the oral agreement. Prior lost suits did not make this one vexatious absent res judicata.

Judge Clark, dissenting, heard no significant resemblance, only short sequences of commonplace notes, and saw no substantial evidence of access against Porter's categorical denial. He objected that Rule 56 contains no copyright exception or presumption against summary judgment and that the majority's factual-doubt formula rewrote a uniform rule. The full brief presents that formula as the historical majority's approach, not today's universal Rule 56 test.

CP-ATLAS-BECHTEL.rule: Under the artful-pleading doctrine, a plaintiff cannot defeat removal by using state-law terminology to conceal a claim's true federal nature, although a federal question must arise from the claim itself and not merely from an anticipated defense.

sections.Parties: Willie D. Bright, an employee, sued his employer, Bechtel Petroleum, and individual agents in California Superior Court for breach of contract, alleging that his paychecks were smaller than his employment contract required. Bechtel removed the case to federal court and sought dismissal and attorney's fees, arguing that the complaint was a frivolous challenge to its compliance with federal tax law. Bright sought remand. Bright then brought two appeals to the Ninth Circuit, one from the judgment and one from the denial of his motion for clarification.
sections.Procedural History: Bright sued in California Superior Court on June 1. Bechtel removed to the Northern District of California and sought dismissal and fees; Bright sought remand, now insisting that he wished to litigate only state withholding. On December 4 the district court denied remand, dismissed the action, and awarded $3,300 in attorney's fees. On December 19 Bright moved for clarification of the grounds of judgment. He appealed the judgment before that motion was ruled on and, after it was denied, appealed that order as well. The Ninth Circuit consolidated the appeals and decided them on January 10, 1986. It affirmed, upholding removal, the dismissal of both the federal-withholding and state-withholding claims, the fee award, and the denial of clarification, and it awarded reasonable appellate attorney's fees and double costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Bright entered an employment contract with Bechtel on November 7, 1983, under a collective bargaining agreement. In January 1984 he supplied a W-4 claiming exemption from federal withholding, which Bechtel forwarded to the IRS. In March the IRS rejected the certificate and directed Bechtel to withhold federal income tax; a California regulation made that federal determination effective for state withholding as well. In 1984 Bechtel withheld $2,486.18 in federal tax and $736 in state tax.

Bright's complaint alleged paychecks smaller than the agreed amounts and described the cause as breach of contract and violation of Christian principles. He had sent two letters threatening contract litigation because Bechtel obeyed the IRS directive. Both challenged the directive's legality and cited federal revenue statutes, and one referred to an earlier Ninth Circuit decision dismissing a similar withholding suit as frivolous. Affidavits identified substantially identical wording in another Bechtel employee's recently dismissed complaint. Bright's demand exceeded $100 million, against approximately $3,222 withheld.
sections.Issue: Whether a complaint worded as a state-law breach of contract could be removed to federal court because it actually challenged the employer's compliance with federal tax withholding; whether the federal-withholding claim and the related state-withholding claim were properly dismissed; and whether the district court's fee award and its denial of the clarification motion were proper.
sections.Holding: The Ninth Circuit in 1986, in an opinion by Judge Beezer for a unanimous panel with Judges Wright and Kennedy, held removal proper because the record showed that Bright's actual claim challenged federal withholding despite its state-law wording. It upheld dismissal of the federal-withholding claim and of the pendent state-withholding claim, held that retaining the state claim was not an abuse of discretion, and sustained the $3,300 fee award and the denial of the clarification motion. It awarded reasonable appellate attorney's fees and double costs for a frivolous appeal, without supplying a final dollar amount. The court did not adjudicate Bright's ultimate tax liability or decide the constitutionality of the California regulation.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with the well-pleaded-complaint principle: a federal question had to arise from the claim rather than merely from an anticipated defense, and plaintiffs normally controlled their choice of claim and forum. But the artful-pleading doctrine prevented concealing a claim's true federal nature through state-law terminology, and the removal petition could clarify the action the complaint presented. Bright's letters attacking the IRS directive and citing federal revenue statutes, and the nearly identical wording of another employee's complaint, showed the actual claim. His later assertion that only state tax was at issue did not match the complaint or that history, and the panel viewed it as another effort to evade the federal court. This was a determination about the actual claim on the record, not acceptance of an employer's federal defense as sufficient, and not a conclusion that every contract dispute involving a federal regulation is removable.

On the federal claim, section 3402 imposed withholding duties and Bechtel had complied; circuit precedent treated an employer as satisfying its payment obligation by withholding as required and paying the balance; section 3403 protected the employer against claims for the withheld payment; and the Anti-Injunction Act, section 7421(a), applied to a suit restraining collection. The state claim arose from a common nucleus of operative facts, so the court's power over it survived dismissal of the federal claim. A California decision and California's rule excusing performance made impossible by operation of law supported dismissing it. The action was frivolous, in bad faith, and intended to harass, so the fee award was a permissible deterrent. The clarification motion fell outside the then-applicable ten-day period, and Rule 52(a) did not require findings when deciding motions.

CP-ATLAS-BNSF.rule: A state court may exercise general jurisdiction over a corporation only where it is essentially at home, ordinarily its place of incorporation and principal place of business, and FELA's section 56 governs venue and subject-matter jurisdiction, not personal jurisdiction.

sections.Parties: Robert Nelson, a North Dakota resident, and Kelli Tyrrell, appointed in South Dakota to administer her husband Brent's estate, each sued BNSF Railway in Montana state court under the Federal Employers' Liability Act for employment injuries. BNSF, the defendant in both suits, was incorporated in Delaware with its principal place of business in Texas. It moved to dismiss both suits for lack of personal jurisdiction. In the Supreme Court the plaintiffs defended the Montana Supreme Court's decision upholding jurisdiction, which BNSF challenged.
sections.Procedural History: Nelson sued in March 2011 and Tyrrell in May 2014. BNSF moved to dismiss both suits for lack of personal jurisdiction; the motion was granted in Nelson's case and denied in Tyrrell's. The Montana Supreme Court consolidated the matters and upheld general jurisdiction on two grounds: that 45 U.S.C. section 56 authorized state-court personal jurisdiction over a railroad doing business in the State, and that BNSF was a person found within Montana under the State's Rule 4(b)(1). It distinguished Daimler as involving neither a railroad nor a FELA claim. Justice McKinnon dissented, concluding that Daimler controlled. The Court reversed the Montana Supreme Court and remanded both cases, leaving the plaintiffs' separate consent argument unresolved.
sections.Material Facts:
Nelson alleged knee injuries suffered while working for BNSF as a fuel-truck driver. Tyrrell alleged that exposure to carcinogenic chemicals during her husband's BNSF employment had caused his fatal kidney cancer. Neither plaintiff alleged an injury arising from or related to work in Montana, and the record indicated that neither injured worker appeared ever to have worked for BNSF there. The Court did not adjudicate the merits of these allegations.

BNSF was incorporated in Delaware, had its principal place of business in Texas, and operated in 28 States. In Montana it had 2,061 miles of track and approximately 2,100 employees, which was about six percent of its total track and less than five percent of its workforce. Montana generated less than ten percent of its revenue and contained one of its 24 automotive facilities. BNSF did not dispute that Montana considered it found within the State under its own procedural rule.
sections.Issue: Whether section 56 of FELA confers personal jurisdiction on state courts over railroads doing business in the State, and, if not, whether Montana's alternative exercise of general jurisdiction over BNSF under its own rule, on claims unrelated to BNSF's Montana activity, satisfied Fourteenth Amendment due process.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2017, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg for eight Justices, held that section 56 does not confer personal jurisdiction over railroads; its relevant provisions address federal venue and concurrent state and federal subject-matter jurisdiction. Montana's alternative exercise of general jurisdiction was unconstitutional because BNSF was not essentially at home there and the claims had no connection with its Montana operations. Justice Sotomayor joined the statutory parts but dissented from the constitutional part and the judgment, so the statutory interpretation was unanimous and the constitutional application divided eight to one. The Court expressly left the plaintiffs' consent argument undecided because the Montana Supreme Court had not addressed it.
sections.Reasoning:
The first relevant sentence of section 56, allowing a federal action where the defendant resides, where the cause arose, or where the defendant does business, identifies permissible locations for suit. The Court had already read it as a venue provision; Congress commonly describes venue by saying where an action may be brought and addresses personal jurisdiction through provisions authorizing service of process. The second relevant sentence, making federal jurisdiction concurrent with that of state courts, describes shared subject-matter competence and was added against a Connecticut decision treating FELA claims as exclusively federal. The four precedents Montana invoked did not decide the personal-jurisdiction question, and most preceded International Shoe.

On due process, because neither plaintiff claimed an injury connected to Montana, only general jurisdiction was at issue. The ordinary corporate homes are the place of incorporation and principal place of business, though an exceptional corporation may be at home elsewhere, as in Perkins. That restriction applies regardless of the type of enterprise or claim, so there was no special rule for FELA railroads. The inquiry appraises the corporation's activities as a whole; a multistate corporation is not at home in every State with substantial operations. BNSF's Montana activity could support specific jurisdiction over related claims but not these unrelated ones. The Court announced no numerical ceiling on miles, employees, or revenue.

Justice Sotomayor agreed on FELA but maintained her objection to Daimler's at-home approach, criticized the comparative-contacts analysis as favoring large corporations, and would at least have remanded for Montana to apply the standard.

CP-ATLAS-BREMEN.rule: Federal courts sitting in admiralty treat a freely agreed forum-selection clause as prima facie valid and enforce it unless the resisting party shows that enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust or that the clause is invalid for fraud or overreaching.

sections.Parties: Zapata Off-Shore Company, a Houston-based corporation and owner of the drilling rig Chaparral, sued the German towing company Unterweser personally and its tug, the Bremen, in rem, in admiralty at Tampa, claiming $3.5 million for negligent towage and breach of contract. Unterweser, the defendant, relied on the contract's London forum clause and sought dismissal or a stay; it also sued Zapata for breach of contract in the English High Court. Zapata prevailed in the district court and the Fifth Circuit before the case reached the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: Zapata sued in admiralty at Tampa on January 12, 1968; the tug was arrested and released on security. Unterweser moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction or forum non conveniens, or alternatively for a stay, and sued Zapata in England, where the courts rejected Zapata's jurisdictional challenge. With its motion still undecided and the six-month deadline approaching, Unterweser filed a limitation-of-liability proceeding in Tampa in July 1968, expressly reserving its reliance on the London clause. The district court eventually denied dismissal or a stay, later refused to stay the limitation proceeding, and restrained further London litigation. A divided Fifth Circuit panel affirmed, and the en banc court adopted that opinion with six of 14 judges dissenting. The Court vacated the Fifth Circuit's judgment and remanded.
sections.Material Facts:
In November 1967 Zapata hired Unterweser to tow its self-elevating drilling rig Chaparral from Louisiana to a drilling location off Ravenna, Italy. Zapata had solicited competing bids, and Unterweser was the low bidder. The contract Unterweser submitted designated the London Court of Justice for any dispute. It also disclaimed responsibility for navigation errors and assigned damage to the towed object to its owner. Zapata changed several terms but left the forum and exculpatory clauses intact before executing the contract, and Unterweser accepted the changes.

The tug Bremen departed Louisiana on January 5, 1968. Four days later a severe storm in international Gulf waters caused the rig's raised elevator legs to break off, substantially damaging it. Zapata directed the tug to Tampa as the nearest port of refuge. Zapata had elected to self-insure its rigs, so insurance did not cover the loss. The record suggested materially smaller limitation exposure under English law.
sections.Issue: Whether a federal court sitting in admiralty should enforce a forum-selection clause in a freely negotiated international towage contract designating a London court, and which party bears the burden when enforcement is resisted; and whether Unterweser's filing of a limitation proceeding in Tampa forfeited its reliance on the clause.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1972, in an opinion by Chief Justice Burger joined by Justices Brennan, Stewart, White, Marshall, Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, held that a freely agreed forum-selection clause is prima facie valid in admiralty and should be enforced unless the resisting party establishes adequate grounds to reject it. The lower courts gave the clause too little weight and wrongly made Unterweser prove London more convenient; the burden was on Zapata to show that enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust or that the clause was invalid through fraud or overreaching. The Court vacated and remanded so that Zapata could try to meet that standard; it did not direct a London merits judgment or hold every forum clause enforceable. Justice White qualified his agreement, and Justice Douglas alone dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority rejected the premise that domestic courts must keep international commercial disputes merely because they have jurisdiction and are convenient. Businesses dealing across borders need predictable arrangements, and a sophisticated international transaction may select a neutral forum with relevant expertise, which England supplied. The clause did not oust the Tampa court of jurisdiction; the real question was whether that court should exercise its authority beyond enforcing the parties' legitimate expectations. Here capable companies moved a valuable rig across many jurisdictions with many possible accident locations, and choosing London removed uncertainty beforehand. The majority inferred that forum certainty was part of the bargain.

A clause can be unenforceable if it contradicts a strong public policy of the forum, but Bisso, which disapproved contractual immunity from negligent towage, arose from towage in American waters and did not control this international agreement. Inconvenience remains relevant, but Zapata would have to show that litigating in London would be so gravely difficult that it would effectively lose its day in court. The majority distinguished two Americans sending an essentially local dispute to a remote foreign forum. Unterweser's limitation filing was a defensive response and did not waive the clause, and the clause's language was mandatory and covered the in rem action.

Justice White would have left the remanded issues to the district court without comment. Justice Douglas, dissenting, stressed the limitation court's equitable power, thought the forum clause inseparable from exculpatory terms incompatible with Bisso, and would have affirmed. The casebook's editorial account loosely describes the result as a reversal; the actual disposition was vacatur and remand.

CP-ATLAS-BRISTOL-MYERS.rule: Specific personal jurisdiction requires an affiliation between the forum and the particular claims at issue, and a defendant's extensive but unrelated forum contacts cannot substitute for that connection.

sections.Parties: Plaintiffs in eight complaints, 86 California residents and 592 residents of 33 other States, sued Bristol-Myers Squibb (BMS) in California state court, alleging injury from its prescription blood thinner Plavix. McKesson, a California-based distributor, was also a defendant below. BMS, incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in New York, contested California's jurisdiction over the nonresident plaintiffs' claims and sought to have service quashed as to them. The nonresident plaintiffs defended jurisdiction in the Supreme Court.
sections.Procedural History: BMS moved to quash service on the nonresidents' claims. The superior court denied the motion, initially relying on general jurisdiction. The state court of appeal denied mandamus relief, but after Daimler the California Supreme Court required reconsideration, and the court of appeal then rejected general jurisdiction while sustaining specific jurisdiction. The California Supreme Court unanimously agreed that general jurisdiction was absent but, over three dissents, upheld specific jurisdiction using a sliding scale under which extensive forum contacts permitted a less direct connection between forum activity and each claim. The Court reversed the California Supreme Court and remanded for further proceedings, without deciding the products-liability merits.
sections.Material Facts:
The 678 plaintiffs asserted 13 California-law claims, including products liability, negligent misrepresentation, and misleading advertising. The nonresident plaintiffs did not allege that they obtained Plavix through California physicians or another California source, were injured there, or were treated there.

BMS had substantial operations in New York and New Jersey. In California it had five research and laboratory facilities with approximately 160 employees, about 250 sales representatives, and a small governmental advocacy office. Between 2006 and 2012 it sold nearly 187 million Plavix pills in California for more than $900 million. It had not developed Plavix, created its marketing strategy, manufactured or packaged it, or sought its regulatory approval in California; those activities occurred in New York or New Jersey.

Plaintiffs relied on BMS's contract with McKesson to distribute Plavix nationwide, but did not allege that BMS acted jointly with McKesson in California or was derivatively liable for its conduct, and did not show how their own pills reached the dispensing pharmacies. The casebook's editorial account gives 88 California plaintiffs and more than $1 billion in sales; the official report's figures are used here.
sections.Issue: Whether California's exercise of specific personal jurisdiction over the claims of nonresident plaintiffs, who were not prescribed, sold, or injured by Plavix in California, complied with Fourteenth Amendment due process on the basis of BMS's extensive California business and the similarity of the residents' claims.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2017, in an opinion by Justice Alito for eight Justices, held that California lacked specific personal jurisdiction over the nonresident plaintiffs' claims on this record. Extensive unrelated forum business could not replace the missing affiliation between California and those particular claims, and the sliding-scale approach was rejected. Justice Sotomayor dissented. BMS's amenability to the resident plaintiffs' claims was uncontested. Because this was a state-court Fourteenth Amendment case, the Court expressly left open whether the Fifth Amendment imposes the same restrictions on personal jurisdiction in federal court.
sections.Reasoning:
General jurisdiction permits any claim against a defendant at home in the forum; specific jurisdiction covers only claims arising out of or relating to the defendant's forum contacts and requires an affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy. That distinction would collapse if extensive unrelated business relaxed the required connection, so the sliding scale was an unsupported substitute for general jurisdiction. The nonresidents were not prescribed Plavix, did not buy or ingest it, and were not injured in California. The similar experiences of resident plaintiffs and unrelated California research did not supply the link; a defendant's relationship with third parties, standing alone, is insufficient. Walden illustrated the same limit. Convenience did not cure the defect, because due process also protects defendants from a State's coercive authority and interstate federalism can limit that authority even when litigation would be convenient.

Keeton was distinguished because distribution in New Hampshire allegedly caused injury there. Shutts concerned the due-process rights of absent plaintiff class members, not jurisdiction over a defendant. The McKesson contract fell short because jurisdiction had to be established separately for BMS and no joint conduct, derivative liability, or connection to plaintiffs' own pills was alleged. The majority noted that plaintiffs could sue together where BMS is subject to general jurisdiction, such as New York or Delaware, and that plaintiffs from the same State could probably proceed together in their home State.

Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, thought materially identical nationwide advertising and distribution related the claims to BMS's California conduct, considered consolidated litigation reasonable, and warned of barriers to aggregating small claims. She noted that the case did not address a nationwide class action.

CP-ATLAS-CALDER.rule: A State may exercise personal jurisdiction over nonresident individuals whose own alleged intentional conduct was expressly aimed at the forum and who knew the brunt of the injury would be felt there, with each defendant's contacts assessed individually.

sections.Parties: Shirley Jones, a professional entertainer who lived and worked in California, and her husband sued the National Enquirer, its local distributor, reporter South, and president and editor John Calder for libel, invasion of privacy, and intentional infliction of emotional harm. Her husband later voluntarily dismissed his complaint. The publisher and distributor answered without contesting California jurisdiction. South and Calder, both Florida residents, appeared specially and moved to quash service; they sought Supreme Court review after the California Court of Appeal found jurisdiction over them.
sections.Procedural History: South and Calder were served by mail in Florida, appeared specially, and moved to quash service. The California Superior Court granted the motion; it believed their conduct causing California injury would ordinarily support jurisdiction but gave added weight to the potential chilling effect on reporters and editors and thought Jones could obtain adequate relief from the publisher. The California Court of Appeal reversed, finding jurisdiction based on the defendants' intended and actual tortious effects in California and rejecting the First Amendment barrier. The state supreme court declined further review. The individuals sought review by appeal; the Court held that route unavailable, treated the papers as a certiorari petition, and granted it. The Court affirmed the California Court of Appeal's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The suit concerned an article in the October 9, 1979 issue of the National Enquirer alleging that Jones's drinking interfered with her professional obligations. The Enquirer was a Florida corporation with its principal place of business there. Its circulation exceeded five million, including roughly 600,000 copies in California, almost twice the circulation in the next largest state market.

South and Calder lived in Florida. South wrote the article's first draft, did most of his research in Florida through calls to California sources, and read a draft to Jones's husband by telephone shortly before publication. He regularly traveled to California. Calder approved the proposed subject, edited the final article, and declined Jones's request for a retraction; his two California visits were unrelated to the article. Whether South had made a California research trip for the article was disputed, and the Court did not resolve that dispute or rely on the trip.
sections.Issue: Whether California could constitutionally exercise personal jurisdiction over a Florida reporter and a Florida editor for an allegedly libelous article written and edited in Florida about a California resident, and whether First Amendment concerns should weigh against jurisdiction in the analysis.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1984, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Rehnquist with no separate writings, sustained California's jurisdiction over both individuals. California was the focal point of both the allegedly libelous article and the harm, and the defendants' own alleged intentional conduct was expressly aimed at California. The First Amendment supplied no additional jurisdictional shield. The ruling was jurisdictional only: it did not establish that the article was false, that the defendants committed libel, or that Jones had proved her claims or damages.
sections.Reasoning:
Applying minimum contacts through the relationship among the defendant, the forum, and the litigation, the Court found California the focal point. The story concerned Jones's California activities and a career centered there, drew on California sources, and threatened harm to her professional reputation and emotional well-being primarily in that State. The defendants knew the brunt of the injury would be felt where she lived and worked and where the newspaper had its largest circulation.

South and Calder argued that their employer's circulation could not be attributed to them and that merely foreseeing the article would reach California was not enough, comparing themselves to a Florida welder whose employer sells a boiler into California. The Court distinguished alleged intentional targeting from untargeted negligence. The two were primary participants in the challenged conduct, one writing and the other editing the article, so the connection was their own role in an alleged wrong expressly aimed at California, not the predictable movement of an employer's product. They could reasonably anticipate answering there.

The Court agreed that each defendant's contacts must be assessed individually rather than inferred from the employer's activities, but that same principle meant acting in an official capacity did not insulate an employee whose own conduct established the required relationship.

On the First Amendment, constitutional safeguards already limit the substantive law of defamation. Reintroducing those concerns at the jurisdictional stage would complicate the contacts analysis and double count the protections; the defendants remained free to raise substantive speech defenses in the forum.

CP-ATLAS-COHEN-BENEFICIAL.rule: An order is immediately appealable under section 1291 when it conclusively resolves a claimed right separate from the merits that would probably be irreparably lost if review waited until final judgment.

sections.Parties: A shareholder, represented after his death by the petitioners, brought a derivative action in the right of Beneficial Industrial Loan Corporation, a Delaware corporation, against the corporation and certain managers and directors, seeking recovery for alleged mismanagement and fraud. Another shareholder intervened. Beneficial, relying on a New Jersey statute, sought an order requiring the plaintiffs to post security for its expenses. In the Supreme Court the shareholder side sought review of the Third Circuit's decision for the corporation, and the corporation pursued a companion mandamus request.
sections.Procedural History: The suit began in federal court in New Jersey in 1943 under diversity jurisdiction. After New Jersey enacted its expense-security statute in 1945, Beneficial requested a $125,000 bond. The District Court held the state statute inapplicable in federal court and declined to require security. The Third Circuit reversed. The shareholder side sought certiorari, and the corporation also pursued a companion request for mandamus to compel security. The Court, deciding the case on June 20, 1949, affirmed the Third Circuit's judgment requiring application of the New Jersey statute and dismissed the companion mandamus petition in No. 512 because appeal provided review.
sections.Material Facts:
The shareholder alleged eighteen years of mismanagement and fraud, including diversion or waste exceeding $100 million, and alleged that those controlling the corporation prevented it from acting despite his demand. These were pleaded allegations, not findings. He held 100 shares and the intervenor another 150, out of more than two million outstanding; their combined position was approximately 0.0125 percent, with market value never exceeding $9,000.

In 1945 New Jersey enacted an expense-security statute applicable to pending actions without final judgment. It entitled a corporation to demand security for reasonable expenses, including counsel fees and amounts it might owe other defendants, where the suing holders had less than 5 percent of the outstanding capital measure, unless their shares' market value exceeded $50,000. The court could adjust the security as circumstances changed. Beneficial invoked its indemnification bylaws and requested a $125,000 bond; the Court did not itself fix that amount.
sections.Issue: Whether the District Court's refusal to recognize the statutory right to security was immediately appealable under section 1291 although the derivative merits remained pending; whether the New Jersey statute was constitutional under the federal objections presented; and whether it applied in a federal diversity action despite the Federal Rule governing derivative suits.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1949, in an opinion by Justice Jackson, held the order immediately appealable because it conclusively resolved a claimed right separate from the merits that would probably be irreparably lost if review waited until final judgment. It distinguished denial of the right to security from discretionary adjustment of an admitted security amount and did not make every security order appealable. The federal constitutional objections did not invalidate the statute as the Court construed it, and the statute had to be applied in this diversity action; the then-existing Rule 23 did not conflict with it. Justice Douglas, joined by Justice Frankfurter, dissented in part, and Justice Rutledge dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1291 ordinarily consolidates review into an appeal from the final judgment; tentative rulings are not appealable, and completed intermediate rulings ordinarily wait if they will merge into the merits judgment. Here the refusal to apply the statute was complete, independent of the derivative claim, and could not be effectively repaired after the corporation incurred the unprotected expenses. The right to security presented a serious, unsettled question separate from liability, placing the order in a small class of decisions on collateral rights.

On constitutionality, the Court recognized derivative suits as an equitable remedy but also an opportunity for nuisance-value settlements, so the legislature could impose accountability on a shareholder who chooses to act for others. The Contract Clause challenge failed because no contractual right was impaired; reasonable expense liability and adjustable security did not violate due process; and using the size of a shareholder's financial interest as a measure of responsibility did not deny equal protection. The Court did not construe the statute to impose liability for expenses incurred before enactment and reserved that question.

On the diversity question, the procedural or substantive label was not decisive. The statute created a new liability for defense expenses exceeding ordinary costs and secured it in advance, so treating it as merely procedural would disregard its substantive operation. Rule 23 neither imposed nor exempted the plaintiff from expense liability, so a federal court could comply with both.

Justices Douglas and Frankfurter viewed the statute as regulating only the method of enforcing an existing claim and would have let the Federal Rule govern. Justice Rutledge agreed and objected to decisions ceding control of federal litigation to the States.

CP-ATLAS-CONCEPCION.rule: The Federal Arbitration Act preempts a state rule, even one framed as generally applicable unconscionability, that conditions enforcement of an arbitration agreement on the availability of class procedures and so interferes with arbitration as the parties agreed to it.

sections.Parties: Vincent and Liza Concepcion, cellular telephone customers, sued their carrier in federal court alleging false advertising and fraud. The carrier was Cingular, which AT&T acquired in 2005 and renamed in 2007. AT&T Mobility, the defendant, moved to compel individual arbitration under the customers' service agreement. The Concepcions resisted, relying on California's Discover Bank rule. AT&T lost in the district court and the Ninth Circuit before the Supreme Court reviewed the case.
sections.Procedural History: The Concepcions filed a federal action in the Southern District of California in March 2006, and it was consolidated with a putative class action. AT&T moved to compel arbitration in March 2008. The district court denied the motion under California's Discover Bank rule, despite finding the individual arbitration procedures favorable and the likely recovery potentially better than participation in a class. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, treating California's rule as an application of ordinary unconscionability rather than a rule discriminating against arbitration. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion, without deciding the merits of the false-advertising claims.
sections.Material Facts:
The Concepcions purchased cellular service in February 2002. Their dispute concerned phones advertised as free: they were charged $30.22 in sales tax calculated from the phones' retail value. Their agreement required arbitration of disputes, barred either party from proceeding as a class member or representative, and barred an arbitrator from consolidating claims of more than one person. The controlling version resulted from AT&T's December 2006 revision under its contractual power to amend.

The agreement gave individual claimants favorable procedures. A customer submitted a one-page notice and could demand arbitration after 30 days without resolution. AT&T paid the costs of nonfrivolous claims; proceedings occurred in the customer's billing county; claims of $10,000 or less could proceed in person, by telephone, or on documents; and small-claims court remained available. AT&T could not seek reimbursement of its attorney's fees. If an award exceeded AT&T's last written settlement offer, the claimant received a minimum of $7,500 plus twice the attorney's fees.

California's Discover Bank rule treated a class waiver as unconscionable in a consumer contract of adhesion where disputes predictably involved small damages and the stronger party allegedly schemed to cheat many consumers of individually small sums.
sections.Issue: Whether the Federal Arbitration Act preempts California's Discover Bank rule when that rule prevents enforcement of an agreement requiring individual arbitration, even though California characterizes the rule as ordinary unconscionability and applies it to class waivers in litigation as well as arbitration.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2011, in a 5-4 opinion by Justice Scalia joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, held that the FAA preempts the Discover Bank rule. Requiring the availability of class arbitration through that rule interfered with attributes of arbitration protected by the FAA, even though the State characterized its rule as ordinary unconscionability and applied it to class litigation waivers too. The Court did not hold that parties may not agree to class arbitration; the distinction was between consent and a state-imposed change to the agreed procedure. Justice Thomas concurred separately, and Justice Breyer dissented with Justices Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 2 of the FAA lets arbitration agreements be invalidated by generally applicable defenses such as fraud, duress, and unconscionability, but not by defenses aimed at arbitration. That did not end the inquiry, because a nominally general defense can obstruct the FAA when applied to demand procedures inconsistent with arbitration; hypothetical rules requiring judicially supervised discovery, ordinary evidence rules, or a jury would do so even if applied to litigation too. The saving clause could not preserve a state rule that defeats the statute's objective of enforcing agreements according to their terms.

Discover Bank's limits were weak in practice: consumer contracts are commonly adhesive, the small-damages condition was flexible, and the wrongdoing condition required only an allegation, so class arbitration was the rule's practical consequence. Imposed class arbitration differs fundamentally from bilateral arbitration. It adds complexity and delay through certification disputes, requires formal protections for absent members, and combines enormous aggregate exposure with the limited review available under section 10, which could make companies unwilling to arbitrate. The policy of protecting small claims could not justify procedures inconsistent with the FAA, and these terms were likely to make customers whole.

Justice Thomas joined reluctantly and proposed reading section 2 to preserve only defenses concerning formation of the agreement; that theory was his own. Justice Breyer, dissenting, viewed the rule as the kind of nondiscriminatory contract defense section 2 preserves, argued that the right comparison was class arbitration against class litigation, and questioned whether AT&T's terms gave any real incentive to pursue a $30.22 claim. The casebook's opening describes free phone service, whereas the opinion concerned free phones.

CP-ATLAS-CONLEY.rule: Under Rule 8(a)(2) a complaint needs only a short and plain statement giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds, and should not be dismissed unless it appears beyond doubt that no set of supporting facts could entitle the claimant to relief.

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Black railroad workers employed at the Texas and New Orleans Railroad's Houston Freight House. They brought a federal class suit in Texas against the Brotherhood of Railway and Steamship Clerks, its Local Union No. 28, which was their bargaining representative, and officers of both, seeking declaratory relief, an injunction, and damages for breach of the Railway Labor Act's duty of fair representation. The union defendants sought dismissal. The railroad was not a party.
sections.Procedural History: The defendants moved to dismiss on three grounds: that the National Railroad Adjustment Board had exclusive jurisdiction, that the railroad had not been joined as an indispensable defendant, and that the complaint failed to state a claim. The district court dismissed on the jurisdictional ground, and the Fifth Circuit apparently relied on the same ground in affirming. The Court granted review and also addressed the two alternative defenses, which both parties had briefed and argued. On November 18, 1957, the Court reversed and remanded to the district court for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts: A collective bargaining agreement protected the workers' jobs and seniority. According to the complaint, in May 1954 the railroad purported to abolish forty-five jobs held by Black employees, discharged or demoted them, and actually gave the jobs to white workers. A few Black workers allegedly regained their former jobs without their seniority. The workers charged that the union deliberately refused their repeated requests for protection comparable to that given white workers and, more generally, failed to represent them equally and in good faith. They sought no relief from the railroad. The Court did not determine that the discrimination allegations were true or award the requested relief.
sections.Issue: Whether the National Railroad Adjustment Board had exclusive jurisdiction over the workers' claim against their union; whether the railroad was an indispensable party; and whether the complaint, which alleged discriminatory representation without detailed facts, stated a claim on which relief could be granted under the Federal Rules.
sections.Holding: The Court in 1957, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Black, held that dismissal for want of jurisdiction was erroneous because the Adjustment Board did not have exclusive jurisdiction over this dispute between employees and their bargaining agent. The railroad was not indispensable to the action as framed. The complaint was sufficient: dismissal was inappropriate unless it appeared beyond doubt that no set of supporting facts could entitle the claimant to relief, and Rule 8(a)(2) required only a short and plain statement giving fair notice of the claim and its grounds, not detailed factual allegations.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 3 First (i) governs disputes between employees and carriers arising from grievances or the interpretation or application of bargaining agreements. This was instead a dispute between employees and their bargaining agent over its statutory obligation to represent them without racial discrimination; the agreement was at most incidentally involved, and the Board lacked authority to protect employees against this asserted union discrimination.

The railroad was not indispensable because the workers sought no relief from it and none available on this claim would bind it or affect its interests. If its participation later became necessary, the railroad or the defendants could request joinder.

On sufficiency, the Court's earlier fair-representation decisions made the alleged discrimination actionable. The representative's duty continues after an agreement is negotiated into its administration, grievance handling, and protection of existing contractual rights. The Court did not decide whether a union must handle any grievances at all, only that having undertaken to act for some represented employees it could not refuse comparable good-faith action for others because of race. The allegations, if proved, would establish a breach of that duty.

The Court rejected the demand for detailed facts. Notice pleading depends on the rest of the procedural system: the illustrative forms, discovery, amendment, pretrial definition of issues, and similar mechanisms clarify the dispute after the pleadings. Former Rule 8(f) directed that pleadings be construed to do substantial justice, and the Rules favor decisions on the merits over pleading as a technical contest.

The casebook editors separately recount exchanges between Justices Black and Harlan over draft language, which is not part of the opinion, and later assigned Twombly material reexamines the no-set-of-facts formulation.

CP-ATLAS-DAIMLER.rule: A court may exercise general jurisdiction over a corporation only where its affiliations make it essentially at home, paradigmatically its place of incorporation and principal place of business; a substantial, continuous, and systematic course of business in the State is not enough.

sections.Parties: Twenty-two residents of Argentina, all but one Argentine citizens and the other a Chilean citizen, sued Daimler AG in the Northern District of California, seeking to hold it vicariously liable for the alleged conduct of its Argentine subsidiary. Daimler, a German public stock company headquartered in Stuttgart, was the only defendant named in the operative complaint and contested personal jurisdiction. Its United States distributor, Mercedes-Benz USA (MBUSA), was not a defendant. The Ninth Circuit ultimately ruled for the plaintiffs, and the Supreme Court reviewed that judgment.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in 2004. After jurisdictional discovery, the district court dismissed, finding Daimler's own California contacts insufficient for general jurisdiction and declining to attribute MBUSA's contacts through agency. A Ninth Circuit panel initially affirmed, with Judge Reinhardt dissenting. On rehearing the panel withdrew that opinion and adopted Reinhardt's contrary approach, treating MBUSA as Daimler's agent and exercising jurisdiction. The court later denied rehearing and rehearing en banc over eight judges' dissent. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's judgment, without deciding the underlying human-rights claims.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that Mercedes-Benz Argentina, a subsidiary of Daimler's predecessor, collaborated with Argentine security forces during the 1976-1983 military dictatorship to kidnap, detain, torture, and kill workers, including plaintiffs or their relatives. The alleged conduct centered on the subsidiary's Argentine plant; none occurred in California or elsewhere in the United States. The claims rested on the Alien Tort Statute, the Torture Victim Protection Act, and California and Argentine law. These were allegations, not findings.

MBUSA was a Delaware entity with its principal place of business in New Jersey. As Daimler's exclusive United States importer and distributor, it bought vehicles in Germany and distributed them to independent dealerships nationwide. It had a regional office, a vehicle preparation center, and a classic center in California and was the largest supplier of luxury vehicles to that market; its California sales were 2.4 percent of Daimler's worldwide sales. The distribution agreement described MBUSA as an independent contractor, not Daimler's agent, without authority to bind Daimler.

Plaintiffs never attempted to establish specific jurisdiction and did not claim MBUSA was Daimler's alter ego. Daimler had not contested below that MBUSA was itself subject to general jurisdiction in California, so the Court assumed it was.
sections.Issue: Whether due process permitted California courts, whose long-arm statute reaches the constitutional limit, to exercise general, all-purpose jurisdiction over Daimler, a German corporation, for claims arising entirely in Argentina, on the basis of the California contacts of its United States subsidiary MBUSA.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2014, in an opinion by Justice Ginsburg joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, held that California could not exercise general personal jurisdiction over Daimler. The Ninth Circuit's agency rationale was unsustainable, and even assuming MBUSA was at home in California and its contacts could be attributed to Daimler, those contacts did not render Daimler itself essentially at home there. Justice Sotomayor concurred only in the judgment, so all nine Justices agreed on the result. The Court did not resolve whether agency could ever support general jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
The Ninth Circuit asked whether the subsidiary performed services so important that the parent would perform them itself if the subsidiary did not exist. That test was predisposed to find agency, since a corporation would usually arrange another way to do what a contractor, distributor, or subsidiary does, and it would expose foreign corporations to all-purpose jurisdiction wherever they had affiliates.

More decisively, general jurisdiction has kept a narrow role since International Shoe. Perkins was the exceptional example; Helicopteros and Goodyear rejected purchases or dispersed sales as sufficient. A corporation's place of incorporation and principal place of business are the paradigm forums, clear and readily ascertainable. They are not an exclusive list: an exceptional corporation's operations elsewhere might be so substantial and of such a nature as to make it at home there, but Daimler's California activities did not approach that level. The Court rejected a test of substantial, continuous, and systematic business, language International Shoe used for claims connected to the forum activity. Corporate activities must be appraised in their entirety, nationwide and worldwide; a corporation operating in many places cannot ordinarily be at home in all of them merely because its sales are sizable. Neither Daimler nor MBUSA was incorporated or headquartered in California. When a corporation is genuinely at home, a second-step reasonableness inquiry is superfluous. International comity reinforced the conclusion.

Justice Sotomayor would have rejected jurisdiction as unreasonable in this dispute, objected that the at-home ground had not been argued or decided below, and criticized measuring forum contacts by their proportion of a global enterprise as favoring multinational companies.

CP-ATLAS-DART.rule: A notice of removal under section 1446(a) needs only a plausible allegation that the amount in controversy exceeds the jurisdictional threshold; evidence establishing the amount is required only when the plaintiff contests, or the court questions, the allegation.

sections.Parties: Brandon Owens filed a putative class action in Kansas state court against Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Company and Cherokee Basin Pipeline, alleging that they had underpaid royalties owed under oil and gas leases. Dart, a defendant, removed the case to federal district court under CAFA. Owens moved to remand and prevailed in the district court. Dart then sought permission to appeal from the Tenth Circuit, was refused, and obtained Supreme Court review.
sections.Procedural History: Dart removed the case under CAFA. Owens moved to remand because the notice contained no evidence establishing more than $5 million in controversy. Reading Tenth Circuit precedent to require proof within the removal notice itself, the district court remanded. CAFA permits a court of appeals to accept an appeal from a remand order, but a divided Tenth Circuit panel denied Dart permission to appeal, and an evenly divided court denied rehearing en banc over a dissent by Judge Hartz. The Court granted certiorari on the notice's required contents. It vacated the Tenth Circuit's judgment and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts: Owens requested fair and reasonable compensation for the alleged royalty underpayments without specifying a dollar amount. Dart's notice of removal alleged the required class size and minimal diversity and stated that the underpayments exceeded $8.2 million. Owens moved to remand because the notice contained no evidence that more than $5 million was in controversy. Dart responded with an executive's detailed declaration calculating more than $11 million, excluding interest. Owens did not challenge that calculation; he argued that the evidence came too late to cure the original notice. The district court, relying partly on a presumption against removal, remanded. The Tenth Circuit's order denying permission to appeal said that it had considered the parties' submissions and the applicable law but did not otherwise explain its reasons.
sections.Issue: Whether a defendant's notice of removal must include evidence supporting the amount in controversy or need only plausibly allege it, and whether the Court could reach that question when the Tenth Circuit had exercised its discretion to deny permission to appeal the remand order.
sections.Holding: The Court in 2014, in a 5-4 opinion by Justice Ginsburg joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Breyer, Alito, and Sotomayor, held that a removal notice needs a plausible allegation of the jurisdictional amount, not supporting evidence attached to the notice. The defendant's allegation should be accepted unless the plaintiff contests it or the court questions it. The Tenth Circuit's denial of permission to appeal was infected by the district court's erroneous legal requirement and was therefore vacated; the Tenth Circuit remained free on remand to identify a permissible basis for declining the appeal. Justice Scalia dissented, joined by Justices Kennedy and Kagan and by Justice Thomas except for the final sentence; Justice Thomas also dissented separately.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 1446(a) requires a short and plain statement of the grounds for removal, language borrowed from Rule 8. Legislative history confirms that Congress wanted liberal pleading rules to govern removal allegations. A plaintiff invoking federal jurisdiction may rely on a good-faith allegation of the amount, and requiring proof from defendants would impose an unexplained asymmetry. Evidence becomes necessary when the allegation is disputed: section 1446(c)(2)(B) supplies a preponderance standard, both sides submit proof, and the court decides. Because the parties did not dispute it, the Court assumed without deciding that those provisions, which refer to section 1332(a), apply to CAFA cases. The Court rejected any presumption against removal in CAFA cases and left open whether one applies in ordinary diversity cases.

On reviewability, a point raised by an amicus, the majority concluded that Dart's application made the case one in the court of appeals within section 1254, so it could review what the Tenth Circuit did. Discretion must rest on a legally sound basis, and relying on an erroneous view of law can be an abuse of discretion.
