The California Supreme Court, divided 4-2, treated Ezra's consent to his daughter's move as an out-of-state act causing an effect in California and sustained jurisdiction for the support of both children. The Court dismissed the formal appeal but treated the papers as a certiorari petition and granted review. It rejected Sharon's argument that Ezra's later request to continue proceedings waived his objection. The Court reversed the California Supreme Court because the motion to quash on the support issue had been erroneously denied.
sections.Material Facts:
Ezra and Sharon were New York domiciliaries who married in California in 1959 during Ezra's three-day military stopover en route to Korea. Their children, Darwin and Ilsa, were born in New York in 1961 and 1962, and the family lived there until the spouses separated in March 1972. Sharon moved to San Francisco and returned to New York to sign a September 1972 separation agreement under which the children would live with Ezra during the school year and visit their mother during specified vacations. Sharon waived her own support, and Ezra agreed to pay $3,000 annually for the periods when the children were in her care. Sharon then obtained a Haitian divorce incorporating the agreement and returned to California.

In December 1973 Ilsa told Ezra she wanted to remain in California after her Christmas visit; Ezra agreed and bought her a one-way ticket, and she thereafter spent the school year with her mother. In January 1976 Darwin asked his mother to let him join her; Sharon sent him a ticket without Ezra's knowledge. Shortly after Darwin arrived, Sharon sued in California. Adequate notice was undisputed.
sections.Issue: Whether California could, consistent with due process, exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident, nondomiciliary father in an action to increase child support, on the basis that he agreed to his daughter's move to live with her mother in California.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1978), in an opinion by Justice Marshall for six Justices, with Justice Brennan dissenting joined by Justices White and Powell, held that California's exercise of personal jurisdiction over Ezra for this support action violated due process, because he lacked a sufficient connection with California. The Court reversed the California Supreme Court. It did not eliminate the children's right to support, set a support amount, or decide the uncontested custody jurisdiction issue.
sections.Reasoning:
Minimum contacts required a fair and reasonable connection attributable to the defendant, assessed on the circumstances rather than by a mechanical rule. The brief military stopovers and the wedding could not support this later, unrelated support action. Treating agreement to children's visits as purposeful forum activity could discourage reasonable visitation arrangements and expose a parent to suit wherever the other parent chose to live.

Ilsa's move did not change the result. Accommodating a child's preference for the sake of family harmony was not an effort to obtain California's benefits and protections; schools, hospitals and other services principally benefited the child, not the father. Any reduction in his household expenses came from her absence from his New York home rather than her presence in California specifically, and whether more support was owed could be litigated in New York.

The effects approach drawn from Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 37 contemplated wrongful out-of-state conduct causing in-state injury or commercial activity affecting residents, subject to reasonableness. Ezra had inflicted no such injury and sought no commercial benefit; the dispute arose from a New York separation and an agreement negotiated and signed there. Forcing him to defend roughly 3,000 miles away could penalize cooperative parenting. California's substantial interest in its resident children did not itself establish jurisdiction, and whether California law might govern was distinct from adjudicative power. Reciprocal support statutes in California and New York let Sharon initiate proceedings in California and have them adjudicated in New York.

Justice Brennan accepted the same standard, regarded the case as a close application to its facts, and agreed with California that Ezra's connection was sufficient. The casebook's note is editorial and emphasizes why the effects theory failed in this domestic setting.

CP-ATLAS-LEXECON.rule: A district court conducting coordinated pretrial proceedings under 28 U.S.C. § 1407(a) may not use § 1404(a) to assign a transferred case to itself for trial, because § 1407(a) obligates the Panel to remand each action to its original district.

sections.Parties: Lexecon Inc., a law-and-economics consulting firm, was the plaintiff. It sued the plaintiff-side law firms Milberg Weiss Bershad Hynes & Lerach and Cotchett, Illston & Pitre for malicious prosecution, abuse of process, tortious interference, commercial disparagement and defamation. Lexecon wanted its case remanded to the Northern District of Illinois, where it had filed; the firms opposed remand and asked the Arizona transferee court to keep the case for trial. Lexecon sought reversal in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: Lexecon filed a diversity suit in the Northern District of Illinois. In June 1993 the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation transferred it under § 1407 to the District of Arizona and assigned it to Judge Roll. Lexecon repeatedly asked Judge Roll to suggest remand to the Panel. He dismissed or granted summary judgment on the claims except a defamation claim against Milberg, dismissed Milberg's counterclaims, entered a separate Rule 54(b) judgment for Cotchett, and assigned the surviving case to himself for trial under § 1404(a). The Ninth Circuit denied mandamus, Judge Kozinski dissenting. Milberg won at trial, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed over another Kozinski dissent. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Lexecon and one of its principals had been defendants in litigation arising from the failure of Lincoln Savings and Loan, accused of giving banking regulators misleading reports about the financial condition of Lincoln Savings and its parent, American Continental Corporation. That litigation was transferred to the District of Arizona for coordinated pretrial proceedings under § 1407, and the claims against Lexecon were dismissed in August 1992 under an agreement described as a resolution. Lexecon then sued the law firms in Illinois, characterizing the earlier claims as a meritless vendetta that had ended in its favor.

In transferring the new suit to Arizona, the Panel pointed to shared factual questions about the earlier settlement, a large Arizona document depository and a pending Ninth Circuit appeal. The appeal was later dismissed and the depository closed, and the remaining Lincoln Savings litigation settled, with judgment entered in March 1994. The Panel's Rule 14(b) expressly recognized self-assignment by transferee courts, and courts had followed the practice for decades. Lexecon continuously objected to trial in Arizona; it did not challenge subject-matter jurisdiction or allege an independent error in the conduct of the trial.
sections.Issue: Whether a district court to which an action has been transferred under § 1407(a) for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings may invoke § 1404(a) to assign the action to itself for trial, and whether such an assignment over a preserved objection is harmless error.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1998), in an opinion by Justice Souter with the judgment unanimous, Justice Scalia joining all but Part II-C on legislative history, held that a district court receiving an action under § 1407(a) could not use § 1404(a) to assign it to itself for trial. The statute's mandatory command that the Panel remand each transferred action to its original district at or before the conclusion of pretrial proceedings controlled, and the Panel's self-assignment rule was invalid. The error was not harmless. The Court reversed and remanded, leaving Cotchett's Rule 54(b) dismissal in place.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court acknowledged that respondents' position was initially plausible: the Panel's rule recognized the practice, courts had long followed it, and a § 1404 motion ordinarily occurs before trial. The difficulty appeared when the statute was read as a whole. Self-assignment would prevent the Panel from obeying Congress's separate command to remand. Respondents said that command governed the Panel, not the district judge, but that division would let one statutory actor disable another's mandatory duty. The Panel's rulemaking authority required consistency with Acts of Congress, and longstanding practice could not overcome the statute.

Lexecon had not waived its protection by asking the transferee judge for a remand suggestion rather than moving before the Panel, whose rules strongly discouraged remand without such a suggestion. A § 1404 self-assignment did not terminate the action so as to end the remand duty; the statute referred to termination of the civil action itself. Section 1407(h), expressly allowing trial transfer of certain Clayton Act actions, showed that Congress knew how to authorize trial consolidation. In Part II-C, which Justice Scalia did not join, the opinion found no support for respondents in the legislative history. Efficiency arguments belonged before Congress. The Court reserved whether § 1404, considered alone, permits self-transfer.

On remedy, the Court rejected harmless error. Congress had categorically protected the plaintiff's entitlement to remand, and ignoring a continuously preserved objection would make an impermissible trial its own justification. Caterpillar was distinguished because the defect there had been cured before judgment; here the violation persisted through trial. The casebook's later waiver and choice-of-circuit-law discussions are editorial context, not holdings of the case.

CP-ATLAS-LIVINGSTON.rule: An action for trespass to land is a local action that can be brought only where the land lies, and a court does not acquire jurisdiction over it merely because the defendant resides or can be found in its district.

sections.Parties: Edward Livingston, a New York citizen, was the plaintiff. He sued Thomas Jefferson, a Virginia citizen, in the federal circuit court in Virginia for alleged trespasses on land in New Orleans, attributing the acts to Jefferson while he was President. Jefferson, the defendant, pleaded that the Virginia court lacked jurisdiction because the land was in the Territory of Orleans; Livingston sought damages and argued that confining jurisdiction to where the land lay would leave him unable to sue Jefferson, who had stayed outside the Orleans courts' jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: The suit began in 1810, after Jefferson's presidency ended, in the United States Circuit Court for the District of Virginia. Jefferson demurred to several counts, pleaded the general issue and justifications, and separately pleaded to the court's jurisdiction on the ground that all the land lay in the Territory of Orleans, where a court competent to hear trespass actions existed. Livingston replied that Jefferson had remained outside the Orleans courts' jurisdiction and resided within the Virginia court's reach. Jefferson demurred to that reply and Livingston joined in the demurrer. On December 5, 1811, both judges sustained the jurisdictional objection: Tyler said the cause must leave the court, and Marshall concluded that the law on the demurrer favored Jefferson.
sections.Material Facts:
The dispute concerned the Batture of the Suburb St. Mary in New Orleans, then in the Territory of Orleans. Livingston's declaration alleged entry onto land he claimed, destruction of tools and materials, removal of soil, his expulsion, interruption of canal and embankment construction, and resulting damage. These were allegations, not findings that Jefferson acted unlawfully or that Livingston owned the property.

The eight counts used the traditional pleading device of identifying New Orleans as the place of the events and then adding a fictional Virginia venue: Richmond, in Henrico County. Jefferson's justifications included that he acted under congressional authority as President and without malice; the court did not decide those merits defenses. Livingston's reply rested on the point that Jefferson had stayed out of the Orleans courts' reach since the cause of action arose, so that confining jurisdiction to where the land lay would leave him unable to sue this defendant there.
sections.Issue: Whether the federal circuit court in Virginia could hear a claim for trespass to land situated outside its district when the defendant lived, and could be found, in Virginia.
sections.Holding: The United States Circuit Court for the District of Virginia (1811), with District Judge John Tyler and Circuit Justice John Marshall each giving an explanation, answered no. Trespass to land was a local action, and the defendant's presence in the district did not convert it into a transitory one. The decision was a jurisdictional defeat for Livingston; it did not adjudicate that Jefferson's conduct was lawful, determine ownership of the batture, establish presidential immunity, or decide that every claim connected to land is local.
sections.Reasoning:
Tyler relied on the longstanding common-law distinction. Although many formerly local actions had become transitory, trespass to land, quare clausum fregit, remained local, and a venue fiction useful in a transitory contract action could not move a New Orleans parcel into Richmond. He gave practical reasons: such a case can require examining title and boundaries, a survey, and process reaching a surveyor, sheriff or jury at the place, which a court without authority there could not command. He rejected Livingston's appeal to general or universal law and refused to change the rule solely to prevent a failure of justice; a competent court existed where the trespass allegedly occurred, and occasional gaps did not authorize a new jurisdictional rule.

Marshall concurred in the result but was more skeptical. Common-law actions originally depended on a jury of the vicinity, and judicially created venue fictions later allowed personal tort and contract claims arising elsewhere to be heard where the defendant was found. He saw no satisfactory nontechnical reason why a contract action involving land, which might require the same inquiry into title and boundaries, could be maintained where the defendant was found while a land-trespass action for damages could not. Nevertheless the authorities treated causes necessarily tied to a location as local, and the line was too firmly established to disregard. Lord Mansfield's contrary efforts did not displace it: Mostyn v. Fabrigas was a personal-injury action, his land-trespass decisions were at nisi prius, and Doulson v. Matthews later rejected the expansion. Marshall thought it weighty that the rule could leave a plaintiff with a right but no remedy against a defendant who never entered the land's district, but held that precedent required judgment for Jefferson.

The casebook describes the case as the leading American land-trespass precedent and highlights Marshall's dissatisfaction.

CP-ATLAS-MATSUSHITA.rule: To survive summary judgment, an antitrust plaintiff must present evidence tending to exclude the possibility of independent action, and when the claimed conspiracy makes no economic sense the plaintiff needs more persuasive evidence than conduct equally consistent with lawful competition.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were Zenith Radio Corp., which manufactured and sold television sets in the United States, and National Union Electric, successor to Emerson Radio, which left television manufacturing in 1970 after substantial losses. The defendants were Japanese television manufacturers and their American affiliates; the 21 petitioners in the Court were those remaining after the Third Circuit upheld judgment for three of the original 24. The plaintiffs sought a trial on their antitrust conspiracy claims; the defendants sought reinstatement of summary judgment.
sections.Procedural History: National Union Electric sued in New Jersey in 1970 and Zenith in Pennsylvania in 1974; the cases were consolidated in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania that year. After years of discovery, the district court required final pretrial statements, excluded much of the plaintiffs' proposed evidence, including governmental records, business documents and expert material, and granted summary judgment. The Third Circuit restored substantial excluded evidence and reversed the pertinent summary judgment. The Court's grant excluded the evidentiary rulings and the separate Antidumping Act decision. The Court reversed the Third Circuit and remanded, allowing that court to consider whether other sufficiently unambiguous evidence of the alleged predatory conspiracy existed; absent such evidence the defendants were entitled to reinstatement of summary judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs alleged that the Japanese manufacturers and their American affiliates conspired over many years to eliminate American competitors by combining artificially high prices in Japan with low prices in the United States, using Japanese profits to fund American losses; once American competitors disappeared, the conspirators would raise American prices and recover those losses through monopoly profits. National Union Electric dated the conspiracy from 1960 and Zenith from 1953. These were allegations, not findings. The claims invoked the Sherman Act, Robinson-Patman Act, Wilson Tariff Act and a separately adjudicated Antidumping Act theory.

The Third Circuit pointed to a concentrated Japanese market with barriers to American entry, relatively high fixed costs and excess capacity, export minimum or check prices arranged with Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry, a five-company rule limiting each producer's American distributors, and rebates that undercut check prices and were concealed from governmental authorities.

The alleged campaign had continued for roughly two decades. RCA and Zenith retained the two largest individual retail shares, together around 40 percent, even as the Japanese companies' collective share approached 50 percent.
sections.Issue: Whether, on a Rule 56 motion, the record permitted a rational factfinder to find both a predatory-pricing conspiracy among the defendants and resulting antitrust injury to the plaintiffs, and what inferences substantive antitrust law permits a plaintiff to draw from ambiguous conduct in resisting summary judgment.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1986), in a 5-4 opinion by Justice Powell joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Marshall, Rehnquist and O'Connor, held that antitrust law limits the inferences available from ambiguous evidence on summary judgment: conduct equally consistent with independent price competition and unlawful conspiracy does not, standing alone, establish the conspiracy, and plaintiffs need evidence tending to exclude independent action. Finding the alleged predatory conspiracy economically implausible, the Court reversed and remanded for the Third Circuit to consider any other sufficiently unambiguous evidence. It adopted no universal cost test for predatory pricing and did not decide sovereign compulsion.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority first separated proof of concerted conduct from proof of a conspiracy causing cognizable injury. Cartelization confined to competitive conditions in Japan would not alone support these claims, and agreements raising American prices or restricting output could be unlawful yet benefit competing American producers. Check prices and distributor restrictions were therefore not direct evidence of a conspiracy injuring these plaintiffs; only the alleged low-price campaign supplied a potentially injurious theory.

Under Rule 56, once the movant meets its burden the opponent must identify specific facts creating a genuine issue; speculative doubt is insufficient, and the whole record must permit a rational factfinder to return a favorable verdict. Reasonable inferences still favor the opponent, but a theory that makes no economic sense requires more persuasive support.

Predation imposes present losses for uncertain future gains and succeeds only by eliminating competitors, gaining monopoly power, preventing entry and holding high prices long enough to recoup. A many-firm cartel adds coordination problems, since each member has reason to let others bear the losses. Two decades had passed without success, and the majority saw no demonstrated barriers ensuring that monopoly prices could be sustained. Japanese monopoly profits and excess capacity showed ability, not motive. Mistaken inferences are especially costly where the conduct is low pricing, because chilling discounts undermines what antitrust law protects. The majority discounted expert below-cost evidence built on constructed cost assumptions.

Justice White, dissenting with Justices Brennan, Blackmun and Stevens, argued that comparing the plausibility of conspiracy against independent action could become judicial weighing, that economist DePodwin's report created a genuine issue on injury, and that the majority's criticisms were arguments for trial; he would have affirmed. The casebook's account emphasizes the inference standard and compresses the parties and procedural result.

CP-ATLAS-MCGEE.rule: Due process permits a state to exercise personal jurisdiction over a foreign insurer in a suit on a contract that has a substantial connection with the state, even when that single contract is the insurer's only shown business there.

sections.Parties: Lulu B. McGee, the mother and beneficiary of the insured, Lowell Franklin, was the plaintiff. She sued International Life Insurance Company, a Texas corporation, first in California to recover on the policy and then in Texas to enforce the California judgment. International resisted enforcement on the ground that the California judgment was void for want of jurisdiction over it. McGee sought reversal of the Texas courts' refusal to enforce her judgment.
sections.Procedural History: McGee sued International in a California state court under a California statute permitting suits against foreign insurers on insurance contracts with California residents even when the insurer could not be served within the state. International received process by registered mail at its principal place of business in Texas, and McGee obtained a California judgment. Unable to collect it there, she sued on the judgment in Texas. The Texas courts refused enforcement, holding the California judgment void under the Fourteenth Amendment because service outside California had not given its courts jurisdiction over International. The Court reviewed the judgment of the Texas Court of Civil Appeals, reversed, and remanded to that court for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Lowell Franklin lived in California when he bought a life insurance policy from Empire Mutual Insurance Company, an Arizona corporation, in 1944. In 1948 International Life agreed to assume Empire Mutual's insurance obligations and mailed Franklin a reinsurance certificate offering to insure him on the terms of his existing policy. Franklin accepted the offer in California and mailed premiums from his California home to International's Texas office until his death in 1950. McGee submitted proof of death, but International refused payment on the ground that Franklin had committed suicide; that was the insurer's asserted defense, not a finding by the Court.

Neither insurance company had an office or agent in California, and the record showed no California insurance business by International beyond this one policy. The California statute McGee relied on became law in 1949, after International assumed the policy. International did not claim that it lacked adequate notice or sufficient time to prepare its defenses and appear. The parties did not dispute that, if California's jurisdiction was valid, Texas had to recognize the judgment under the full faith and credit requirement implemented by 28 U.S.C. § 1738.
sections.Issue: Whether California could, consistent with due process, enter a binding personal judgment against an insurer whose relevant California activity consisted of a single insurance contract conducted by mail, and whether applying the 1949 California statute to a policy assumed in 1948 impaired the obligation of the insurer's contract.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1957), in an opinion by Justice Black, with Chief Justice Warren not participating and the other eight Justices deciding without separate opinion or recorded dissent, held that California's exercise of jurisdiction satisfied due process because the suit concerned a contract with a substantial connection to California. It also rejected the impairment objection. The Court reversed the Texas judgment and remanded. It did not try the insurance claim, make a finding about suicide, or calculate policy proceeds, and it did not say the single policy made International answerable in California on unrelated claims.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court traced the constitutional evolution from Pennoyer v. Neff to International Shoe Co. v. Washington. Rather than treating corporate presence or in-state service as the exclusive basis of judicial power, International Shoe asked whether the defendant had minimum contacts consistent with fair play and substantial justice. The Court tied this development to changes in interstate commerce: contracts increasingly crossed state lines by mail, and modern transportation and communication made defending in a distant state less burdensome.

The contract had a substantial connection with California: it was delivered there, Franklin mailed premiums from there, and he lived there when he died. California had a substantial interest in providing an effective remedy when an insurer refused payment to its residents. Requiring an individual claimant to sue an insurance company in a distant state could make a small or moderate claim too costly to pursue, effectively insulating the insurer from collection. California also offered access to important witnesses; evidence relevant to the suicide defense would often be found where Franklin had lived.

The Court acknowledged that defending in California could inconvenience International, but the inconvenience shown did not amount to a denial of due process, and International did not claim inadequate notice or insufficient time to prepare and appear.

On the impairment objection, the statute changed only the means of enforcing the insurance obligation without enlarging or reducing the parties' substantive contractual rights. It supplied a California forum for whatever rights McGee already had, and International still had a reasonable opportunity to appear and contest liability, so it had no vested right to avoid suit in California. The casebook's editorial account omits this explanation of why the 1949 statute could apply to the existing policy.

CP-ATLAS-MOORE.rule: Under Rule 15(b), an unpleaded issue is tried by implied consent only if the record shows the opposing party recognized it was being litigated and had a fair chance to contest it; evidence relevant to an already pleaded issue does not establish consent.

sections.Parties: Reuben Moore, the father, filed the District of Columbia custody suit and was the appellant. Sidney Moore, the mother, was the defendant; after trial she moved to add a counterclaim for custody, child support, separate maintenance and counsel fees, and she received those awards. On appeal Reuben argued that Sidney had requested no affirmative relief before trial and that he lacked notice and an adequate opportunity to contest the counterclaim's subjects; he also challenged the custody findings and the monetary awards.
sections.Procedural History: In April 1976 Reuben opposed Sidney's D.C. habeas petition and filed this custody suit. Sidney at first challenged D.C. jurisdiction, then withdrew the objection and answered after a New York court suggested resolving custody in D.C. The Family Division of the Superior Court tried the case in October 1976. A week after trial Sidney moved under the domestic-relations counterpart of Rule 15(b) to conform the pleadings to the evidence. The February 1977 written order granted the amendment and made the awards; the court then denied Reuben's stay and new-trial motions. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals affirmed custody, reversed separate maintenance, and remanded child support, counsel fees, and visitation rights and bond for further proceedings, findings and conclusions.
sections.Material Facts:
Reuben and Sidney married in the District of Columbia in 1968, and their daughter Jessica was born in 1973. In December 1975 Sidney took Jessica to her parents' home in Schenectady, New York. Reuben sought custody there; the New York court orally awarded temporary custody to Sidney and visitation to Reuben. In February 1976 Reuben, assisted by a detective, took Jessica from her maternal grandfather and brought her to Washington. Sidney filed a D.C. habeas proceeding seeking custody. Reuben took Jessica to Europe and the Bahamas; after his return, Sidney and her parents took the child back to Schenectady.

At the end of trial the court orally awarded Sidney custody and $500 per month in child support and gave Reuben visitation conditioned on a $7,500 bond. It did not then award spousal support, recognizing there was no affirmative pleading requesting it, and reserved attorney fees for motion papers. The written order awarded custody, $500 monthly child support, another $500 monthly in separate maintenance and $5,916.65 in counsel fees, and retained the bond. Sidney's answer had asserted that Jessica's best interests favored her custody, and she had introduced evidence of Jessica's financial needs and of D.C. counsel expenses without objection.
sections.Issue: Whether the trial court could, under Rule 15(b), permit a post-trial amendment adding a counterclaim for custody, child support, separate maintenance and counsel fees on the ground that those issues were tried by express or implied consent, and whether the custody and monetary awards were adequately supported.
sections.Holding: The District of Columbia Court of Appeals (1978), in an opinion by Judge Ferren on a panel with Judge Gallagher and Superior Court Judge Moultrie and with no separate opinion, held that custody, child support, the visitation bond and counsel fees were properly before the trial court because they had been tried by consent or without prejudicial surprise, but that the trial court abused its discretion in permitting the amendment for separate maintenance and awarding it. The court affirmed custody, reversed separate maintenance, and remanded child support, counsel fees, and visitation rights and bond because the findings on the parents' financial abilities were inadequate.
sections.Reasoning:
The D.C. domestic-relations rule incorporated a civil Rule 15(b) identical to the then-existing Federal Rule. Matters tried by express or implied consent are treated as though pleaded, and an amendment can formalize that even after judgment. The court read the rule to favor decision of the real controversy while preserving fair notice and an opportunity to respond. For implied consent, the record must show that the opposing party recognized the introduction of the unpleaded matter and had an adequate chance to litigate it. Evidence relevant specifically to the new issue can support the inference, as can a failure to object, but incidental evidence that only inferentially suggests another issue is not enough. The inquiry proceeds issue by issue.

Custody: Reuben knew the court would decide Jessica's placement; Sidney's answer, both parents' evidence, the New York court's suggestion and the habeas petition supplied notice. Child support was inherent in a custody contest centered on the child's best interests, and Sidney's evidence of Jessica's needs came in without a relevance objection. Reuben conceded visitation belonged in the custody determination, and his history of taking the child supported requiring security. Fees were allowable under D.C. precedent as a necessary expense for the child, and the judge reserved the question, received a motion and opposition, and held a hearing.

Separate maintenance was different. The marital relationship was not being litigated, and evidence of Sidney's finances was also relevant to custody and child support, so its admission did not signal a separate claim for herself.

The custody evidence supported placement with Sidney, and no maternal presumption was used. But the findings did not adequately establish the parents' financial abilities for support, fees or the bond's amount. The casebook excerpt develops the amendment question and omits much of the review of the monetary amounts.

CP-ATLAS-MUSSAT.rule: In a nationwide Rule 23 class action under a federal statute, the named representative must establish personal jurisdiction over the defendant, but no separate showing of specific jurisdiction is required for each absent class member's claim.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was the professional services corporation through which Florence Mussat, an Illinois physician, operated; the opinion uses Mussat as shorthand for the corporation. It sued IQVIA, Inc., a Delaware corporation headquartered in Pennsylvania, under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, proposing to represent itself and people throughout the country who had received similar IQVIA faxes. IQVIA, the defendant, moved to strike the nationwide class definition. Mussat was the appellant under Rule 23(f); IQVIA defended the order and contested appellate jurisdiction.
sections.Procedural History: Mussat sued in the Northern District of Illinois. IQVIA moved to strike the nationwide class definition, arguing under Bristol-Myers Squibb that the court lacked specific jurisdiction for unnamed members injured outside Illinois. The district court agreed that each class member's claim needed minimum contacts between IQVIA and Illinois and struck the non-Illinois portion of the proposed class; an Illinois-only class remained possible. Mussat obtained permission to appeal under Rule 23(f), and IQVIA disputed the appellate court's authority to review the order. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Florence Mussat received two unsolicited faxes from IQVIA that lacked the opt-out notice required by federal statute. The corporate plaintiff sued under 47 U.S.C. § 227 and proposed a class of people throughout the country who had received similar IQVIA junk faxes during the preceding four years.

IQVIA was not subject to general jurisdiction in Illinois. The district court's order was made on a Rule 12 motion to strike rather than on a motion labeled class certification, and it left open the possibility of an Illinois-only class while eliminating any possibility of certifying the nationwide class Mussat actually sought. The district court invoked the Fourteenth Amendment even though the relevant due-process provision for a federal court was the Fifth; the panel noted the labeling error without making it dispositive. Neither class certification nor liability under the statute had been adjudicated.
sections.Issue: Whether an order striking the nationwide portion of a proposed class is reviewable under Rule 23(f), and whether Bristol-Myers Squibb or Rule 4(k) requires a federal court to have specific personal jurisdiction over the defendant for the claim of each unnamed member of a nationwide class.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit (2020), in a unanimous opinion by Chief Judge Wood for a panel of Wood, Kanne and Barrett, held that striking the nationwide portion of the proposed class was functionally a partial denial of certification reviewable under Rule 23(f), and that a nationwide Rule 23 action under a federal statute does not require a separate showing of specific personal jurisdiction for each absent member's claim. The named representative must establish personal jurisdiction. The court reversed and remanded; it did not certify the class or decide liability.
sections.Reasoning:
On appealability, the panel looked to the order's effect. Its earlier Bemis decision treated a ruling resolving a dispute about representative litigation as the functional equivalent of a certification ruling, and Microsoft v. Baker endorsed that approach. The order eliminated the nationwide class, and leaving a smaller class available did not erase the denial as to everyone excluded.

On the merits, Bristol-Myers involved individually named plaintiffs in a California mass action, not unnamed members represented through a certified class, so it did not decide the question. Nationwide classes had long been entertained without examining each absent member's forum contacts. Rule 23 requires representatives to satisfy subdivision (a) and one branch of (b); those safeguards, underscored by Taylor v. Sturgell's rejection of virtual representation, distinguish a class from ordinary joinder. Under Devlin, unnamed members are parties for some purposes and not others: their citizenship ordinarily does not defeat complete diversity, supplemental jurisdiction can cover their claims when the named representative meets the amount requirement, and venue need not be established for each. Personal jurisdiction follows the same representative focus.

Rule 4(k) did not require otherwise. It addresses how and where process establishes personal jurisdiction, not whom a representative action must treat as a separately appearing litigant; Rule 17's provision for representatives and Rule 82 pointed the same way, and Rule 23(b)(3)'s forum-concentration factor contemplates concentrating claims.

The panel noted that Bristol-Myers reserved whether the Fifth Amendment imposes the same limits in federal court and that Justice Sotomayor's dissent observed that class actions were not addressed. The casebook extract omits the Rule 4(k) and appellate-jurisdiction discussions, and its following question about absent members' standing is editorial, not a holding.

CP-ATLAS-ORTIZ.rule: A mandatory limited-fund class under Rule 23(b)(1)(B) presumptively requires a fund independently shown to be insufficient for all claims, devotion of the whole fund to those claims, and inclusion and equitable treatment of the claimants, with conflicts addressed by separately represented subclasses.

sections.Parties: Fibreboard Corp., an asbestos manufacturer facing thousands of personal-injury claims, and its insurers, Continental and Pacific, agreed with counsel for asbestos claimants to a global settlement on behalf of a mandatory settlement class principally made up of people with unfiled or withdrawn claims and people who might develop future injuries. Objectors challenged the class certification and the representation; the settlement's proponents defended certification as a limited-fund class.
sections.Procedural History: The Eastern District of Texas certified a mandatory settlement class under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), finding a limited fund, and approved the settlement after an eight-day fairness hearing. The Fifth Circuit affirmed. After Amchem, the Court returned the case for reconsideration, and the Fifth Circuit again sustained certification, reasoning that the mandatory-class setting differed from Amchem's opt-out class and that the allocation did not discriminate among injury groups. The Court reversed the Fifth Circuit's judgment and remanded for proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
Fibreboard manufactured asbestos products from the 1920s until 1971. Its own assets were much smaller than its projected liability, but two old insurance policies were a possible source of recovery: Continental's, covering May 1957 to March 1959 with no aggregate limit, and Pacific's disputed policy for an earlier period. California coverage litigation had produced a trial judgment for Fibreboard, which the insurers had appealed.

During 1993 negotiations, counsel for existing claimants arranged separate settlements for approximately 45,000 inventory claims, at least some of which made full payment contingent on approval of the global settlement or favorable resolution of the insurance dispute; the same lawyers negotiated for the class. On August 26, 1993, agreement was reached on a $1.535 billion trust: $1.525 billion from the insurers and $10 million attributed to Fibreboard, of which only $500,000 came from its own assets. A separate backup Trilateral Settlement Agreement provided $2 billion from the insurers if the global settlement failed.

The class excluded the inventory plaintiffs and more than 53,000 pending claimants. Class members could not opt out; litigation recovery against the trust was capped at $500,000, with no punitive damages or prejudgment interest and payment over five to ten years. Fibreboard retained nearly all its net worth.
sections.Issue: Whether this global settlement of present and future asbestos claims against Fibreboard could be certified as a mandatory limited-fund class under Rule 23(b)(1)(B), when the fund's limit rested on negotiated figures, many claimants were excluded, and class counsel represented groups with conflicting interests.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1999), in an opinion by Justice Souter for seven Justices (Rehnquist, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg joining), held that this settlement could not be certified as a mandatory limited-fund class: the fund was not independently shown to be limited, and exclusions and conflicting representation defeated the required protections. The Court reversed and remanded. It did not decide whether Rule 23(b)(1)(B) could ever aggregate unliquidated mass tort claims, did not resolve the Article III or constitutional objections, and did not decide whether Fibreboard's retention of its net worth alone would invalidate certification.
sections.Reasoning:
A limited-fund class binds claimants who cannot all recover in full from one inadequate resource, and because it is mandatory, absent members lack the opt-out right of Rule 23(b)(3). The traditional cases shared three characteristics: definite maximums for the claims and the fund showing insufficiency; the whole inadequate fund devoted to the claims; and inclusion and equitable treatment of claimants sharing the recovery theory. These were presumptively necessary, and a proponent departing from them had to justify it. The Rule's history, the Rules Enabling Act, and jury-trial and due-process concerns supported caution, though the Court did not hold every mandatory limited-fund settlement unconstitutional.

Applying this, an agreed payment figure shows what parties will pay, not the maximum available; the district court needed an independent evidentiary basis for the limit and insufficiency, and a later fairness hearing could not substitute. Settlement value might be evidence after disinterested bargaining, but class counsel also represented inventory clients whose payments depended on a global deal. The Court did not find the policies sufficient to pay everyone; it held insufficiency unproven.

A mandatory class should include the competing claims on the fund, yet the inventory and pending claimants were outside it and appeared to receive better terms. Within the class, present and future claimants, and those exposed before and after Continental's policy expired in 1959, had conflicting interests requiring homogeneous subclasses with separate representation; a Rule 23(e) fairness review could not swallow Rule 23(a)'s adequacy requirement.

Rehnquist, concurring with Scalia and Kennedy, said the asbestos crisis called for legislation. Breyer, dissenting with Stevens, would have deferred to the district court's findings and treated the disputed insurance asset as a genuine limited fund. The casebook's assigned excerpt substantially compresses the majority.

CP-ATLAS-PERKINS.rule: When a foreign corporation carries on continuous and systematic corporate activities in a state, due process permits, but does not require, that state to exercise jurisdiction over it on causes of action entirely distinct from those activities.

sections.Parties: Idonah Slade Perkins, who did not reside in Ohio, was the plaintiff. She brought two Ohio actions against Benguet Consolidated Mining Company, a corporation organized under Philippine law, and other defendants, seeking dividends allegedly owed to her as a stockholder and damages for the company's alleged failure to issue share certificates. Benguet obtained an order quashing service; Perkins sought review of the Ohio courts' refusal to exercise jurisdiction over the company.
sections.Procedural History: The Ohio trial court quashed service on the company, and Ohio's intermediate appellate court and supreme court affirmed. Under Ohio practice the supreme court's syllabus stated the court's approved law, and it denied jurisdiction over this unrelated claim without clearly identifying whether Ohio law or the Fourteenth Amendment required that result; the accompanying opinion relied unequivocally on a federal constitutional prohibition. The Court vacated Ohio's judgment and remanded for further proceedings in light of its opinion, so that Ohio could decide the state-law question for itself.
sections.Material Facts:
Benguet owned profitable gold and silver mines in the Philippines. Perkins sought approximately $68,400 in dividends and $2.5 million in damages, principally for the alleged failure to issue certificates for 120,000 shares. Neither claim arose in Ohio or related to the company's Ohio activities.

Japanese occupation halted the Philippine mining operations. The company's president, who was also its general manager and principal stockholder, returned to his Ohio home and directed the company's limited continuing business there. He kept corporate files, handled business correspondence, issued salary checks to himself and two secretaries, maintained substantial corporate bank balances, and held directors' meetings at his office or home. An Ohio bank served as stock transfer agent. From Ohio he supervised plans to rehabilitate the Philippine properties and dispatched funds for machinery. The company mined no Ohio property.

The president was served in Ohio while acting for the company. The company had neither obtained a foreign-corporation license nor appointed a statutory agent in Ohio, but those omissions did not themselves prevent it from being sued under Ohio law.
sections.Issue: Whether the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment prohibits, or compels, Ohio's exercise of jurisdiction over a foreign corporation on causes of action that did not arise in Ohio and are unrelated to the corporation's activities there, where its president carried on continuous corporate management in the state.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (1952), in Justice Burton's opinion for six Justices, with Justice Black concurring only in the result and Justice Minton dissenting joined by Chief Justice Vinson (7-2), held that the corporation's Ohio activities were sufficiently substantial to make jurisdiction over these unrelated claims constitutionally permissible. Federal due process neither prohibited Ohio from entertaining the claims nor compelled it to do so; Ohio remained free to choose a narrower policy under its own law. The Court vacated and remanded. It did not order Ohio to take jurisdiction or decide the stock claims.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court faced a risk that Ohio had declined jurisdiction in the mistaken belief that federal law left it no choice, so it decided only the federal boundary. The Constitution did not require Ohio to open its courts to every properly notified foreign corporation, nor to treat a foreign corporation as it treated a properly served nonresident natural person sued on an out-of-state cause of action.

Older decisions involving attempted service on public officials without authority to bind the foreign corporation in an unrelated action concerned inadequate service and notice, and their broader assumptions about corporate jurisdiction had been modified by International Shoe. Here actual service on the president resolved the notice concern, and the company's own substantial Ohio activities resolved the separate fairness concern.

International Shoe required attention to the quality and nature of the defendant's activities and whether jurisdiction was fair and reasonable. Corporate licensing criteria could help identify relevant activity but were not conclusive. Management, banking, correspondence, salary payments, stock administration and directors' meetings were meaningful activities even though the mines were elsewhere. Looking at the whole Ohio operation, the Court found continuous and systematic supervision of the necessarily limited wartime business; given that concentration of corporate management, due process allowed Ohio to adjudicate causes of action entirely distinct from the Ohio activities. The holding rested on those combined circumstances, not on a rule that an officer's presence or a few local purchases suffice.

Justice Minton agreed the constitutional premise in the Ohio opinion was erroneous but considered the syllabus an adequate and independent state ground; he regarded the majority's clarification as advisory and would have dismissed the writ as improvidently granted. The casebook discusses Perkins within its later Goodyear opinion rather than printing it separately.

CP-ATLAS-PIMENTEL.rule: Under Rule 19(b), when a required party is a sovereign entitled to immunity and its claims to the disputed property are not frivolous, the action must be dismissed if there is a potential for injury to the absent sovereign's interests.

sections.Parties: Merrill Lynch, the stakeholder, was the plaintiff in a statutory interpleader action over a brokerage account. The competing claimants were defendants: the Republic of the Philippines and its Presidential Commission on Good Governance, which claimed the assets as forfeited; Arelma, the Panamanian corporation that opened the account; the Philippine National Bank (PNB); the Pimentel class of about 9,539 human-rights victims holding a judgment against Marcos and his estate; and other claimants. The Republic and Commission asserted sovereign immunity and sought dismissal; the Pimentel class sought the fund.
sections.Procedural History: Merrill Lynch filed interpleader under § 1335 in federal court in Hawaii. The Republic and Commission invoked the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and moved to dismiss; Arelma and PNB also sought Rule 19(b) dismissal. The district judge initially rejected the sovereigns' request without deciding immunity. On a first appeal the Ninth Circuit held them immune and required parties under Rule 19(a) and stayed proceedings pending the Sandiganbayan's decision. The district judge later vacated the stay and awarded the fund to the Pimentel class. On a second appeal the Ninth Circuit affirmed, predicting the sovereigns' claims would fail under a New York six-year limitations period. The Court reversed and remanded with instructions to order the district court to dismiss the interpleader action.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1972 Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos incorporated Arelma under Panamanian law, and Arelma deposited $2 million in a Merrill Lynch brokerage account in New York. By 2000 the account held approximately $35 million. The Pimentel class had obtained a nearly $2 billion judgment in federal court in Hawaii against Marcos and his estate and sought to attach the Arelma assets.

The Republic and the Commission claimed that Philippine law forfeited assets derived from misuse of public office to the Republic from the moment of misappropriation. After Marcos fled in 1986, the Commission pursued assets in Switzerland, including Arelma shares; the assets were frozen and later placed in escrow at PNB pending proceedings in the Sandiganbayan, the Philippine court with special jurisdiction over corruption cases, where forfeiture proceedings had begun in 1991. The Republic and Commission asked Merrill Lynch to transfer the brokerage assets into a comparable escrow account; it instead filed the interpleader. A week after the district court awarded the fund to the Pimentel class, the Republic asked the Sandiganbayan specifically to declare the Arelma assets forfeited; that court had not ruled when the Court decided the case. Required-party status and sovereign immunity were uncontested in the Court.
sections.Issue: Whether, under Rule 19(b), an interpleader action over disputed assets may proceed in the absence of a foreign sovereign and its commission that are required parties, have successfully asserted sovereign immunity, and claim the assets, on the basis of a court's prediction that their claims would fail on the merits.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of the United States (2008), in an opinion by Justice Kennedy joined in full by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer and Alito, held that where required parties asserting sovereign immunity have nonfrivolous claims to disputed assets and adjudication could injure their interests, a court cannot effectively adjudicate those claims in their absence by predicting they will lose; Rule 19(b) required dismissal. Seven Justices ordered dismissal. Justice Souter joined except Parts IV-B and V, and Justice Stevens joined Part II only. The Court did not award the assets to the Philippines or undo the victims' judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court left open whether the Republic and Commission could seek review after obtaining dismissal on immunity grounds, because Arelma and PNB were proper petitioners; all nine Justices joined that holding. Rule 19(b) asks whether equity and good conscience permit proceeding, through nonexclusive factors; the 2007 wording changes were stylistic. The Court reserved the standard of review because the lower courts' legal errors required reversal under any standard.

On prejudice, sovereign immunity protects comity and dignity, and the Philippines had a concrete interest in adjudicating claims arising from historically significant abuses. The Ninth Circuit's prediction that the Republic would lose under New York limitations law effectively adjudicated a consequential interest without its consent. Dismissal is required when an immune required sovereign has nonfrivolous claims and there is potential injury to its interests; frivolous claims may be disregarded. The limitations prediction was itself uncertain. Second, no alternative that would lessen the prejudice had been proposed or appeared available. Third, adequacy refers to the public interest in settling the dispute as a whole, and a judgment would not bind the absent sovereigns. Fourth, the relevant plaintiff was Merrill Lynch, the interpleader plaintiff, which in later suits could try to join the sovereigns and seek Rule 19(b) dismissal; any remaining prejudice to it was outweighed. The equities might change if the Sandiganbayan unreasonably delayed or ruled.

Justice Stevens agreed the limitations analysis was faulty but opposed giving immunity near-dispositive force and preferred a stay or reassignment to a new district judge. Justice Souter preferred vacatur and a reasonable stay awaiting the Sandiganbayan, with proceedings before a new judge. The casebook's criticism and questions about public rights are commentary, not holdings.

CP-ATLAS-POLLER.rule: Summary judgment should be used cautiously in complex antitrust litigation where motive and intent are central, the proof lies largely with the alleged conspirators and credibility may matter; the record must be viewed favorably to the party opposing the motion.

sections.Parties: Lou Poller, the plaintiff, held the rights of Midwest Broadcasting Company, a dissolved corporation that had operated WCAN, a Milwaukee UHF television station affiliated with CBS. He sued for treble damages under section 4 of the Clayton Act, alleging restraint of trade and monopolization under sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act. The defendants were CBS, its television division and officers, management consultant Thad Holt, and Bartell Broadcasters, which owned the competing UHF station WOKY. The defendants won summary judgment below; Poller sought reversal in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment to the defendants. It reasoned that CBS could legally purchase WOKY with FCC approval and exercise its contractual right to cancel WCAN's affiliation, so Poller's resulting economic injury did not establish actionable wrongdoing. The D.C. Circuit affirmed, with Judge Washington dissenting. The Court then considered whether the record left a genuine dispute of material fact under then-Rule 56(c); it did not conduct the antitrust trial. By a vote of 5 to 4, the Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded for trial.
sections.Material Facts:
WCAN broadcast on ultra high frequency (UHF), which was relatively new: ordinary receivers initially received VHF signals and needed modification to receive UHF. Poller claimed WCAN had become a successful operation worth $2 million, but its affiliation agreement permitted CBS to cancel on six months' notice.

Poller alleged a coordinated plan. While the FCC considered allowing networks to own additional UHF stations, Holt obtained an option on WOKY. CBS could take that option after the regulatory change, acquire WOKY, and terminate WCAN's affiliation. Losing network programming would leave WCAN unable to compete and force it to sell its recently improved facilities cheaply, so that CBS could operate under WOKY's license using WCAN's superior equipment. Poller alleged a $1.45 million loss to Midwest and an equipment exchange that required Midwest to acquire WOKY's inferior facilities at excessive prices. WCAN continued operating for only ten days after CBS began its broadcasts on February 17, 1955. CBS abandoned UHF broadcasting in Milwaukee in 1959 and affiliated with a VHF station, which Poller treated as evidence of a design to destroy UHF competition and protect CBS's VHF interests. These were allegations and disputed inferences, not findings.
sections.Issue: Did the record leave a genuine dispute of material fact under then-Rule 56(c), so that summary judgment for the defendants was improper, where CBS's cancellation of the affiliation and purchase of a competing station could each be lawful when considered separately but were alleged to be parts of a scheme to restrain trade and monopolize?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1962, in an opinion by Justice Clark for a five-Justice majority (5 to 4), reversed and remanded for trial. The Court accepted that CBS's cancellation and acquisition could be lawful when considered separately, but held that a contractual privilege did not authorize its use as part of an unlawful agreement or purpose to restrain trade, control a market, or monopolize. Viewing the record favorably to Poller, a material dispute remained, and affidavits should not replace a trial. The Court did not award treble damages, establish a conspiracy, or resolve the relevant-market question, and it left the section 2 monopolization issues for trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The defendants' abstract entitlement to change affiliates did not dispose of the allegation that the entire course of conduct served a prohibited end. The majority found circumstances from which a trial could develop evidence of coordination: Holt had participated in CBS's plans, had relationships with CBS executives, and obtained an option that contemplated CBS's purchase but that he could retain if CBS did not buy. Because a finding of independent participation was possible, the Court did not decide whether a corporation could conspire with its own division or subsidiary. The majority read parts of CBS's market analysis as permitting an inference that its UHF investment was temporary and related to protecting its VHF position. WCAN's initial success, the purchase and disaffiliation, and CBS's later withdrawal suggested more than an entirely fanciful accusation, though the Court acknowledged the proof might ultimately fail. In complex antitrust litigation motive and intent were central, much of the proof lay with the alleged conspirators, and credibility could matter. The case does not hold that every antitrust plaintiff is entitled to trial merely by alleging an improper motive. Continued television service from another station would not itself negate a restraint.

Justice Harlan, joined by Justices Frankfurter, Whittaker, and Stewart, dissented and would have affirmed. Discovery was complete, including depositions of CBS's president and vice president, Holt, and Poller. Allegations, disbelief of defense witnesses, and hope for a different story on cross-examination were not affirmative evidence of unlawful intent, and he saw no reason for a specially restrictive antitrust version of Rule 56. He also disputed the majority's inferences and considered the conduct shown legally insufficient under sections 1 and 2.

The casebook's discussion of Poller's later influence is editorial history, not a holding of the 1962 Court.

CP-ATLAS-RAGAN.rule: In a diversity action on a state-created claim, a state rule making service an integral part of the limitations scheme governs the life of the claim; filing under Federal Rule 3 does not give the claim a longer life than state law allows.

sections.Parties: Ragan, the plaintiff, sought damages from Merchants Transfer & Warehouse for injuries sustained in a highway accident, invoking diversity jurisdiction in the federal District Court in Kansas. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse, the defendant, pleaded the Kansas statute of limitations and sought summary judgment. Ragan won a verdict at trial; the defendant prevailed in the Tenth Circuit, and the case came to the Court on certiorari.
sections.Procedural History: The defendant pleaded limitations and sought summary judgment. The District Court struck the defense and denied the motion, and Ragan obtained a verdict at trial. The Tenth Circuit reversed, holding after examining Kansas decisions that timely service was an integral part of the state limitations scheme and that summary judgment should have been granted. The Court granted certiorari and affirmed the Tenth Circuit's reversal of Ragan's trial recovery. The disposition sustained the limitations defense; it made no independent finding about the merits of the accident claim.
sections.Material Facts:
The highway accident occurred on October 1, 1943. Ragan filed his complaint in federal court on September 4, 1945. A summons issued on September 7 and was subsequently served but quashed. Effective service occurred on December 28, 1945, after the two-year Kansas tort limitations period had run. Filing, issuance, and effective service therefore occurred at different times.

Kansas law specified when an action commenced for limitations purposes by reference to service. Its provision included a sixty-day allowance for an attempt accompanied by faithful, proper, and diligent efforts to obtain service. The Court did not announce that all attempted service lacked legal effect; it accepted that this particular case would be barred in a Kansas court, and it was conceded that Ragan could not recover there.
sections.Issue: Did timely filing of the complaint under Federal Rule 3 toll the Kansas limitations period for this state-created tort claim in a diversity action, although Kansas law required service and the claim would be untimely in a Kansas court?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1949, in an opinion written by Justice Douglas and announced by Justice Reed, held the action barred. The state limitations rule governed the life of the state-created cause of action, and proper commencement of the action in federal court under Rule 3 did not itself give the claim a longer life than Kansas law allowed. The Court accepted the Tenth Circuit's determination that the Kansas service requirement was integral to the limitations scheme. Justice Rutledge dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
Erie and York sought to prevent diversity litigants from obtaining materially different state-law rights merely by choosing a federal forum. It was conceded that Ragan could not recover in a Kansas court, and allowing him to recover in federal court would create the advantage those decisions rejected.

The Court acknowledged that the Federal Rules determined how an action began in federal court and that Ragan properly followed that procedure. But it distinguished commencing the federal proceeding from preserving the state claim. The claim carried the same limitations burden and defenses in either forum, and local law determined when it accrued and ended.

Ragan relied on Bomar v. Keyes, which treated filing as tolling. The Court distinguished that case because it involved rights under a federal statute, whereas Ragan concerned a locally created claim. It did not matter that the state limitation expired after the federal filing rather than before: either way, extending the claim's life solely in federal court would add to the state-created right. Finally, the Court declined to disturb the Tenth Circuit's careful reading of Kansas law, so its treatment of the service provision rested on that local-law interpretation rather than a new national rule.

Justice Rutledge's dissent, published with Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. and addressing Cohen, Woods, and Ragan together, accepted Erie for substantive state law but rejected the assumption that federal doors must close whenever state doors closed; he would have reversed in Ragan.

The casebook note asks whether federal or state law determines commencement in a suit enforcing federal law; Ragan's distinction of Bomar means its holding is not a rule that state service law always governs federal causes of action.

CP-ATLAS-SCOTT.rule: At summary judgment the evidence and reasonable inferences favor the nonmovant only where the dispute is genuine; a court need not adopt a version of the facts so plainly contradicted by the record that no reasonable jury could believe it.

sections.Parties: Harris, the plaintiff, was a driver left quadriplegic when a police pursuit ended in a crash. He sued Deputy Timothy Scott and others under 42 U.S.C. section 1983; the claim before the Court alleged excessive force in an unreasonable seizure under the Fourth Amendment. Scott, the defendant, moved for summary judgment based on qualified immunity, lost in both lower courts, and sought reversal in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: The district court denied Scott's motion for summary judgment based on qualified immunity, finding material disputes. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed on interlocutory appeal, reasoning that a jury could find an unconstitutional use of deadly force and that the unlawfulness was sufficiently established to defeat immunity. Other claims against Scott or other defendants were outside the Court's review. The Court reversed the Eleventh Circuit, 8 to 1, and held Scott entitled to summary judgment on the Fourth Amendment claim before it. The judgment rested on the absence of a constitutional violation rather than on a separate determination that an established violation was excused by qualified immunity.
sections.Material Facts:
In March 2001 a Georgia deputy recorded Harris driving 73 miles per hour in a 55-mile-per-hour zone. When the deputy activated his lights, Harris fled. Scott joined the pursuit after hearing radio communications. The chase reached speeds above 85 miles per hour and lasted approximately six minutes and nearly ten miles. In a shopping-center parking lot Harris evaded police vehicles trying to contain him, collided with Scott's car, and returned to the highway. Scott sought permission to use a Precision Intervention Technique, and his supervisor authorized intervention. Scott instead applied his push bumper to the rear of Harris's car, saying the speed made the planned technique unsafe. Harris lost control, left the road, overturned, and was left quadriplegic.

The chase was recorded. Harris's account, accepted for summary-judgment purposes by the lower courts, portrayed speeding but controlled driving, little actual threat to others, and a largely clear roadway when Scott intervened. The majority described the video as showing an extraordinarily dangerous chase: movement around numerous vehicles, crossing the center line, red-light violations, and substantial risks to motorists and police. No party alleged the recording was altered or disputed that it depicted the actual events.
sections.Issue: First, did Rule 56 require the courts to accept Harris's version of the facts despite the video recording of the chase? Second, on the facts the Court regarded as established, was Scott's use of force in ramming Harris's car objectively reasonable under the Fourth Amendment?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 2007, in an opinion by Justice Scalia for eight Justices (8 to 1), held that a version of events so plainly contradicted by the record that no reasonable jury could believe it need not be adopted at summary judgment, and that the lower courts should have used the factual picture supplied by the recording. On those facts, Scott's intervention in this dangerous pursuit was objectively reasonable, there was no Fourth Amendment violation, and he was entitled to summary judgment. Justices Ginsburg and Breyer joined the Court and concurred separately; Justice Stevens alone dissented.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court reaffirmed that evidence and reasonable inferences favor the nonmovant, but that protection applies to a genuine dispute, not every verbal disagreement. The video conclusively defeated the proposition that Harris's driving posed little danger. This was not a general license to disregard a plaintiff whenever a defendant supplies video; the premise was that the account was untenable for any reasonable jury. The Court noted that no other vehicle or pedestrian was threatened at the precise instant Scott rammed Harris, but treated the ongoing pursuit's broader danger as decisive. Once the supportable facts were determined, reasonableness was a legal question.

Scott conceded a seizure. The Court rejected using the deadly-force label as a mechanical trigger for the Tennessee v. Garner preconditions; Garner concerned shooting an unarmed person fleeing on foot. The Court balanced the serious risk to Harris against the imminent danger to motorists, possible pedestrians, and officers, considering the number of lives endangered and relative culpability: Harris intentionally created the dangerous flight. It rejected a constitutional obligation to end the pursuit, since withdrawal would not reliably communicate that Harris could stop fleeing and would let especially reckless driving secure escape.

Justice Ginsburg, concurring, stressed that the decision was not a mechanical rule authorizing force in every fast chase. Justice Breyer, concurring, said watching the video changed his assessment and proposed freeing lower courts from Saucier's mandatory sequence, a proposal not adopted here. Justice Stevens, dissenting, read the recording as showing controlled passing, pointed to alternatives such as later arrest or stop sticks, and regarded disagreement among judges who had seen the recordings as evidence that reasonable jurors could disagree; he would have let a jury decide.

CP-ATLAS-SHAMROCK.rule: Under a removal statute authorizing removal by the defendant or defendants, an original state-court plaintiff cannot remove on diversity grounds merely because the defendant asserts an independent counterclaim, and federal courts must keep removal jurisdiction within the limits Congress prescribed.

sections.Parties: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp., a noncitizen of Texas, was the original plaintiff in a Texas state court, suing to recover an alleged indebtedness. The Texas defendant asserted a counterclaim against Shamrock for breach of a separate contract and, after Shamrock removed, moved to remand. Shamrock won in the federal district court, lost in the Fifth Circuit, and sought to preserve its removal in the Court.
sections.Procedural History: Shamrock sued in Texas state court and, after the defendant counterclaimed, removed the case to the federal district court for Northern Texas. The district court denied the defendant's motion to remand, tried the merits, and entered judgment for Shamrock on both its original claim and the counterclaim. The Fifth Circuit reversed and ordered the case remanded to the state court, reasoning that an original plaintiff was not a defendant within the meaning of Judicial Code section 28. The Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among federal courts on that statutory question and affirmed the Fifth Circuit. It did not affirm Shamrock's favorable federal judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Shamrock brought an action in a Texas state court to recover an alleged indebtedness. The Texas defendant asserted a counterclaim, also described as a cross-action, demanding more than $3,000 for breach of a contract separate and distinct from the indebtedness Shamrock sought to collect. Shamrock therefore faced an affirmative demand for damages although it had initiated the lawsuit. The asserted basis for removal was diversity of citizenship; the opinion does not describe the counterclaim as a federal cause of action.

The Court assumed that removal had been timely and procedurally regular if Shamrock was eligible to remove, and that the counterclaim was an independent cause of action exceeding the jurisdictional amount. Those assumptions left only the question whether Congress had given this original plaintiff a right of removal at all. Under Texas procedure the counterclaim could operate as an independent suit and produce an affirmative judgment against Shamrock.
sections.Issue: Does the statutory authorization in Judicial Code section 28 permitting removal by the defendant or defendants include an original plaintiff who must defend against an independent counterclaim asserted by the state-court defendant?
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court in 1941, in an opinion by Justice Stone with no dissent, concurrence, or nonparticipation recorded, answered no. For the ordinary diversity removal sought here, Shamrock remained the original plaintiff and could not acquire removal eligibility merely because the state defendant asserted a counterclaim against it. Congress's statutory language and its deliberate narrowing of the earlier removal law excluded that route. The holding rests on the removal statute then in force, Judicial Code section 28, and construes ordinary diversity removal; it does not declare that no statute could ever permit removal by a plaintiff.
sections.Reasoning:
First, federal law supplied the governing classification. Texas might call a counterclaim a separate suit and its target a defendant, but the federal removal statute operated nationwide and Congress intended its eligibility criteria to apply uniformly rather than vary with state procedural terminology.

Second, the statutory history showed a deliberate restriction. The Judiciary Act of 1789 allowed a defendant to remove, and West v. Aurora City held that an original plaintiff facing a counterclaim could not use that authorization because the plaintiff had voluntarily submitted to the state court. In 1875 Congress allowed either party to remove. In 1887 it changed the authorization back to the defendant or defendants and tied timing to the defendant's obligation to plead. The Court treated these coordinated changes as an intended return to the narrower rule, presuming Congress knew the earlier history. The House committee's explanation that a plaintiff should ordinarily abide by the forum it selected reinforced that inference. Had Congress intended to preserve removal for an original plaintiff confronted with a counterclaim, it could have said so.

Third, Shamrock's waiver argument confused possession of a right with loss of one. A party cannot acquire a statutory right merely by showing that it never waived one; Congress must first confer it, and the amount of the original demand was immaterial.

Finally, the Court tied this reading to Congress's policy of restricting removal jurisdiction: federal courts must respect the independence of state courts by keeping their jurisdiction within the limits Congress prescribed.

The casebook's introductory reference to a federal counterclaim conflicts with the opinion, which identifies an independent contract counterclaim and diversity removal, and its use of modern section 1441(a) is the textbook's later framework.

CP-ATLAS-SHOSHONE.rule: The mere fact that Congress authorized an action, such as an adverse suit to determine the right of possession of a mining claim, does not confer federal-question jurisdiction; jurisdiction requires a genuine federal question or another independent basis under the ordinary rules.

sections.Parties: Shoshone Mining Company and the Rutter side were competing claimants to mining property in proceedings connected with obtaining a federal mineral-land patent. Each side commenced an adverse suit under Revised Statutes sections 2325 and 2326 to establish the right of possession before the Land Department issued a patent: the Rutter side in federal court, and Shoshone in Idaho state court, which the Rutter side removed. Diverse citizenship did not exist.
sections.Procedural History: Two similar proceedings were consolidated for trial in the federal Circuit Court in Idaho and then taken to the Ninth Circuit. The Rutter side had commenced one action, numbered 81, in federal court. Shoshone had commenced the other in the Idaho state district court for Shoshone County, and the Rutter side removed it; the official report calls that second action No. 103 in its procedural description but No. 102 in its final mandate. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and directed a remand to the federal Circuit Court, Northern Division, District of Idaho, with instructions to reverse its decree, dismiss the action originally filed in federal court, and remand the removed action to state court.
sections.Material Facts:
The case concerned an adverse suit under Revised Statutes sections 2325 and 2326, through which competing claimants to mining property could establish the right of possession before the Land Department issued a patent. The Court's opinion concentrates on jurisdiction and does not supply a detailed chronology of discovery, location, or competing ownership claims. It expressly states that diverse citizenship did not exist, which made the alleged federal character of the adverse suit decisive.
