Transient jurisdiction ordinarily met the fairness standard because voluntary visitors have notice of the rule and enjoy real benefits from the forum's laws and services, while modern travel and communications reduce defense burdens and devices such as forum non conveniens can address exceptional inconvenience.

Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, finding the historical evidence, the continuing consensus, fairness and common sense collectively sufficient to affirm.

CPR-010.rule: Before a proceeding that is to be accorded finality, due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections.

sections.Parties: Central Hanover Bank and Trust Company, a New York trust company, was trustee of a common trust fund and the petitioner in the state accounting proceeding; it was an appellee in the Supreme Court. Mullane, the appellant, had been appointed by the Surrogate's Court as special guardian and attorney for all persons, known or unknown and not otherwise appearing, who had or might have an interest in the fund's income. Vaughan, also an appellee, represented those interested in the principal. The beneficiaries never appeared. The trust company sought a decree approving its account that would bind every beneficiary; Mullane sought to defeat it on the ground that the beneficiaries had not received constitutionally adequate notice.
sections.Procedural History: In March 1947 Central Hanover petitioned the Surrogate's Court, New York's court for estates and trusts, to settle its first account. Mullane appeared specially and objected that the statutory notice was inadequate under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, so that the Surrogate's Court lacked jurisdiction to enter a final and binding decree. The Surrogate overruled the objections and entered a final decree accepting the accounts. The Appellate Division affirmed, and the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, holding the notice constitutionally sufficient. The case reached the Supreme Court on appeal, the route then available when a state's highest court upheld a state statute against a federal constitutional challenge. The Court reversed the judgment of the New York Court of Appeals and remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with its opinion, while overruling the objections made on behalf of beneficiaries whose interests or addresses were unknown to the trustee.
sections.Material Facts:
New York Banking Law § 100-c allowed a trust company to pool the assets of many trusts into a single common fund for investment. Each participating trust shared ratably in income, gains, losses and expenses. The trustee had to account to the court twelve to fifteen months after establishing a fund and every three years after that, and a decree settling an account was binding and conclusive on everyone with an interest in the fund or in any participating trust.

Central Hanover established a common fund in January 1946. During the accounting period 113 trusts participated, with gross capital of nearly three million dollars. The beneficiaries were many, and some lived outside New York. The only notice of the accounting was the one § 100-c(12) required: publication in a local newspaper for four successive weeks, giving the trust company's name and address, the fund's name and date of establishment, and a list of the participating trusts. It named no beneficiary.

Earlier, when each trust first entered the fund, the trust company had mailed notice under § 100-c(9), enclosing the statutory provisions on notice and judicial settlement, to every beneficiary of full age and sound mind whose name and address were then known and who was entitled to share in income or, if the relevant event had already occurred, in principal. The decree would terminate every claim the beneficiaries might have against the trust company for improper management during the accounting period, and their interests also bore the guardians' fees and expenses.
sections.Issue: Did New York have power to bind beneficiaries who lived outside the state and were not personally served, when the decree adjudicated personal claims against the trustee rather than title to specific property? If so, was notice by newspaper publication constitutionally adequate for each category of beneficiary: those whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence, those whose interests were conjectural or future, and known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had on its books?
sections.Holding:
The U.S. Supreme Court, in 1950, in an opinion by Justice Jackson, with Justice Burton dissenting and Justice Douglas taking no part, held that the State's power to settle the account did not depend on whether the proceeding was labelled in rem, quasi in rem or in personam. New York's interest in closing trusts that exist by the grace of its laws and are administered under the supervision of its courts gave its courts the right to determine the interests of all claimants, resident or nonresident, provided the procedure gave them full opportunity to appear and be heard.

Publication was sufficient for beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts could not be ascertained with due diligence and for those whose interests were conjectural or future. It was insufficient for known present beneficiaries of known residence, who were entitled at least to notice by ordinary mail to the addresses in the trustee's records. Personal service was not required.
sections.Reasoning:
Mullane argued from Pennoyer that the decree was in personam and could not bind nonresidents served only by publication. The Court declined to decide by classification: the Fourteenth Amendment's requirements do not depend on a classification so elusive and so variable from state to state, and the State's interest in closing trusts created under its law justified adjudicating all beneficiaries' claims if they had full opportunity to be heard.

The question therefore became one of opportunity. A deprivation of property by adjudication must be preceded by notice and an opportunity for hearing appropriate to the nature of the case. The accounting could cut off the beneficiaries' claims against the trustee and diminish their interests through guardians' fees. Personal service is the classic form of notice but had never been held indispensable. The Court stated a functional standard, adding that "when notice is a person's due, process which is a mere gesture is not due process." The means must be those that a person who actually wanted to inform the absentee might reasonably use.

Publication alone is not a reliable means of informing known people, and this notice did not even name the beneficiaries. Publication is traditionally acceptable as a supplement to action likely to warn an owner, such as attachment of a chattel or entry upon real estate, but here the beneficiaries' caretaker, the trustee, had become their adversary. Publication remained acceptable where nothing better was reasonably possible, and due process did not require costly searches for conjectural or future beneficiaries. Where names and addresses are at hand, however, the reasons for less reliable means disappear; the mails were efficient and inexpensive. Because each beneficiary's interest was identical to that of the class, notice reasonably certain to reach most would safeguard all, so personal service was unnecessary.

Justice Burton dissented, regarding the question whether further notice should supplement what New York provided as within the State's discretion.

CPR-011.rule: Contracting parties may agree in advance to submit to a court's jurisdiction, and a person a contract designates to receive process is an agent authorized by appointment under the Federal Rule when she promptly accepts and transmits the process, even without an express promise to do so.

sections.Parties: National Equipment Rental, Ltd., a corporation with its principal place of business in New York, leased farm equipment to the respondents. It was the plaintiff in the district court and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The Szukhents, Michigan farmers who had leased the equipment, were the defendants and respondents. Florence Weinberg, the person the lease designated to receive process for them in New York, was not a party. The lessor sought to sue the Szukhents in New York for unpaid rent; the Szukhents sought to quash service on the ground that Weinberg was not their agent.
sections.Procedural History: In 1962 the petitioner sued in federal district court in New York, alleging that the Szukhents had failed to make the periodic payments the lease required. On the Szukhents' motion, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York quashed service. It reasoned that although Weinberg had promptly notified the Szukhents and sent them the papers, the lease did not explicitly require her to do so, so there was a "failure of the agency arrangement to achieve intrinsic and continuing reality." The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded, leaving the Szukhents subject to suit in the Eastern District of New York.
sections.Material Facts:
In 1961 the Szukhents leased farm equipment from the petitioner on a printed form less than a page and a half long, containing eighteen numbered paragraphs. The last paragraph, printed just above the respondents' signatures in the same type as the rest of the form, provided that the agreement would be deemed made in Nassau County, New York, and governed by New York law, and that the lessee designated Florence Weinberg, of 47-21 Forty-first Street, Long Island City, New York, as agent for the purpose of accepting service of any process within New York. The Szukhents did not know Weinberg. The dissent noted that she was chosen by the company, had never met the Szukhents, received nothing from them, undertook no obligation to them, and was revealed after the suit began to be the wife of one of the company's officers.

When the petitioner sued in 1962, a United States marshal delivered two copies of the summons and complaint to Weinberg. The same day she mailed them to the Szukhents with a letter stating that the documents had been served on her as their agent under the lease. The petitioner also notified the Szukhents by certified mail that process had been served on Weinberg.
sections.Issue: Was a person designated in a printed lease to receive process for the lessees, who was a stranger to them and whose appointment did not expressly require her to forward process, "an agent authorized by appointment" to receive service within Federal Rule 4(d)(1) (now Rule 4(e)(2)(C)), where she in fact promptly transmitted the summons and complaint to them?
sections.Holding: The U.S. Supreme Court, in 1964, in an opinion by Justice Stewart for a five-Justice majority, held that Weinberg was an agent authorized by appointment within the Rule and that service on her was valid. Parties to a contract may agree in advance to submit to the jurisdiction of a given court, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or even to waive notice altogether. Under general principles of agency law, an appointed agent's prompt acceptance of process and transmittal of it to the principal validates the agency even without an explicit promise to transmit. The Court limited its holding to a case in which prompt notice was actually given; a different case would be presented if Weinberg had not promptly notified the Szukhents.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court first set aside Wuchter v. Pizzutti, on which the Szukhents relied. That case concerned the limits the Fourteenth Amendment places on a state statute designating a public official to receive process for nonresidents; the question here was whether a party to a private contract may appoint an agent to receive service within the meaning of the Federal Rule.

The purpose of the clause was clear: to ensure that any litigation under the lease would take place in New York. It was settled that contracting parties may agree in advance to submit to a court's jurisdiction, to permit notice to be served by the opposing party, or to waive notice altogether. No question of subject-matter jurisdiction or venue was presented.

Applying general principles of agency law, the Court held that Weinberg's prompt acceptance of the papers and her transmittal of them, under the authority the lease conferred, was itself sufficient to validate the agency. The Rule is a uniform federal standard, and even assuming it should give way to contrary state policy, neither Michigan nor New York law required an express undertaking to notify the principal.

The Court rejected the argument that Weinberg had a conflict of interest. She was appointed for the single purpose of receiving service, and lessor and lessees had an equal interest in ensuring that the lessees received adequate and timely notice. The Court expressly did not reach a case in which the defendant received no personal notice.

Justice Black dissented. He would have held the appointment invalid under New York law or under a federal definition of agency, thought upholding service raised serious due process questions, and called the notion that the Szukhents knowingly consented to suit in New York "a fiction—not even an amiable one." Justice Brennan, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justice Goldberg, dissented on the ground that federal standards should bar agents with conflicting interests, require an explicit condition that the agent transmit process forthwith, and require proof beyond a signature of understanding consent.

CPR-012.rule: A judgment obtained by serving a defendant who was fraudulently induced to enter the state for service is void for want of personal jurisdiction and may be attacked collaterally when its enforcement is sought in another state.

sections.Parties: Wyman was the plaintiff. She had obtained a Florida state-court default judgment against Newhouse and sued on that judgment to enforce it; she was the appellant in the Second Circuit. Newhouse, a New York resident who had never lived in Florida, was the defendant. His answer asserted that Wyman had fraudulently induced him to enter Florida solely to serve him, and he sought dismissal of the enforcement complaint.
sections.Procedural History: Wyman obtained a Florida state-court default judgment against Newhouse after a jury assessed damages. The underlying claims sought recovery for money loaned, money advanced for Newhouse, and seduction under a promise of marriage. She then sued on that judgment. Newhouse's answer pleaded that she had fraudulently induced him to enter Florida solely to serve him. Wyman moved to strike that defense and for summary judgment under Rule 113 of the New York Rules of Civil Practice; for purposes of that motion the answer's alleged facts were taken as true, and the motion was denied. Both parties submitted affidavits. Newhouse then moved to dismiss the complaint, and that motion was granted before trial. Wyman appealed. The Second Circuit affirmed the judgment dismissing her complaint. The assigned caption also records that certiorari was denied.
sections.Material Facts:
The facts in Newhouse's affidavits were deemed true for reviewing the dismissal, and Wyman did not deny making the representations. The parties had known one another for years and maintained a sexual relationship outside marriage.

On October 25, 1935, while Newhouse was in Salt Lake City, Wyman sent a telegram asking him to visit on his return because of illness and her planned departure. After he returned to New York, she wrote that her mother was dying in Ireland, that she would leave the United States permanently, and that she needed to see him once more and discuss her affairs. She repeated this in a distressed telephone conversation, and he promised to visit Florida within a week or ten days. A further affectionate letter and exchanged telegrams arranged accommodations in Miami.

At six in the morning Newhouse arrived at the Miami airport and saw Wyman and her sister about seventy-five feet away. A deputy sheriff identified and served him in an action demanding $500,000, and a photographer attempted to take his picture. A stranger offered to take Newhouse to the stranger's home, saying he knew a lawyer acquainted with Wyman's attorney; that lawyer came there, appeared to know about the case, and invited Newhouse to his office, where one of Wyman's lawyers was waiting. Newhouse retained no Florida lawyer and returned to New York that evening. His New York counsel advised him to ignore the Florida summons; he did so and defaulted. Wyman never made the claimed trip to Ireland.
sections.Issue: Could Wyman enforce the Florida default judgment despite fraud that manufactured Newhouse's presence in the jurisdiction for service? Did Newhouse have to challenge the judgment or defend the underlying claim in Florida before resisting enforcement elsewhere?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 1937, in an opinion by Judge Manton for a panel with Judges Learned Hand and Swan and with no separate opinion, held that this fraud affected jurisdiction over Newhouse's person. A judgment procured through that jurisdictional fraud was void and could be challenged collaterally in the enforcement action. Newhouse's equitable defense was sufficient; he did not have to seek relief in Florida or establish a defense to the merits of the original action. The judgment dismissing Wyman's complaint was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court concluded that the circumstances and reasonable inferences convincingly established a fraudulent inducement to enter Florida for service. The professed affection conflicted with the airport arrangements, Wyman never went to Ireland, and the court questioned whether her mother had been ill at all. Its conclusion concerned the scheme to procure Newhouse's presence, not the underlying loan or seduction claims.

Wyman relied on Article IV, § 1 and its then-applicable implementing statute, which required authenticated judicial proceedings to receive the faith and credit they had in the rendering state. The court therefore first asked how Florida would treat the judgment and believed the fraudulent service would have been vacated there. Because neither a Florida statute governing such service nor a controlling Florida decision had been supplied, the court applied the forum's law, under which the service would be set aside as fraudulent.

The defect concerned the acquisition of jurisdiction rather than an irregularity after jurisdiction existed. Fraud inducing entry into the state for service was treated as equivalent to lack of personal jurisdiction. The court relied on authorities allowing a defendant to raise that jurisdictional fraud when the judgment was offered for enforcement in another state; it acknowledged contrary authority but considered the weight of authority opposed to enforcement.

Jaster v. Currie did not help Wyman because it had found no fraudulent inducement into the jurisdiction, and other cited cases concerned procedural irregularities that did not void a judgment. Rules requiring a merits defense when fraud is alleged after valid personal and subject-matter jurisdiction has attached did not apply, because the Florida court had not duly acquired jurisdiction over Newhouse.

The casebook's following note asks about a defendant already in the state who is tricked out of hiding; those are editorial questions that Wyman does not decide.

CPR-013.rule: A prejudgment attachment procedure is tested under a modified Mathews v. Eldridge balance weighing the private interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation and value of added safeguards, and principally the interest of the party seeking the remedy, with any ancillary government interest.

sections.Parties: John F. DiGiovanni, who planned to sue Brian K. Doehr for assault and battery, obtained a prejudgment attachment on Doehr's home. Doehr, the homeowner, was the plaintiff in the federal suit and the respondent in the Supreme Court; he sought a declaration that Connecticut's attachment statute violated due process. The State of Connecticut intervened in the Court of Appeals, at that court's invitation, to defend the constitutionality of its statute. Connecticut and DiGiovanni were the petitioners and defended the statute.
sections.Procedural History: Instead of seeking the post-attachment hearing the statute offered, Doehr sued DiGiovanni in federal district court, claiming that the statute violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court upheld the statute and granted summary judgment to DiGiovanni. A divided panel of the Second Circuit reversed in an opinion by Judge Pratt. It held that a prior hearing may be postponed only where exceptional circumstances justify the delay and sufficient additional safeguards are present, and it emphasised that an assault claim turned on disputed facts a judge could not reliably assess on the plaintiff's version alone. Judge Pratt concluded, in his own view, that the lack of a bond was an independent defect. Connecticut intervened after oral argument there, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
On March 15, 1988, DiGiovanni applied to the Connecticut Superior Court for an attachment of $75,000 on Doehr's home in Meriden, Connecticut, in connection with a civil action for assault and battery he was bringing against Doehr in the same court. The suit did not involve Doehr's real estate, and DiGiovanni had no pre-existing interest in the home or in any of Doehr's other property.

Connecticut law allowed a judge to authorize prejudgment attachment of real property without a hearing, on verification by oath that there was probable cause to sustain the validity of the plaintiff's claim. The statute did not require the plaintiff to post a bond. DiGiovanni's affidavit, in five one-sentence paragraphs, stated that the facts in his complaint were true, that Doehr had willfully, wantonly and maliciously assaulted him, that the assault broke his left wrist and bruised his right eye among other injuries, that he had incurred medical expenses, and that in his opinion these facts showed probable cause that judgment would be rendered for him.

On March 17 a Superior Court judge found probable cause and ordered the attachment. The sheriff attached the property four days later. Only then did Doehr receive notice, and he had not yet been served with the complaint. The notice told him he could seek a hearing to argue that there was no probable cause, to ask that the attachment be vacated or modified or a bond substituted, or to claim an exemption.
sections.Issue: Does a state statute that authorizes prejudgment attachment of real estate without prior notice or hearing, without a showing of extraordinary circumstances, and without requiring the plaintiff to post a bond satisfy the Due Process Clause when invoked by a tort plaintiff who has no pre-existing interest in the property? Must due process also require a bond?
sections.Holding:
The U.S. Supreme Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Justice White with a unanimous judgment, held that the Connecticut statute violated due process as applied. The adequacy of a prejudgment attachment procedure is judged by a modified version of the Mathews v. Eldridge test. Here the homeowner's interest was significant, the risk of error was substantial, and the plaintiff's interest in an ex parte attachment was minimal because he had no pre-existing interest in the property and did not allege that Doehr was about to transfer or encumber it.

A four-Justice plurality would further have held that due process requires the plaintiff to post a bond or other security in addition to a hearing or a showing of exigency, and that a bond does not excuse the need for a hearing. That part commanded only four votes and is not a holding of the Court.
sections.Reasoning:
The Court placed the case in the line from Sniadach through Fuentes, Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing. Because prejudgment remedies ordinarily arise between private parties, it adjusted the third Mathews factor to focus principally on the interest of the party seeking the remedy rather than on the government's.

The private interest was significant. Attachment clouds title, impairs the ability to sell, taints the owner's credit rating, reduces the chance of a home equity loan or additional mortgage, and can place an existing mortgage in technical default. Due process protection is not limited to complete, physical or permanent deprivations.

The risk of erroneous deprivation was substantial. The meaning of the probable-cause standard was obscure, and under any reading offered the risk was too great: the judge received only a skeletal, one-sided affidavit, and an assault case does not lend itself to documentary proof as a debt does. The post-attachment hearing, judicial review and double-damages action did not adequately reduce the risk; unlike in Mitchell, there was no vendor's lien, no documentary dispute and no bond, and a later hearing could not cure the temporary deprivation.

The interests favouring ex parte attachment were slight. DiGiovanni's only interest was ensuring assets to satisfy a judgment, and he alleged no exigency; a properly supported allegation of one would permit postponing the hearing. History and the practice of nearly every state supported the result.

In Part IV the plurality reasoned that without a bond the risk of wrongful deprivation remains unacceptably high, and that a bond cannot fully undo the harms of an erroneous attachment.

Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justice Blackmun, concurred in part and in the judgment, noting that the holding broke new ground because earlier cases involved seizure of personal property, distinguishing mechanics' liens and lis pendens, and declining to decide hypothetical questions about bonds. Justice Scalia concurred in part and in the judgment, agreeing that the procedure, not recognized at common law, failed Mathews.

CPR-014.rule: Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns a court's competence to entertain the category of action, not the plaintiff's ability to establish the substantive conditions for relief, so an error about a statutory element of the claim does not render the judgment void.

sections.Parties: Harold G. Lacks, the husband, was the plaintiff in the matrimonial action and sought to preserve his final divorce judgment. Irene R. Lacks, the wife, was the defendant in that action, later the movant seeking to vacate the judgment, and the appellant before the Court of Appeals. She sought to reopen the completed litigation on the theory that the divorce judgment was jurisdictionally void.
sections.Procedural History:
The husband commenced the action on August 10, 1965. After a nonjury trial, the Supreme Court dismissed the separation complaint on June 28, 1967. The Appellate Division reversed on March 26, 1968, and ordered a new trial, which resulted in a divorce judgment on March 16, 1970. The Appellate Division affirmed that judgment, with modifications irrelevant here, on October 26, 1972, and both the Appellate Division and the Court of Appeals denied permission for a further appeal.

Almost two years after the appellate process ended, the wife moved under CPLR 5015(a)(4) to vacate the final judgment for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Special Term granted the motion in 1975. The Appellate Division modified that order by denying the motion and reinstating the divorce judgment. The wife appealed that postjudgment order to the Court of Appeals, which affirmed the Appellate Division without costs, leaving the divorce judgment in place.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties married in New York in 1938. Their marital dispute produced repeated litigation beginning in 1953. On August 10, 1965, the husband commenced the action at issue, seeking a separation on the ground of cruelty. While that action was pending, New York liberalized its divorce law. At the second trial the husband added a request for an absolute divorce, relying on the same allegations and proof that had supported his request for separation.

The wife's later jurisdictional theory rested on Domestic Relations Law § 230. She asserted that the husband had not resided in New York for a full year before the original action began and that the failure to satisfy that statutory requirement deprived the court of power to grant a divorce.

The asserted defect remained only an assertion. The Court of Appeals expressly declined to assume that the earlier courts had made a legal or factual error about residence. It noted considerable evidence of the husband's residence and the possibility that the residence questions had already been considered and determined. Its point was that even an erroneous determination of the statutory requirement would not make the judgment void for lack of subject-matter competence.
sections.Issue: Does an alleged failure to satisfy the durational residence requirements of Domestic Relations Law § 230 deprive New York's Supreme Court of subject-matter jurisdiction over a divorce action, so that a final divorce judgment may be vacated under CPLR 5015(a)(4) after ordinary appellate review has ended? Or is the residence requirement an element of the right to obtain a divorce that the competent trial court may determine correctly or incorrectly?
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, in 1976, in an opinion by Chief Judge Breitel in which Judges Jasen, Gabrielli, Jones, Wachtler, Fuchsberg and Cooke concurred, held that the wife could not reopen the final divorce judgment on the jurisdictional theory she advanced. Section 230's residence requirements regulate the divorce cause of action; they do not withdraw the Supreme Court's competence to adjudicate matrimonial causes. An error concerning those requirements therefore does not make the judgment void under CPLR 5015(a)(4). The court did not hold that residence requirements are optional, that every statutory requirement is nonjurisdictional, or that consent supplies subject-matter power. It held that this particular condition was substantive rather than a restriction on the court's adjudicative competence.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began by explaining that judicial opinions use the word jurisdiction to describe very different limitations: absence of a cause of action, inability to grant a particular remedy, or a fundamental absence of adjudicative competence. CPLR 5015(a)(4) addresses only the fundamental kind, and calling the residence condition jurisdictional does not put it in that category.

Precision matters because of the consequences. If an ordinary error in deciding a claim were treated as a defect in subject-matter competence, the losing party could try to reopen a final judgment after the normal avenues of review had closed. Because jurisdictional defects are usually described as nonwaivable and as rendering judgments void, an overly expansive definition would be especially disruptive.

New York's Supreme Court is a court of general original jurisdiction. The wife relied on statements that matrimonial relief is statutory, but the absence of an entitlement to relief under a statute does not necessarily establish the absence of jurisdiction over actions invoking it. A competent court can decide that a claimant has failed to prove a required fact, and it does not lose its competence by deciding that question incorrectly.

Section 230 provided that an action for divorce or separation could be maintained only when specified residence conditions were met. It did not say that the Supreme Court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction when they were not. Read against the constitutional grant of general jurisdiction, it supplied substantive restrictions on obtaining relief.

The wife's interpretation would make competence depend on the court's reaching the correct answer to an element of the claim, turning every failure of proof into a potential failure of power. Ordinary legal and factual mistakes must be corrected through the procedures for correcting them. Treating substantive elements as perpetual jurisdictional objections would undermine res judicata and the certainty of final judgments. The court also stated that the federal constitutional connections needed to make the divorce secure against attack in other states were satisfied.

CPR-015.rule: For diversity purposes a natural person is a citizen of a state only if a United States citizen domiciled there; domicile persists until the person takes up residence elsewhere intending to remain, and citizenship is determined when the complaint is filed.

sections.Parties: Jean Paul Mas, a citizen of France, and Judy Mas, an American whose established domicile was Mississippi, were the plaintiffs and appellees. Oliver H. Perry, their landlord and a Louisiana citizen, was the defendant and appellant. The Mases sought damages for Perry's observation of them through concealed two-way mirrors. On appeal Perry challenged the federal court's subject-matter jurisdiction rather than the substantive basis of the verdict.
sections.Procedural History: The Mases sued in federal district court and tried the case to a jury. Immediately before their last witness testified, Perry made an oral motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, which by stipulation approved by the court was treated as made at the close of their case. The district court denied the motion. The jury awarded $5,000 to Jean Paul and $15,000 to Judy, and final judgment was entered. Perry appealed solely on jurisdictional grounds, arguing that complete diversity had not been established and that Jean Paul's claim failed the required amount in controversy. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, and certiorari was denied. The casebook excerpt omits the court's discussion of the amount in controversy, which the complete opinion contains.
sections.Material Facts:
Before their marriage, Jean Paul and Judy were graduate assistants at Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge, Jean Paul for approximately nine months and Judy for approximately one year. They married at her home in Jackson, Mississippi, then returned to Baton Rouge to resume their graduate-assistant work and remained there approximately two more years.

After returning to Baton Rouge they rented an apartment from Perry. They discovered two-way mirrors in the bedroom and bathroom. Perry had watched them through the mirrors during three of the first four months of their marriage. The complaint was filed within several days of the discovery, well before the move to Illinois. Both spouses initially claimed $100,000, and the statutory threshold was then more than $10,000.

The Mases later moved to Park Ridge, Illinois. At trial they intended to return to Baton Rouge while Jean Paul completed his doctorate but had not decided where they would live afterward. Judy testified that she did not intend to return to her parents' Mississippi home after marrying. The court found that she had not established a new domicile in Louisiana, because she and Jean Paul were there as students and lacked the intention to remain.
sections.Issue: Was Judy Mas a Louisiana citizen for diversity purposes because she lived and studied there, or had her Mississippi domicile continued? Did marriage to a French citizen automatically change her domicile or citizenship? With Jean Paul a French citizen and Perry a Louisiana citizen, were § 1332's citizenship requirements met when the complaint was filed? The complete opinion also asks whether Jean Paul's recovery below the then-applicable statutory minimum defeated jurisdiction.
sections.Holding:
The United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, in 1974, in an opinion by Judge Ainsworth for a panel with Judges Wisdom and Clark and with no separate opinion, upheld jurisdiction over both claims. Judy remained a Mississippi citizen: her presence in Louisiana as a graduate student, without the necessary intention to remain, did not change her domicile, and neither did marriage to an alien. Her claim against the Louisiana defendant qualified under § 1332(a)(1), and Jean Paul's claim qualified under § 1332(a)(2).

In the part of the opinion the casebook omits, the court also held that the amount claimed in good faith controls unless the claim is legally certain to fall below the jurisdictional amount, so the $5,000 verdict for Jean Paul did not eliminate jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning:
The court analysed the two plaintiffs separately. Jean Paul's French citizenship gave his dispute with a Louisiana defendant an alienage basis. Judy was an American, so her state citizenship had to be determined under the domicile rule: a person must be a United States citizen and domiciled in the state, and domicile, not mere residence, controls. The party invoking jurisdiction bears the burden of pleading it and, when properly challenged, proving it.

Changing domicile requires taking up residence in a new place and intending to remain there; until then the old domicile persists. Judy had lived and worked in Louisiana for substantial periods, which established residence but not, on this record, the intent needed to replace her Mississippi domicile. Her lack of intention to return to her parents' home did not itself establish a new domicile elsewhere.

The court acknowledged the then-used generalization that a wife's domicile followed her husband's but refused to extend that fiction here. Treating Judy as domiciled in France would not make her an alien and could leave her outside the state-citizen category despite her United States citizenship; treating her as domiciled in Louisiana would destroy diversity. An American woman did not lose United States citizenship by marrying an alien, and her state citizenship likewise did not change automatically.

Diversity is determined under federal law at the time of filing, and later changes in citizenship do not destroy it. The later move to Illinois therefore could not change jurisdiction, though it remained relevant as evidence that the couple lacked intent to stay permanently in Louisiana.

On the amount objection, what mattered was the amount genuinely at stake when suit began under the good-faith and legal-certainty standard; a lower verdict did not show the original claim was insufficient. The court closed by observing that the spouses' claims arose from the same operative facts with overlapping proof, making joint adjudication sensible, but it had already found a separate citizenship basis for each.

CPR-016.rule: The amount a plaintiff claims in apparent good faith controls unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less than the jurisdictional amount, and the court must give the plaintiff a reasonable opportunity to show otherwise before dismissing.

sections.Parties: A.F.A. Tours, Inc., doing business as Alumni Flights Abroad, was the plaintiff and appellant. It operated a travel business specializing in deluxe overseas tours. Desmond Whitchurch, its former tour escort who began offering competing services, was the defendant and appellee. AFA sought damages and an injunction for alleged misappropriation of confidential business information. The assigned excerpt does not specify the parties' citizenships; the jurisdictional dispute concerns the amount in controversy.
sections.Procedural History: AFA filed the diversity action in the Southern District of New York. Whitchurch moved for summary judgment on whether the information qualified as confidential trade secrets. At oral argument on that motion, the district judge raised the amount in controversy on the court's own initiative. At the conclusion of the same hearing, the judge granted summary judgment and dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, reasoning that AFA could not prove damages exceeding $50,000. AFA appealed, arguing that it had not received a reasonable opportunity to make a jurisdictional showing and that the district court had valued the damages claim and the requested injunction incorrectly. The Second Circuit vacated the judgment and remanded for further proceedings. In the complete opinion it also rejected the proposed alternative basis for affirmance on the trade-secret merits, because material factual disputes remained.
sections.Material Facts:
AFA arranged deluxe tours for United States residents to destinations including Australia, New Zealand and New Guinea. It alleged that it had invested substantial money, time and labor in developing customer lists, marketing information and tour information that it regarded as confidential trade secrets. Whitchurch served as its exclusive tour escort in those regions from 1972 through 1989 and had access to some of that information.

AFA alleged that Whitchurch resigned around October 1989, misappropriated the confidential information, created a competing tour business, and solicited or intended to solicit AFA's customers. It requested an injunction against any use of the information, compensatory damages not yet ascertainable but believed to exceed $50,000, and punitive damages of at least $250,000. These were allegations, not findings.

At the hearing, Whitchurch's lawyer reported that Whitchurch had mailed solicitations to between 100 and 200 former AFA participants and obtained favorable responses from only two. AFA's lawyer argued that this did not measure the whole threatened loss: Whitchurch had escorted about 1,500 AFA customers over the years and intended to organize further tours. The record indicated approximately seven tours per year over seventeen years, usually with ten to fifteen participants. AFA's lawyer also relied on the high tour prices, and the court of appeals accepted that a participant might pay about $10,000. The jurisdictional threshold at the time was more than $50,000.
sections.Issue: May a district court dismiss a diversity action for failing the amount-in-controversy requirement when it first raises the issue at a hearing on a different ground and does not give the plaintiff a reasonable opportunity to submit supporting evidence? In evaluating the amount, may the court consider only losses already realized, or must it also consider legally available punitive damages and the value of preventing future harm through the requested injunction?
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Kearse with no separate opinion, held that the district court's immediate dismissal and narrow valuation were erroneous on this record. Under the St. Paul Mercury standard, the amount the plaintiff claims controls if apparently asserted in good faith, unless it appears to a legal certainty that the claim is for less than the jurisdictional amount, and the court must give the plaintiff an appropriate and reasonable opportunity to show a good-faith basis for believing that recovery above the threshold is reasonably possible. In a trade-secret action, damages may be measured by the plaintiff's losses or the defendant's unjustly obtained profits, legally available punitive damages can count, and an injunction is valued by the right being protected and the impairment it would prevent. The court did not decide that AFA had established liability or proved a particular jurisdictional value.
sections.Reasoning:
A court may raise a jurisdictional question itself, but the plaintiff must have an opportunity to answer it. AFA had prepared for a motion about the confidentiality of its information, not an evidentiary dispute over jurisdictional value, so the lack of a developed valuation record could not fairly be held against it.

The standard was legal certainty, not a prediction of the most likely verdict. That AFA had not yet shown actual losses approaching $50,000 did not establish that the full value of the legally available relief necessarily fell below the threshold. A good-faith allegation did not, however, remove the plaintiff's obligation to substantiate jurisdiction when the issue was properly presented.

The record already suggested a larger possible customer base. Whitchurch's years of escorting, the number of trips and the typical group size supported the estimate of roughly 1,500 customers, the first solicitation's two favorable responses could not conclusively establish the results of every future solicitation, and AFA's evidence indicated repeat customers.

The court separated gross receipts from profits. A $10,000 tour price did not mean $10,000 in profit. As a conditional illustration, if the operator earned seventeen percent of a $10,000 trip and thirty former AFA customers, two percent of 1,500, were diverted, the resulting profit would be $51,000. Neither the margin nor the diversion was found as fact; the illustration showed why the record did not establish a legally certain ceiling below $50,000.

The injunction sought protection against any use of the information, including possible sale or disclosure to other operators better able to exploit it, so it could not be valued solely by the small loss already realized. Controlling New York law apparently permitted punitive damages for sufficiently gross and wanton conduct in a trade-secret case, and the record did not foreclose them.

On the merits, drawing reasonable inferences for AFA as the party opposing summary judgment, the court found genuine factual disputes about confidentiality.

CT-ATLAS-KLAR.rule: A bailee for hire relying on a liability limitation printed on a claim check must show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent; accepting a ticket issued to identify property does not establish that assent as a matter of law.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs sued over a lost package of valuable furs; Ellis acted for them in checking it, and Sidney R. Klar later presented the claim check. The defendant, H. & M. Parcel Room, Inc., operated a parcel room on the concourse of the Hudson & Manhattan Railroad's 33rd Street station in New York City. The plaintiffs wanted $1,000, the alleged value of the package. The parcel room, with ordinary negligence conceded, wanted its responsibility reduced to $25 under the terms printed on the check. The plaintiffs were the appellants in the Appellate Division.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in Municipal Court for $1,000. After a trial without a jury they obtained a judgment of $939.50. The Appellate Term reduced the recovery to $25 because it regarded the printed limitation as sufficiently communicated to form a contract. The plaintiffs then appealed by permission to the Appellate Division, First Department. On April 5, 1946, by a vote of three to two, that court reversed the Appellate Term's determination and affirmed the Municipal Court's $939.50 judgment, awarding the plaintiffs costs in both appellate courts. The Court of Appeals later affirmed with costs and without opinion, so it supplied no further written rationale.
sections.Material Facts:
Ellis, acting for the plaintiffs, deposited a brown-paper package containing valuable furs at the parcel room and received claim check 34-971. The cardboard check measured three inches by two and a half inches. Its identifying number appeared prominently in red, and the word CONTRACT also appeared in red near the top. Beneath that word, finer print stated that acceptance bound both parties, that checking cost ten cents per twenty-four hours or fraction, and that no claim exceeding $25 could be made for loss or damage to any piece. The limitation was on the face of the check, not hidden on its reverse.

Ellis testified that he neither read the check nor was asked to read it, and thought it was simply a receipt. No evidence showed any further notice or explanation of the limitation. When Sidney R. Klar presented the check two days later, an employee admitted that the parcel had mistakenly been delivered to someone presenting a differently numbered receipt. Ordinary negligence was conceded.
sections.Issue: Whether a limitation of liability to $25, printed on the face of a parcel-room claim check that the bailor accepted without reading, had become part of the parties' agreement, and in particular whether acceptance of the check established assent to the limitation as a matter of law.
sections.Holding: The New York Appellate Division, First Department, in 1946, in an opinion by Justice Cohn joined by Justices Townley and Glennon, with two justices dissenting, held that printing the limitation on the face of the ticket, followed by its acceptance, did not compel a finding of agreement as a matter of law. Whether acceptance of this check constituted assent was a question for the trial judge, and the finding that no such agreement existed had ample evidentiary support. The Appellate Term erred by treating acceptance as establishing the limitation. The majority did not hold that every unsigned ticket is unenforceable, that failure to read always excuses assent, or that every liability limitation is contrary to public policy.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority accepted that a bailee for hire owes ordinary care and, absent an effective special agreement, answers for the reasonable value of property lost through negligence. It also accepted that parties may contract to reduce that obligation within the limits of law and public policy. To establish the limitation, however, the bailee had to show reasonable notice of its terms and the bailor's assent. A ticket issued as a means of identifying property does not necessarily communicate that it also changes substantive rights. The record contained no conspicuous signs, placards, other notice of special terms, or evidence that the plaintiffs were given an opportunity to assent or dissent. Relying on Madan and Healy, the majority said an omission to read a parcel receipt is not invariably negligence or assent. Healy involved fine print on the reverse of a check, but its reasoning applied: the customer could reasonably regard the paper as identification rather than an agreement limiting recovery.

Justice Dore, joined by Presiding Justice Martin, dissented and would have affirmed the $25 recovery. He viewed the conspicuous word CONTRACT, the brief text beneath it, the time available to read and the ten-cent charge as adequate notice of a reasonable limitation, and treated the failure to read as inexcusable. He also questioned the credibility of the account of how the furs came to the parcel room.

The assigned reading is a casebook account rather than a reproduced opinion. Its comparison with Restatement section 211(3) is the casebook's editorial point, not a rule announced by this court.

CT-ATLAS-TOLOSA.rule: Under Texas law, a loan agreement over $50,000, including a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, must be in a signed writing, and promissory estoppel avoids that requirement only if the promisor promised to sign a complying written document.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs were borrowers who had obtained a loan to buy property in Sugar Land, Texas, and who sued after a completed foreclosure sale in order to delay eviction. The defendant was HSBC Bank USA, N.A. The plaintiffs wanted an injunction and relief on several claims, including promissory estoppel based on an alleged promise not to foreclose while a loan modification was under review. The defendant wanted the suit dismissed, arguing among other things that the statute of frauds barred all the claims.
sections.Procedural History:
In September 2011 the plaintiffs filed suit in state court. They said the state court issued a temporary restraining order before removal. The defendant removed the suit to federal court on diversity grounds and moved to dismiss. The federal district court, Judge Nancy F. Atlas, granted the motion to dismiss and dismissed the case; the reproduced order does not state whether the dismissal was with or without prejudice.

This account covers only the abridged text printed in the casebook. The excerpt jumps from section I to section III.B, and the complete opinion has not been recovered, so the court's other grounds for dismissal and its treatment of the restraining-order argument cannot be given.
sections.Material Facts:
The plaintiffs obtained a $276,000 loan to buy property in Sugar Land, Texas. A promissory note evidenced the debt and a deed of trust secured it. They defaulted on their payment obligations, and the property was sold at a foreclosure sale in April 2011. In September 2011 they sued to delay eviction following the completed foreclosure; the action followed the sale and did not prevent it.

Besides an injunction, they sought relief for fraud, wrongful foreclosure due to fraud, slander of title, promissory estoppel, unreasonable collection, and an accounting. Their relevant allegation was that the defendant had promised not to foreclose while reviewing a loan modification. That promise is an allegation recorded by the court, not a finding that the bank made it. The excerpt does not give the promise's wording, speaker or date, or a detailed account of reliance. The plaintiffs did not allege that the defendant promised to sign a written agreement embodying the postponement.
sections.Issue: Whether an alleged oral agreement to delay foreclosure on a $276,000 loan could be enforced notwithstanding the writing requirement of section 26.02(b) of the Texas Business and Commerce Code, and whether promissory estoppel supplied a route around that requirement.
sections.Holding: The United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, in 2011, Judge Nancy F. Atlas, held in the reproduced portion of its opinion that the alleged foreclosure delay was a financial accommodation covered by the statute of frauds and could not be enforced on the pleaded basis because it lacked the required statutory form. The promissory-estoppel theory failed because the plaintiffs had not alleged a promise to sign a written agreement that would satisfy the statute. The defendant was therefore entitled to dismissal of the promissory-estoppel claim. The court granted the motion to dismiss and dismissed the case.
sections.Reasoning:
Section 26.02(b) required a loan agreement involving more than $50,000 to be in writing and signed by the party to be bound or its authorized representative. The $276,000 loan exceeded that threshold. The statutory definition of a loan agreement included a financial institution's promise to delay repayment or make a financial accommodation, so the court did not treat the alleged postponement as a separate undertaking outside the statute merely because it concerned the timing of foreclosure.

The court then stated a further requirement for promissory estoppel in this setting: the promisor must have promised to sign a written document that would satisfy the statute of frauds. It applied that requirement both to estoppel as an affirmative claim and to estoppel used to oppose the statute-of-frauds defense, citing Burnette v. Wells Fargo Bank and Ford v. City State Bank of Palacios. Alleging the underlying oral accommodation did not itself allege that additional promise.

The ruling concerns enforceability and pleading on a motion to dismiss. It is not a finding that the promise was never made, and it does not establish that a bank may always disregard a loan-modification agreement or that every foreclosure-related tort claim fails.

The casebook editors, not the court, go on to ask whether an accurately remembered oral promise ought to be enforceable, to distinguish estoppel as a source of obligation from estoppel as a way to enforce an otherwise unenforceable agreement, and to discuss the statute's notice provisions. Because only the excerpt was available, the reasoning on the other claims cannot be supplied.

CT-CB-0002.rule: When a physician guarantees a specified result, damages for breach are the difference between the value of the promised condition and the value of the actual condition, plus incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation, and not the pain ordinarily incident to the agreed operation.

sections.Parties: Hawkins was the patient, who sought contractual compensation for a surgeon's allegedly guaranteed result. McGee was the defendant physician. Hawkins's theory depended on proving an undertaking to produce a specified condition of his hand. McGee disputed whether his words could create that obligation and challenged the jury instructions governing both contract formation and damages.
sections.Procedural History: The formation question was submitted to a jury. On damages, the trial judge instructed the jury to consider the patient's operative pain and suffering and injury beyond the preexisting condition, and McGee objected. The trial court later set aside the verdict under its own assessment of damages, regarding an award exceeding $500 as excessive. McGee had also requested instructions that would have required an identical subjective understanding by physician and patient and barred liability unless a further operation could not correct the condition. The Supreme Court of New Hampshire, deciding the case on June 4, 1929, rejected the damages instruction and ordered a new trial.
sections.Material Facts:
An electric-wire burn about nine years before the treatment had left scar tissue on the palm of Hawkins's right hand. McGee operated by removing a substantial quantity of scar tissue and grafting skin from Hawkins's chest.

The evidence included two kinds of statements. Asked about hospitalization, McGee predicted three or four days in the hospital and a return to work a few days later. Separately, witnesses attributed to him a guarantee of a completely good or perfect hand, made before the decision to operate and in Hawkins's presence; this alleged guarantee was the substantial basis of the contract claim.

There was evidence that McGee had repeatedly solicited the opportunity to perform the operation, and Hawkins's counsel suggested in cross-examination that McGee wanted experience in skin grafting. The court treated that as a theory the jury could accept, not as an established fact. The evidence also permitted the conclusion that Hawkins and his father took the alleged guarantee seriously. There was evidence that McGee had refused to perform another operation.
sections.Issue: Whether the evidence of the physician's words and surrounding conduct could support a finding that he undertook a contractual obligation to achieve a specified result; and, if so, whether damages should restore the patient's preoperative position, reimburse the burden of undergoing treatment, or compensate for the difference between the promised result and the actual result.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of New Hampshire, in 1929, in an opinion by Justice Branch in which the participating judges concurred, Justice Marble not sitting, held that the alleged guarantee could create a contractual undertaking and that the evidence justified submitting that question to the jury, while the estimates of hospitalization and recovery time were predictions rather than promises on this record. If a good or perfect hand was promised, the measure of damages is the difference between the value to the patient of the promised hand and the value of the actual hand, together with incidental consequences within the parties' contemplation. Pain necessarily incident to the agreed operation is not a separate item. The court ordered a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first separated statements that could reasonably bear a promissory meaning from ordinary medical forecasts. Whether language is capable of the asserted contractual meaning is initially a question of law for the judge; once that threshold is met, the jury decides whether the words were spoken and what the circumstances establish. The alleged explicit guarantee cleared the threshold and the recovery predictions did not. McGee argued that, given the uncertainty of surgery, no reasonable person would take a guarantee literally. The court did not decide whether that argument would be conclusive in every case; here the alleged solicitation and possible wish for experience, if the jury accepted them, made a result warranty plausible.

On damages, the promised improvement defines the protected interest. A comparison of the hand before and after the operation would miss the loss where an operation fails to improve the hand without making it worse, and where the hand is worsened the promised-versus-actual measure already captures the deterioration, so adding it again would count harm twice. The court drew an analogy to a machine warranted to perform a specified function. Ordinary pain of the operation would have been suffered even with the promised result and was part of what the patient agreed to bear.

The rejected instructions were wrong. Assent is judged by an external standard, so an undisclosed mental reservation does not undo an objectively manifested guarantee. The corrective-surgery request was inconsistent with evidence that McGee had refused another operation. The court did not decide whether the evidence otherwise supported the $500 assessment. There was no separate opinion.

CT-CB-0004.rule: A seller's statement creates an express warranty only if it is an affirmation, promise or description relating to the goods actually sold that forms part of the basis of the bargain; statements about differently configured goods and general commendation do not.

sections.Parties: John R. Crow bought a sport-fishing boat and was the prevailing plaintiff at trial. Bayliner Marine Corporation manufactured the boat and appealed the warranty judgment against it. Tidewater Yacht Agency was the authorized local dealer; Crow nonsuited his claim against it before trial. Brunswick, the diesel-engine manufacturer, had also been sued, but the final trial order dismissed the negligence claim against it. Bayliner challenged both liability and damages.
sections.Procedural History: After a bench trial, the circuit court found that Bayliner had breached an express warranty, the implied warranty of merchantability, and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. It awarded $135,000 plus prejudgment interest, consisting of the $120,000 purchase price and approximately $15,000 toward the claimed costs of storing, maintaining, insuring and financing the boat. Bayliner appealed. The Supreme Court of Virginia, deciding the case on January 8, 1999, viewed the evidence in the light most favorable to Crow, held it insufficient to support any of the three warranty findings, reversed, and entered final judgment for Bayliner without a remand. It did not reach the damages assignments.
sections.Material Facts:
In the summer of 1989 Crow took a short ride on a Bayliner 3486 Trophy Convertible offered through Tidewater and asked the dealer's representative, John Atherton, about maximum speed. Atherton could not answer from his own experience, so he gave Crow two manufacturer 'prop matrixes' from the dealer's manual. The thirty-mile-per-hour figures in them concerned boats with propellers different from the 20-by-17 propeller on Crow's boat, and the data specified testing with approximately 600 pounds of passengers and gear. Atherton also showed a sales brochure promoting the model's performance for reaching offshore fishing grounds.

Crow bought the boat for $120,000 before taxes, with about 2,000 pounds of added equipment, and did not test it again before delivery. On delivery in September 1989 its maximum speed was thirteen miles per hour; after repeated repairs it generally reached seventeen, and briefly about twenty-four. In July 1990 Bayliner wrote that the performance representations at purchase had been incorrect and that twenty-three to twenty-five miles per hour was the boat's maximum capability. Crow testified that he would not have bought it even at that speed. The boat logged approximately 850 engine hours over five years, and Crow had used it for offshore fishing in the first years.
sections.Issue: Whether the numerical matrices or the brochure's general language created a thirty-mile-per-hour express warranty for Crow's boat; whether failure to reach that speed established unmerchantability in the trade or unfitness for the boat's ordinary purpose; and whether the seller knew of Crow's particular thirty-mile-per-hour requirement so as to support an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia, in 1999, in an opinion by Justice Barbara Milano Keenan with no separate opinion, held that the evidence did not support any of the three warranty findings. Under Virginia's version of UCC section 2-313, the matrices did not warrant the performance of Crow's differently configured boat, and the brochure's general praise was commendation and opinion rather than a description promising a specific speed. Under section 2-314, Crow did not establish a relevant trade standard or show the boat was generally unacceptable or unfit for ordinary offshore fishing. Under section 2-315, he did not show that the seller had reason to know of his precise speed requirement. The court reversed and entered final judgment for Bayliner.
sections.Reasoning:
The court began with express warranty. The thirty-mile-per-hour figures were definite numbers, so the problem was not puffery but what they referred to: boats with different propellers and materially different equipment weight. A precise statement about a differently configured product does not automatically become a warranty about the buyer's actual boat. The court contrasted an earlier jewelry case in which an appraisal described the very diamonds being sold. The brochure, by contrast, identified no specific speed or other measurable characteristic; section 2-313(2) preserves the distinction between an affirmation or description and an opinion commending the goods, and on this record the sentence was commendation.

On merchantability, the court considered two statutory aspects separately. For acceptance in the trade, Crow offered no evidence of the offshore-boat trade's standard or that a substantial segment of buyers would reject a boat of this capability; his testimony that travel to the Gulf Stream took too long described his own preferences. For fitness for ordinary purposes, the evidence of actual offshore fishing and substantial engine hours undermined any inference of general unfitness, and his explanation that many hours were spent on repairs did not prove otherwise.

On fitness for a particular purpose, Crow identified the purpose as offshore fishing in a boat capable of thirty miles per hour. He had discussed fishing and speed, but the record did not show that Atherton knew a slower boat was unacceptable to him, and that failure defeated the claim. Because every ground of liability failed, the court did not decide the damages questions. The casebook excerpt omits the implied-warranty discussion.

CT-CB-0013.rule: A patient may recover on a physician's clearly proved promise of a specific result even without negligence, and the damages may include out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of the patient's condition, and pain and mental distress beyond what the promised treatment would have entailed.

sections.Parties: Alice Sullivan, the patient, sued physician James H. O'Connor for breach of a promise concerning the result of cosmetic surgery and, separately, for negligent treatment. On appeal O'Connor sought to confine her compensation to her out-of-pocket expenses. Sullivan had objected that the instructions did not grant full compensation for the promised result, but she offered to abandon those objections if the verdict in her favor stood.
sections.Procedural History: The case was tried to a jury. The jury found for Sullivan on the contract count and for O'Connor on the negligence count. The damages instructions then allowed out-of-pocket expenses, the worsening of her appearance and associated mental distress, and pain and suffering from the third operation, and excluded pain from the first two operations and unproved lost earnings. The jury awarded $13,500. O'Connor excepted to the refusal to restrict recovery to expenditures and to the inclusion of disfigurement and third-operation suffering. Sullivan conditionally waived her own exceptions. The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, on May 9, 1973, overruled the defendant's exceptions and treated the plaintiff's as waived, so the verdict stood and no new trial was ordered.
sections.Material Facts:
Sullivan was a professional entertainer, as O'Connor knew. The jury could find that he undertook to improve her appearance by making her relatively long, prominent nose shorter and more pleasing in relation to her other features. The contemplated treatment was two operations. He performed three, and the result worsened her appearance: the opinion describes a concave upper line, a bulbous lower portion, flattening and broadening, and an asymmetrical tip. Further surgery evidently could not improve it.

Sullivan incurred stipulated physician and hospital expenses totaling $622.65. She did not prove lost employment or earnings attributable to the changed nose, and the trial judge excluded lost earnings from the damages calculation. The two contemplated operations already entailed some pain and distress; the third operation was additional. She no longer sought on appeal the improvement above her preoperative condition, and she waived any claim for suffering from the first two operations.
sections.Issue: Whether damages for breach of a physician's promise of a result may include physical deterioration, mental distress and the pain of an additional operation when the physician was not negligent, or are limited to a refund of expenditures; and whether the case required a choice between expectation damages and reliance damages.
sections.Holding: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, in 1973, in an opinion by Justice Kaplan with no separate opinion reported, held that Massachusetts recognizes an action on a physician's promise of a specified result, on clear proof that the promise was made, and that the jury's rejection of negligence does not defeat it. The award could include Sullivan's expenditures, the worsening of her condition, and the suffering and distress associated with the third operation. Those items were recoverable under either an expectation or a reliance approach, and because Sullivan waived the claims that would distinguish the two measures, the court did not select one as the exclusive formula. It overruled the defendant's exceptions, and the $13,500 verdict stood.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Kaplan first addressed whether such promises should be enforced at all. Medical results are uncertain, disappointed patients may recast optimistic reassurance as a guarantee, and broad liability could encourage defensive practice; yet refusing to enforce genuine promises would let practitioners induce patients with commitments they never intend to honor. Massachusetts takes an intermediate position: the action exists, but the jury should scrutinize whether an actual undertaking, rather than an opinion or therapeutic assurance, was proved. Absence of negligence goes to the quality of treatment; the contract count goes to the content of the undertaking.

The court then distinguished three interests. Restitution returns the benefit conferred on the physician, most obviously the fee. Reliance reverses detrimental changes incurred because of the agreement, including payments to third parties and a worsened condition. Expectation compares the actual result with the promised one; on the Hawkins model it captures failure to improve and deterioration but ordinarily excludes pain the patient would have endured in any event. A fee-only recovery might protect too little, while the full value of the promised appearance might be hard to estimate and disproportionate to the fee, so the court spoke favorably of reliance without holding that it excludes expectation in every medical case.

The deterioration and the extra operation were compensable on either view. Mental distress was recoverable because an agreement to operate on a person's body, unlike an ordinary merchandise transaction, makes bodily change and the attending distress central to what the parties contemplate; her known professional circumstances were relevant to that appraisal. The footnotes warn against double recovery.

CT-CB-0021.rule: Contract damages ordinarily compensate the injured party's own loss; the breaching party's gains can sometimes help measure that loss, but gains that do not correspond to it are not automatically recoverable in an ordinary contract action, and a supported estimate of the loss suffices despite uncertainty.

sections.Parties: The United States Naval Institute held the author's copyright in The Hunt for Red October and marketed the hardcover edition. It licensed paperback rights to Charter Communications and Berkley Publishing Group, treated collectively as Berkley. Naval was the plaintiff and appellant; Berkley was the defendant and cross-appellant. Naval sought relief for premature paperback retail sales and, on this appeal, wanted a larger recovery of Berkley's profits, additional interest and attorney's fees. Berkley wanted the judgment eliminated or reduced.
sections.Procedural History: Naval unsuccessfully sought preliminary relief, and the district court initially entered judgment against it after trial. In 1989 the Second Circuit, in Naval I, reversed on contract liability and remanded for appropriate relief. On remand the district court treated the conduct as copyright infringement and awarded $35,380.50 in lost hardcover profits, $7,760.12 of Berkley's profits, and $15,319.27 in prejudgment interest on the compensatory award, plus costs; it denied attorney's fees and interest on the profit award. Naval appealed and Berkley cross-appealed. On June 18, 1991, the Second Circuit reversed the $7,760.12 profits award and affirmed the judgment in all other respects.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties made their licensing agreement in September 1984. One provision conveyed an exclusive right to publish and sell paperback editions, and another made the license term begin on the date of the agreement. A separate provision prohibited publication before October 1985.

Berkley shipped paperbacks to outlets early, and retail sales began on September 15, 1985. Sales were extensive enough for the book to approach the top of the paperback bestseller lists before the end of September. The earlier appellate decision had held that causing such substantial early retail sales breached the timing provision.

Some buyers of the cheaper paperback in September would otherwise have bought the hardcover, but others would have waited for the paperback and never bought the hardcover. Hardcover sales had been declining before the premature release. Naval proposed $724,300 as the measure of Berkley's profits. The district court estimated Naval's lost September hardcover sales by reference to August hardcover sales. Naval had accepted substantial royalties and renounced rescission.
sections.Issue: Whether Berkley's early retail publication infringed a copyright interest owned by Naval or only breached a covenant governing rights already licensed to Berkley; whether, without copyright remedies, Naval could still recover contract damages and could recover Berkley's profits; and whether the comparison with August hardcover sales was a permissible estimate of Naval's loss.
sections.Holding: The United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, in 1991, in an opinion by Judge Kearse for a panel with Judges Winter and Altimari and no separate opinion, held that an exclusive license transfers ownership of the rights conveyed, so Berkley's premature publication breached the agreement without infringing copyright, and the Copyright Act supplied no basis for the profits award or attorney's fees. Naval could still recover contract damages. Berkley's paperback profits did not measure Naval's lost hardcover profit and were not recoverable. The $35,380.50 estimate based on the prior month's hardcover sales was not clearly erroneous, and prejudgment interest followed under New York law. The court reversed the $7,760.12 award and otherwise affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The district court had treated October 1985 as the date the license took effect, but the agreement tied its beginning to the September 1984 agreement date and referred to first publication elsewhere. Berkley therefore owned the paperback rights when the early sales occurred, and the publication restriction was a contractual covenant; a licensee does not infringe rights already conveyed to it. Since the Copyright Act's route to an infringer's profits depended on infringement, it was unavailable, but the license did not free Berkley from its contractual restriction.

Berkley argued that Naval had abandoned its monetary contract claim. The court answered that Naval I had held Naval entitled to relief for the breach, which was the law of the case, and that Naval had asked for other just and proper relief and Rule 54(c) directs a judgment to grant the relief warranted.

On measure, Naval's proposed figure included profits on sales to buyers who would never have bought the hardcover; those sales enriched Berkley without depriving Naval of corresponding hardcover sales, and awarding them would detach damages from the injury. The court recognized that a defendant's profit can sometimes help define the plaintiff's loss, but that relationship was absent here. The $7,760.12 award rested on the rejected copyright theory, while the separate lost-profit estimate could stand under contract law.

On certainty, there was evidence of actual lost sales, and only the amount was uncertain. Nothing showed purchases were even throughout September, so Berkley's alternative projection was not compelled, and uncertainty caused by the wrongdoer could be resolved against it. An ordinary contract claim gave no basis for attorney's fees.

CT-CB-0026.rule: Although specific performance is ordinarily not the remedy for an agreement to sell personal property, equity may order delivery of a specific chattel when special circumstances give it a peculiar and unique value that makes damages inadequate.

sections.Parties: Archie Sparrow, a cowboy and experienced horse trainer, was the plaintiff and sought delivery of a particular horse, Keno, as promised compensation for ranch work. C. L. 'Chip' Morris, who owned the ranch and the horse, was the defendant and the appellant. Morris argued that Sparrow had not satisfied a condition about the quality of his work, that money rather than delivery was the proper remedy for personal property, and that a final wage check had settled everything between them.
sections.Procedural History: Sparrow brought an action in chancery for specific performance. After hearing testimony from both parties, the chancellor ordered Morris to deliver the horse. Morris appealed the decree to the Supreme Court of Arkansas.
