Nothing showed that the owners demanded the wall's relocation while construction was underway. The contract required written agreement for extras, and none existed.
sections.Issue: Whether the defects and omissions prevented the builder from recovering on the contract, leaving him at most a claim in quantum meruit, and, if performance was substantial, whether the owners' damages for each defect are measured by cost of repair or by diminution in value.
sections.Holding: The Wisconsin Supreme Court in 1960, in an opinion by Hallows with no separate writing reported, affirmed. Plante substantially performed, so he recovered the contract price less damages attributable to incomplete or defective work. The trial court's differentiated treatment of the proven defects stood: repair cost for the plaster cracks, patio floor and patio wall, and no award for relocating the living-room wall, because moving it would substantially destroy completed work and both sides' experts agreed it did not affect market price. Denial of the builder's disputed extras was also affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
Contract recovery requires substantial performance, which the court defined by the essential purpose of the promised performance rather than a mathematical percentage of completion or repair cost. A building need not comply perfectly with every specification unless the parties make particular details essential, although a feature of special or great personal importance could defeat substantial performance if left unperformed. Prior decisions, such as those involving a grossly inadequate boiler or a practically useless boathouse, illustrated failures to accomplish a contract's essential purpose. Here the owners received a usable house built from a stock plan and standard-form specifications, and the record did not show that every detail was essential to their agreement.

On damages, diminution in value compares the building as delivered with the building as properly promised. Small, separable defects that can reasonably be corrected without destroying substantial completed work may be measured by correction cost, with unreasonable economic waste limiting destructive reconstruction. The defects here could be separated without confusion. Correcting ceiling plaster cracks, mud jacking and repairing the patio floor, and reconstructing a nonstructural patio wall did not involve unreasonable waste, so those repair allowances stood.

Moving the living-room wall was different. It would substantially destroy completed work, damage other portions of the house, and require replastering and redecorating walls and ceilings in at least two rooms. The court treated the diminution measure as contemplating that the wall would remain, and because both sides' experts agreed it did not affect market price, the owners established no recoverable loss for it. That conclusion depended on these facts.

Plante's claimed extras failed because the contract required written agreement, none existed, the evidence about waiver conflicted, and he carried the burden.

CT-NEXT-CM-0147.rule: When a contractor deliberately fails to perform a construction obligation, the owner's damages are the reasonable cost of performing the promised work, even if that cost exceeds the value of the completed land; economic waste concerns only destroying a completed or substantially completed structure.

sections.Parties: Frank Groves was the plaintiff and the appellant. He sued as assignee and successor to the rights of S. J. Groves & Sons, the landowner and lessor, and sought damages measured by the cost of completing the grading that had been promised. John Wunder Co., the lessee that had promised to grade the site, was the defendant. Liability for breach was not the disputed question on appeal; the dispute was the measure of damages.
sections.Procedural History:
The trial findings established that Wunder failed to perform the grading covenant. The trial court applied a market-value measure and entered judgment of slightly more than $15,000 including interest, rather than awarding the cost of completion. The plaintiff appealed the measure of damages.

The Minnesota court reversed and ordered a new trial. It did not render a fixed award above $60,000. The first question on remand was what the grading language actually demanded, an interpretation the court expressly withheld because the issue had not been argued on appeal. Justice Olson, joined by Justice Holt, dissented and would have affirmed the existing judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
S. J. Groves & Sons owned twenty-four acres of suburban Minneapolis land zoned for heavy industry, with existing or readily available railroad access. Limited development in the neighborhood made the sand and gravel deposit the property's principal immediate asset. Groves operated an excavating and screening plant there, and Wunder operated a nearby competing plant.

In August 1927 the parties' transaction gave Wunder a seven-year lease, the screening plant and rights to remove sand and gravel, and eliminated Groves as a competitor. Wunder paid $105,000 and promised to leave the site at a uniform grade substantially matching the existing roadway, using stripped overburden to establish and maintain that grade.

Wunder removed the richest gravel and left the land broken, rugged and uneven. Under the interpretation used at trial, completion required moving 288,495 cubic yards of overburden off the property at a reasonable cost above $60,000. The land's value if properly graded was only $12,160.
sections.Issue: Whether the promised grading was compensable at its reasonable completion cost even though that cost exceeded the value of the completed land, or whether recovery was limited to a market-value measure.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota court, 1939, in a prevailing opinion by Stone, with Olson and Holt dissenting and Hilton and Loring not participating, held that cost of performance was the appropriate measure for this deliberate failure to perform a construction obligation, subject to determining on remand exactly what work the contract required. The prevailing opinion represented a majority of the sitting quorum, although a minority of the full membership. The judgment was reversed and a new trial ordered. The court did not fix an award; whether every point had to be lowered to roadway level, even if that required hauling material away, remained for initial determination below.
sections.Reasoning:
The aim was to give the promisee, so far as money could do so, the promised accomplishment. A landowner may purchase an improvement for reasons not exhausted by current market value, including future development or personal preferences, and a contractor who has received the agreed consideration cannot escape the cost of the promised work simply because the land is worth little. Stone characterized the breach as willful and in bad faith and distinguished cases of good-faith substantial performance.

The opinion separated contractual loss from tort valuation. Tort generally compensates the decrease in an asset's money value, but this contract entitled the owner to a specified alteration of the property, so the loss was the promised work. Drawing on grading and farm-improvement precedents, the court treated reasonable performance cost as the value of that lost accomplishment and refused to confine that treatment to municipal construction agreements. Its illustration of a monument to an owner's taste showed why the promisor's opinion of economic benefit did not replace the bargain.

The court acknowledged the Restatement's economic-waste limitation but construed it narrowly, as addressing destruction of a completed or substantially completed structure to cure a defect. Here the grading had not been performed, and a large gap between completion cost and land value did not itself establish that kind of waste.

Olson, dissenting, regarded damages as compensation for actual loss, not punishment for motive. He disputed the majority's use of willfulness, saw no showing of a unique personal use, and favored diminution in value when reconstruction expense was disproportionate to its benefit.

CT-NEXT-CM-0148.rule: Reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures damages for omitted remedial work under a coal lease, but where the breached provision is merely incidental to the main purpose and the economic benefit of performance is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to diminution in value.

sections.Parties: Willie and Lucille Peevyhouse, owners of coal-bearing farm property, were the plaintiffs and lessors. Garland Coal & Mining Co., the strip-mining lessee, was the defendant. Both sides appealed the jury's award. The owners sought the cost-of-performance measure for the restoration work Garland omitted, while Garland sought to limit recovery to the value the restoration would add to the farm.
sections.Procedural History:
The owners sued for $25,000. Over their objection, Garland introduced testimony on the difference between the farm's value without restoration and its value if restoration occurred. The trial judge required a verdict for the owners but let the jury consider both performance cost and the other evidence in fixing the amount. The jury awarded $5,000, and both sides appealed.

The Oklahoma court modified the judgment to $300 and affirmed it as modified; it did not remand for a new damages trial. The original judgment was issued December 11, 1962. The report records modification and denial of rehearing on March 26, 1963, with a supplemental opinion by Jackson and the same five-to-four grouping, and denial of a second rehearing on May 28.
sections.Material Facts:
In November 1954 the Peevyhouses leased their farm to Garland for a five-year strip-mining operation. The agreement permitted use of the surface necessary for mining and payment of royalties, and it also imposed specific restoration obligations, including filling pits at property lines to permit fences and access, smoothing the tops of the spoil banks, and leaving no shale or dirt on the high wall of the pits.

The parties stipulated that every contractual obligation had been performed except the remedial work, and Garland conceded that omission. Experts estimated that the omitted work, involving many thousands of cubic yards of dirt, would cost about $29,000. The court found no evidence supporting more than $300 as the increase in value attributable to the restoration, and the owners did not argue for a higher figure under that measure. The owners had tried the claim on the premise that only performance cost mattered: they objected to the valuation testimony, did not cross-examine Garland's valuation witnesses and offered no rebuttal.
sections.Issue: What is the proper measure of damages for a lessee's failure to do promised restoration work under a coal lease when the cost of the work greatly exceeds the increase in the property's market value that the work would produce?
sections.Holding: The Oklahoma court, 1962, in an opinion by Jackson joined by Welch, Davison, Halley and Johnson, with Williams, Blackbird, Irwin and Berry dissenting, a five-to-four division, held that reasonable cost of performance ordinarily measures a lessor's loss from omitted remedial work under a coal lease. Where, however, the breached provision is merely incidental to the agreement's main purpose and the economic benefit of performance to the lessor is grossly disproportionate to its cost, recovery is limited to the diminution in value caused by the omitted work. The $5,000 judgment was modified to $300 and affirmed as modified. The full brief notes that the casebook's bracketed 4-3 disposition conflicts with the actual report.
sections.Reasoning:
The majority characterized the principal bargain as the economical extraction and sale of coal for the parties' profit and treated the restoration provisions as incidental. It thought it unrealistic that an ordinary owner would spend $29,000 for a $300 increase in value. It distinguished the Restatement's concern about destroying a substantially completed structure from a broader inquiry into expense disproportionate to the end attained, and regarded relative economic benefit as an appropriate consideration even though no completed building needed destruction. It compared Groves with decisions applying diminution in value to similar grading arrangements.

Its governing grounds were Oklahoma statutes barring damages greater than the benefit of full performance and requiring reasonable rather than unconscionable, grossly oppressive damages, which it analogized to restrictions on contractual penalties. On its valuation premise, performance-cost recovery would give the owners more economic benefit than completed restoration. Both qualifications matter: the court acknowledged that where a principal contractual purpose is an improvement that reduces resale value, performance cost would ordinarily govern.

Irwin, dissenting, disputed the incidental-purpose characterization: Garland admitted the owners insisted on restoration and would not lease without it, the cost was reasonably predictable when the contract was made, and he considered the breach willful and without good faith. He would have enforced the unambiguous obligations as written and favored the Groves performance-cost approach.

On rehearing the court refused to let the owners change their theory of the case to develop a valuation claim, and it rejected a federal Contract Clause argument raised by amici because the damage statutes predated the 1954 agreement.

CT-NEXT-CM-0150.rule: A subcontractor who justifiably stops work after the other party's material breach may elect restitution for the reasonable value of the performance conferred, less payments received, without deduction for the loss it would have suffered by completing and without the contract price as a ceiling.

sections.Parties: Coastal Steel Erectors, Inc., a steel-erection subcontractor, was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sued in the name of the United States under the Miller Act to recover for labor and equipment it had already supplied. The defendants were Algernon Blair, Inc., the prime contractor on a naval hospital, and its payment-bond surety, United States Fidelity and Guaranty. Blair maintained that the subcontract did not require it to pay crane rental.
sections.Procedural History:
The district court found that the subcontract required payment for crane use and that Blair's refusal to pay was a material breach justifying Coastal's termination; those findings were not challenged on appeal. It estimated that approximately $37,000 remained payable for Coastal's performance under the contract after payments received, but it also found that Coastal would have lost more than $37,000 had it finished. Treating that expected loss as a deduction from contract damages, it denied recovery.

The Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded with instructions to determine accurately the reasonable value of the labor and equipment use Coastal furnished and then enter judgment for Coastal after subtracting prior contractual payments.
sections.Material Facts:
Algernon Blair contracted with the United States to build a naval hospital in Charleston County, South Carolina. It subcontracted steel erection and the supply of associated equipment to Coastal Steel Erectors. Coastal used its own cranes to handle and place the steel. Blair refused to pay crane rental, maintaining that the subcontract did not require payment.

Coastal stopped work after completing approximately twenty-eight percent of its obligations, and Blair hired another subcontractor to finish. The district court estimated that approximately $37,000 remained payable for Coastal's performance under the contract after payments received, and it found that Coastal would have lost more than $37,000 if it had finished the job. The appeal therefore concerned an alternative remedy for a justified cessation after the other party's breach, not whether Coastal itself wrongfully abandoned the project.
sections.Issue: Whether a partly performing subcontractor may elect quantum meruit recovery for the labor and equipment it has already supplied even though completing the contract would have been unprofitable and contract damages would yield no award.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, 1973, in an opinion by Craven for a panel of Chief Judge Haynsworth, Senior Judge Bryan and Craven, with no separate writing, held that it could. Restitution measures the reasonable value of the performance conferred on Blair, without deducting the loss Coastal would have incurred on the unperformed balance. The contract price may be evidence of reasonable value but neither sets the measure nor caps recovery. Amounts already paid remain deductible. The court reversed and remanded for an accurate finding of reasonable value; it did not award $37,000 as the final restitution figure.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished the expectation question, what financial position completion of this bargain would have produced, from the restitution question, what reasonable value Coastal had already supplied at its own expense and Blair retained without full payment. Blair's material breach entitled Coastal to stop and elect recovery of that value. The anticipated loss on the remaining work did not turn the completed labor and equipment use into a benefit Blair could keep unpaid.

The opinion relied on Miller Act and construction precedents recognizing a promisee's option to forgo contract damages and seek reasonable value after the other party's breach. That remedy could be pursued against the payment-bond surety as well as the prime contractor. Imprecision in the complaint's theory did not preclude quantum meruit, which could be pleaded alongside contract damages, though not to collect duplicative awards.

The relevant value was the amount for which the services could have been purchased from someone in Coastal's position at the time and place of performance. The restitution rationale rested on both Coastal's expenditure and Blair's retained gain, but it did not make every expense automatically recoverable. A footnote acknowledged that restitution could exceed the value of the promised return, consistent with refusing to make the contract price a ceiling.

A footnote stated that federal substantive law controls a Miller Act action when federal and state law differ, while the court believed the outcome would be the same under the pertinent state law. The opinion did not decide the separate case of a claimant who has fully performed. The district court's $37,000 approximation was not a precise reasonable-value finding.

CT-NEXT-CM-0151.rule: After receiving an absolute repudiation, a contractor may not continue performing and charge the avoidable cost to the repudiating party; recovery is limited to labor, materials and expenses in partial performance before repudiation plus the profit the contract would have produced.

sections.Parties: Luten Bridge Co., a bridge builder, was the plaintiff. It sued Rockingham County for $18,301.07 allegedly earned under a bridge-building contract through November 3. Rockingham County was the defendant and the appellant. The county initially contested the contract's validity, but on appeal it admitted execution, validity and its own breach, so the ultimate dispute was the amount Luten could recover.
sections.Procedural History:
Three of the original commissioners met privately with an attorney and filed an answer admitting the complaint. After a new board took office, the county sought to strike that answer and filed its own defense. The trial judge treated the commissioners' answer as the county's admission, admitted it in evidence, excluded the county's proffered resignation and cancellation evidence, and directed a verdict for Luten's full claim. The county appealed.

The Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded for a new trial because the unauthorized answer should have been stricken, the county's evidence should have been admitted, and the directed verdict for the full claim was erroneous. It did not finally calculate the county's liability.
sections.Material Facts:
On January 7, 1924 the county's five-member board awarded Luten the bridge contract by a three-to-two division, and public controversy followed. Pruitt, one of the supporters, submitted his resignation to the superior-court clerk on February 11. The county offered evidence that the clerk accepted it before Pruitt tried to withdraw it and appointed Hampton as successor. Hampton took the oath and thereafter regularly conducted county business with Martin and Barber, while the three original supporters attended no further meetings. These details reached the appellate court through affidavits and offers of proof, much of which the trial court excluded.

At a regularly advertised February 21 meeting the functioning board declared the contract invalid, instructed Luten to proceed no further, and abandoned the road for which the bridge was to be a connecting link. The resolution was sent to Luten. Resolutions in March and April warned that construction would be at Luten's risk, and a September resolution refused payment of bridge bills. When the first notice issued, labor and materials on site amounted to about $1,900. Luten nevertheless continued building.
sections.Issue: Whether an answer filed privately by three commissioners bound the county; whether the functioning board's notices were county action; and whether Luten could recover for construction it continued after receiving an effective repudiation. The assigned casebook excerpt concentrates on the third question.
sections.Holding: The Fourth Circuit, 1929, in an opinion by Parker for a panel with District Judges McClintic and Soper and with no separate writing, held that once Luten received the county's repudiation it could not continue building a bridge the county no longer wanted and charge the avoidable expenditure to the county. On proof of duly given notice, the measure is compensation for labor and materials expended and expenses incurred in partial performance before repudiation, plus the profit the contract would have produced. The privately filed answer was unauthorized and should have been stricken, and the county's resolutions and notices could not be excluded for want of authority. The judgment was reversed and remanded for a new trial.
sections.Reasoning:
A county board exercises its corporate powers as a body in a legally convened meeting. Even assuming the three original commissioners were still a numerical majority, their private conference met none of the statutory requirements for a meeting, so their answer was unauthorized as the county's pleading and could not be evidence of a county admission.

The proffered resignation evidence was relevant. If the offered facts were true, acceptance by the proper authority ended Pruitt's ability to withdraw and permitted Hampton's appointment, giving the three acting members a quorum. Independently, Hampton's appointment by the proper official, his oath and his unchallenged exercise of the office made him a de facto commissioner, so acts at lawful meetings were valid for the county and those dealing with it.

The county had no right to rescind the valid bargain without compensation; its notice was a breach. But after receiving the repudiation Luten could not go on building and charge the avoidable expenditure to the county. The abandoned road left the bridge useless to the county, and Luten's compensable interest was its loss from being stopped, including anticipated profit, which did not require completing unwanted work.

The court applied the American rule against increasing damages through continued performance after absolute repudiation, and distinguished authorities allowing an immediate suit for anticipatory breach. The measure did not confine Luten to $1,900 or eliminate its lost profit, and it did not entitle Luten to the $18,301.07 claimed. The opinion spoke of a duty to mitigate; its consequence here was a limit on recoverable damages.

CT-NEXT-CM-0154.rule: A wrongfully discharged employee recovers the agreed compensation less what the employer proves was or could reasonably have been earned in other employment, but only comparable or substantially similar work counts; different or inferior work need not be accepted.

sections.Parties: Shirley MacLaine Parker, who had contracted to play the female lead in a Fox film, was the plaintiff and the respondent on appeal. She sued Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. for the compensation due under her contract and, alternatively, for breach damages. Fox, the defendant and appellant, admitted the agreement's validity, Parker's compliance and readiness to perform, and its own anticipatory repudiation. Its sole defense was that by rejecting a substitute role she unreasonably failed to mitigate her loss.
sections.Procedural History:
Parker sued for compensation due and, alternatively, breach damages, and obtained summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest. Although she had not started performing, the parties stipulated for the motion that she had been discharged, allowing wrongful-discharge damage principles to apply. Fox appealed.

The California court affirmed the judgment for $750,000 plus interest by a six-to-one division, with Acting Chief Justice Sullivan dissenting. Rehearing was denied October 28, 1970; Mosk did not participate in that denial and Sullivan favored granting it.
sections.Material Facts:
In August 1965 Parker contracted to play the female lead in Fox's proposed musical Bloomer Girl. The agreement guaranteed $750,000 for fourteen weeks beginning May 23, 1966, expressed as $53,571.42 weekly. Bloomer Girl was to be produced in California and would use her dancing as well as her acting talents.

Fox decided not to make the film and notified Parker on April 4 that it would not fulfill its obligations. In the same letter it offered her the lead in Big Country, Big Man, a dramatic western to be filmed in Australia. Fox offered the same compensation and thirty-one of the original agreement's thirty-four numbered provisions, but it removed dance-director approval because the replacement was not a musical and replaced her director and screenplay approvals with consultation subject to Fox's final decision. Parker had one week to accept and did not do so.

The original agreement also stated that Fox need not use Parker's services and that its obligation was to pay the guaranteed compensation, subject to the agreement's terms.
sections.Issue: Whether Fox's substitute offer raised a triable mitigation defense that barred summary judgment, or whether the different and inferior character of the substitute employment could be decided as a matter of law.
sections.Holding: The California court, 1970, in a majority opinion by Burke joined by McComb, Peters, Tobriner and assigned Justices Kaus and Roth, with Sullivan dissenting, six to one, held that the musical lead in Los Angeles and the straight dramatic western lead in Australia were different kinds of employment and that, independently, eliminating contractual approval rights made the substitute inferior. Fox's offer therefore could not support its mitigation defense, and summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest was affirmed. The majority expressly did not decide Parker's separate argument that the guaranteed-pay clause and other grounds excused mitigation altogether.
sections.Reasoning:
Normally an employee recovers agreed compensation less earnings the employer affirmatively proves were received or could reasonably have been received from other employment. Before hypothetical earnings from an unaccepted opportunity may reduce recovery, the employer must establish that the work was comparable or substantially similar; different or inferior work need not be accepted.

The majority distinguished reasonable efforts to find comparable employment from the entitlement to reject different or inferior work. Fox raised no issue about Parker's general search; its theory rested exclusively on the replacement offer. Once that offer was legally different or inferior, no further balancing of the reasonableness of rejection was required.

On summary judgment the court could not weigh disputed facts, and doubts favored trial. Fox's declarations calling the new work comparable and not inferior were treated as conclusions about undisputed terms, not facts creating a triable issue, and neither expertise nor judicial notice was needed to recognize the loss of contractual rights. Equal pay did not establish equal employment. The decision supports summary judgment on this record, not a categorical rule that every contested comparability question can be resolved without trial.

Sullivan, dissenting, agreed that different or inferior work need not be accepted but thought the significance of genre, location and approval rights required factual appraisal, since both were starring roles. He warned that a per se rule that any omitted right makes work inferior threatened to displace mitigation almost entirely, criticized the trial court's use of judicial notice without the opportunity to be heard required by Evidence Code section 455, and would have reversed for a trial on comparability.

CT-NEXT-CM-0155.rule: Damages for breach of contract are limited to losses that arise naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or that both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as its probable result, including losses made ordinary by communicated special circumstances.

sections.Parties: Hadley and another proprietor, who operated the City Steam-Mills at Gloucester, were the plaintiffs. They claimed £300 for profits and other losses caused by the late carriage of a broken crankshaft. The defendants operated Pickford & Co., the carriers. They objected that the lost profits were too remote and, after the verdict, obtained a rule nisi for a new trial on the ground of misdirection.
sections.Procedural History:
The declaration contained two counts. The first, alleging a promise to deliver on a specified second day, was discontinued before trial. The surviving count alleged a failure to use due care and diligence to deliver within a reasonable time. The defendants paid £25 into court in satisfaction, and the plaintiffs replied that the sum was insufficient.

At the Gloucester Assizes, Crompton, J., left the case generally to the jury despite the carriers' objection that lost profits were too remote, and the jury awarded another £25 beyond the amount deposited. The carriers obtained a rule nisi for a new trial for misdirection. The Court of Exchequer made the rule absolute and ordered a new trial with an instruction excluding lost profits; it did not enter a final judgment or calculate a replacement award.
sections.Material Facts:
The crankshaft of the plaintiffs' steam engine broke, stopping the mill on May 11; the fracture was discovered on May 12. Joyce & Co., the engineers at Greenwich who had made the engine, needed the old shaft as a pattern for a replacement, so the replacement depended on getting the broken shaft to Greenwich.

On May 13 the millers sent a servant to the office of Pickford & Co. The report's trial narrative says the servant told the clerk that the mill had stopped and that the shaft must be sent immediately, and the clerk answered that a shaft received before noon would reach Greenwich the following day. The plaintiffs delivered it before noon the next day and paid £2 4s for carriage. Neglect delayed delivery, so the new shaft reached the mill several days later than it otherwise would have, prolonging the shutdown and costing the millers profits. The declaration alleged five additional days of delay, lost sales and profits, flour bought to serve customers and wages paid to idle employees.
sections.Issue: What damages instruction should govern a jury assessing breach of this contract of carriage, and whether the reported facts permitted the jury to include the mill's lost profits.
sections.Holding: The Court of Exchequer, 1854, in a judgment of the court delivered by Alderson, B., with no separate concurrence or dissent and no vote reported, held that recoverable damages must fairly and reasonably arise naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or have been reasonably contemplated by both parties when contracting as its probable result. The mill's lost profits fell outside both routes on the circumstances the court treated as communicated, so the jury should have been instructed to exclude them. The rule was made absolute and a new trial ordered.
sections.Reasoning:
A jury's general power to assess compensation needed a definite legal boundary; without a limiting instruction, similar defendants could face radically different awards depending on circumstances they had no reason to anticipate. The court therefore stated a rule covering both ordinary consequences and special risks known at formation. If communicated special circumstances make a loss an ordinary consequence, damages may reflect that knowledge; if they were unknown, the breaching party is taken to contemplate only the loss arising in the multitude of ordinary transactions. Knowledge matters because it lets the parties arrange special terms for the increased risk.

Applying the rule, the court characterized what was communicated as the shipment of a broken mill shaft by the millers who owned it. That did not necessarily reveal that delay would stop the whole mill from earning profits: a mill might have a spare shaft, or other defective machinery might keep it idle anyway. These were hypothetical explanations, not findings about these plaintiffs.

The court accepted the actual causal chain, that the old shaft was the model, the missing replacement was the sole cause of the stoppage and the delay caused the lost profits, but held that causation did not establish compensable remoteness. The decisive point was that it treated the special dependencies as neither communicated nor known when the parties contracted.

The full brief notes a tension between that application and the trial narrative that the clerk was told the mill had stopped. The casebook editors quote Victoria Laundry as reading the judgment to reject the notice evidence; that is a later interpretation, not Hadley's own explanation.

CT-NEXT-CM-0157.rule: Unusual or extraordinary damages are recoverable only if liability for them was contemplated at or before contract formation as a probable consequence of breach, judged by the contract's nature, purpose and circumstances and the liability the defendant consciously assumed or reasonably led the plaintiff to believe it assumed.

sections.Parties: Kenford Co., whose president and sole shareholder was Edward Cottrell, and Dome Stadium, Inc. (DSI), formed by Cottrell and Roy Hofheinz, were the plaintiffs. They sued Erie County for specific performance or damages after the County terminated a contract to build a domed stadium. The County was the defendant and the appellant in the Court of Appeals, where it disputed the legal recoverability of Kenford's claimed appreciation of surrounding land.
sections.Procedural History:
Kenford and DSI sued in June 1971 for specific performance or $90 million, later increased to $495 million. Liability was established by summary judgment. A damages trial of roughly nine months produced $18 million for anticipated peripheral-land appreciation and over $6 million in out-of-pocket expenses for Kenford, plus $25.6 million in management profits for DSI.

In 1985 the Appellate Division sustained much of Kenford's reliance and mitigation award, rejected DSI's lost profits, and ordered a retrial of the land-appreciation amount; two justices dissented. On a separate earlier appeal the Court of Appeals rejected DSI's management profits. The retrial yielded $6.5 million, and the Appellate Division affirmed in 1988. On the County's appeal, the Court of Appeals reversed the relevant portions of the 1988 and 1985 orders, with costs, and struck the land-appreciation award.
sections.Material Facts:
Erie County authorized a domed stadium and $50 million in financing in May 1968. Kenford acquired options on Lancaster land and offered to sell the County a site; the County declined. Kenford then proposed donating the site in exchange for DSI's ability to lease or manage the stadium. The County accepted in June 1969, and Cottrell exercised options on surrounding parcels while negotiations proceeded.

The August 8, 1969 contract called for Kenford to donate 178 acres and for the County to begin construction within twelve months. The County would negotiate a forty-year DSI lease expected to produce at least $63.75 million in revenues, including increased taxes on peripheral lands owned, contracted for or later acquired by Cottrell or Kenford. If no satisfactory lease emerged within three months, the parties were to execute an annexed twenty-year management agreement. The lease was never agreed.

Construction bids reached approximately $72 million, $22 million beyond the authorized financing, and efforts to increase the appropriation failed. The County terminated the contract in January 1971. Kenford had no contractual duty to acquire or retain surrounding land.
sections.Issue: Whether the County had assumed liability for the anticipated appreciation in value of Kenford's land surrounding the proposed stadium site if the stadium was never built, so that the appreciation was recoverable as damages for breach.
sections.Holding: The New York Court of Appeals, 1989, in an opinion by Designated Judge Mollen, with Chief Judge Wachtler and Judges Alexander, Titone and Bellacosa concurring and Judges Simons, Kaye and Hancock taking no part, held that Kenford could not recover the peripheral-land appreciation as a matter of law because the County had not reasonably contemplated liability for that loss. The court struck the award rather than remanding for another appraisal. There was no separate writing, and the decision did not vacate every damages award in the litigation.
sections.Reasoning:
Ordinary damages compensate the natural and probable consequences of breach. Unusual or extraordinary damages require contemplation at or before formation as a probable consequence of breach, assessed from the contract's nature, purpose and known circumstances and from the liability the defendant consciously assumed or reasonably led the plaintiff to believe it assumed.

Kenford argued that the appreciation was actually foreseen and inherent in the bargain, since the contract contemplated higher assessments and peripheral-land tax revenues. The court answered that knowledge that a stadium could raise property values did not establish a promise to compensate Kenford if the increase never occurred. The revenue provisions showed shared expectations of growth, not an assumption by the County of the investment risk in Kenford's peripheral lands. The court drew an analogy to its earlier rejection of DSI's twenty-year profits.

Kenford had no contractual duty to acquire or retain surrounding land; its obligation concerned the 178-acre donation. The County knew of the purchases, but awareness alone did not make those special consequences part of the agreement. The court compared cases on sugar supplies, telegraph delays and Hadley's broken mill shaft.

Kenford bought the peripheral lands voluntarily, hoping to capture the stadium's benefits. Its theory would effectively guarantee the anticipated increase whether or not the stadium was built, and the court found no contractual or evidentiary basis for that guarantee. Limiting damages for unassumed risks also reduces the uncertainty facing businesses entering contracts.

The casebook's discussion contrasting this assumption-of-liability approach with the UCC's rejection of a tacit-agreement test is the editors' point, not a holding of the court.

CT-NEXT-CM-0158.rule: A new business is not automatically barred from recovering lost anticipated profits; it may recover them if the evidence gives a reasonable basis for estimating the loss, without absolute or mathematical certainty, though the jury may not guess.

sections.Parties: Anthony and Frank Fera were the plaintiffs. They had contracted to lease space in a proposed shopping center for a book-and-bottle shop and sued in Wayne Circuit Court, including for anticipated profits, after they were refused the location. The defendants, named in the case title as Village Plaza, Inc., offered evidence that the venture would have lost money.
sections.Procedural History:
The plaintiffs sued in Wayne Circuit Court, and the jury returned a $200,000 verdict against the defendants. The trial judge found enough evidence to move the claim beyond conjecture and denied a new trial. The Court of Appeals ordered a new damages trial on the premise that lost profits were an improper measure for a new business and that the plaintiffs' proof was speculative.

The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and restored the trial court's judgment on the verdict, with costs to the plaintiffs. The report also records that rehearing was denied.
sections.Material Facts:
On August 20, 1965 the Feras contracted for a ten-year lease of a particular location in a proposed shopping center for a book-and-bottle shop. Minimum rent was $1,000 a month, plus five percent of annual receipts over $240,000, and they paid a $1,000 deposit. They later surrendered approximately 600 square feet for another tenant; in exchange, liquor sales were excluded from the percentage-rent calculation.

Work stoppages and other complications delayed the project. After the developers defaulted, Bank of the Commonwealth took a deed in lieu of foreclosure and Schostak Brothers managed the property. When the premises were ready, the plaintiffs were refused their location because the lease had been misplaced and the space let to others. They rejected alternative space as unsuitable.

At trial both profitability and the prospect of a liquor license were extensively litigated. The plaintiffs had no license. Fera projected approximately $270,000 in profits over ten years, while the defendants' evidence predicted the venture would lose money.
sections.Issue: Whether a proposed new business may recover anticipated lost profits as damages for breach of a lease, and whether the plaintiffs' proof of those profits was too speculative to support the jury's verdict.
sections.Holding: The Michigan Supreme Court, 1976, in an opinion by Chief Justice Kavanagh joined by Justices Williams, Fitzgerald and Lindemer, with Justice Coleman concurring in part and dissenting in part and Justices Levin and Ryan taking no part, a four-to-one division over the disposition, held that a new business is not automatically barred from recovering expected profits. The plaintiff must supply a reasonable basis for estimating the monetary loss, and absolute or mathematical certainty is unnecessary. The evidence here sufficed to go to the jury, so the court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the full $200,000 verdict.
sections.Reasoning:
Earlier decisions distinguishing new from interrupted businesses reflected evidentiary differences: an established operation often has a record supporting prediction. A new operation's lack of history makes proof harder but not necessarily inadequate. Uncertainty describes the evidence, not an inherently unrecoverable category of profits. The court read Jarrait's restrictive lease-damages language alongside Isbell's recognition that sufficiently proven prospective profits can be recovered. The inquiry was whether the evidence afforded reasonable inference, not whether the business had begun operating; the plaintiff still needed more than sympathy, conjecture or an unsupported estimate.

The $200,000 verdict fell within the range of the testimony, but the majority relied on substantive testimony from both sides, full cross-examination and the jury's informed credibility assessment. One defense witness had a potential financial interest the jury could weigh. The jury was instructed to reject a speculative claim, and choosing between competing expert accounts, including the license evidence, was a factfinding function.

The justices acknowledged that they might have found the plaintiffs' proof unpersuasive as jurors, but that differed from deciding that reasonable minds could not disagree or that the trial court abused its discretion. Neither ground for displacing the verdict was shown. The court added that once some injury is established, inability to measure it precisely need not defeat recovery, especially where the defendant's conduct contributes to the imprecision.

Justice Coleman agreed that a new business can prove profits and that bookstore losses could go to the jury, but would have excluded liquor profits because the plaintiffs had no license and witnesses testified that none could be obtained. She would have affirmed only on remittitur of the judgment above $60,000, and otherwise reversed for a new trial.

CT-NEXT-CM-0161.rule: A stipulated damages clause is enforceable liquidated damages, not a penalty, when at formation the harm was difficult to estimate, the parties made a reasonable effort to fix fair compensation, and the stipulated sum is reasonably related to probable damages.

sections.Parties: Dave Gustafson & Co., a highway contractor, was the plaintiff and the appellant. It sued the State and its Highway Commission to recover $14,070 that the State had withheld for late completion, contending that the contractual assessment was an unenforceable penalty. The State and its Highway Commission, the defendants, maintained that the withholding was valid liquidated damages.
sections.Procedural History: The contractor sued the State and its Highway Commission to recover the $14,070 withheld for late completion. The trial court determined that the contractual assessment was liquidated damages. On appeal the sole question was whether the assessment was valid liquidated damages or an unenforceable penalty. The South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Material Facts:
On October 5, 1963 Gustafson agreed to construct subbase, base and bituminous surfacing for a new highway between Wessington Springs and Woonsocket. The work exceeded $530,000. The new road replaced a portion of State Highway 34, although the old road remained open during construction and afterward.

The agreement declared time important and identified increased engineering, inspection, supervision and administration costs, together with public inconvenience and deprivation of full use. Section 8.9 authorized deductions for each weather working day after the deadline or an approved extension and described the amount as agreed compensation rather than a penalty. Section 8.10 graduated the daily damages by the size of the project; projects above $500,000 and up to $1 million carried a rate of $210.

Gustafson completed the project sixty-seven working days late without requesting or receiving an extension. The State withheld $210 for each day, totaling $14,070. Asked by interrogatory what damage, loss or expense the delay caused, the State answered that it was unknown.
sections.Issue: Whether the contract's graduated per-day assessment for late completion of the highway work was valid liquidated damages or an unenforceable penalty.
sections.Holding: The South Dakota Supreme Court, 1968, in an opinion by Presiding Judge Hanson in which all judges concurred, held that the $14,070 withholding was enforceable as liquidated damages because delay damages were difficult to measure and the graduated per-day amount fairly approximated anticipated harm. The court affirmed the trial court. It also expressly overruled the portion of its earlier Fitzgerald decision that had declared a daily-delay forfeiture invalid on the ground that municipal damages were readily measurable.
sections.Reasoning:
South Dakota's statutes voided contractual penalties but permitted agreement on presumed damages where fixing actual damage would be impracticable or extremely difficult. With a valid stipulation the agreed sum replaces the factual measure of damages even if actual loss proves larger or smaller, so the court treated actual-loss evidence as immaterial under an enforceable clause. It distinguished an unknown amount of damage from proof of no damage.

The court compared the statutes with the first Restatement and treated the validity of a clause as a legal question. The controlling approach examined, at formation, the difficulty of estimating harm, a reasonable effort to fix fair compensation, and a stipulated sum reasonably related to probable damages. The label mattered less than the provision's substance.

Although the old road stayed open and the State named no actual-loss figure, delayed highway construction caused public inconvenience, postponed use and added administration costs not susceptible to precise measurement. The schedule was a reasonable effort to approximate compensation: it scaled upward with the size of the work, and each extra day increased the amount, tying the assessment to the extent of delay. The amount was not legally disproportionate to the harm reasonably anticipated, and the State did not have to prove $210 of actual expense for each day.

Hanson characterized the Fitzgerald discussion as unnecessary dictum and unrealistic about losses to municipalities, travelers and adjoining owners, and overruled it to that extent only. The opinion contrasted the disfavor of forfeitures with the usefulness of fair liquidated-damages clauses, especially in government work; their capacity to encourage timely performance did not alone make this schedule a punishment.

CT-NEXT-CM-0162.rule: Under Illinois law a liquidated damages clause must be a reasonable estimate, at formation, of likely damages that are difficult to measure; a formula awarding unearned gross revenue without deducting the costs the promisee avoids is an unenforceable penalty.

sections.Parties: Lake River Corp., which bagged, stored and distributed an abrasive powder for Carborundum Co., sued Carborundum for the amount due under the contract's minimum-quantity deficiency formula. Carborundum, the manufacturer, refused to pay, calling the formula a penalty, and counterclaimed that Lake River's retention of its bagged product was conversion, seeking the powder's value and its extra delivery expenses. Both parties appealed the judgment.
sections.Procedural History:
In this diversity action applying Illinois commercial law, Lake River sued for the stipulated amount and Carborundum counterclaimed for conversion. After a bench trial the court awarded each side its requested categories, together with approximately $17,000 in interest on Lake River's award, leaving Carborundum roughly $42,000 ahead. Both parties appealed.

The Seventh Circuit upheld the rejection of Lake River's claimed lien, held the contract's damages formula an unenforceable penalty, and required redetermination of both parties' damages. It affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded, permitting additional evidence and directing each party to bear its own appellate costs.
sections.Material Facts:
Carborundum made Ferro Carbo, an abrasive powder used in steel production. Under a 1979 agreement Lake River would receive bulk powder in Illinois, bag it, store it and distribute it to Carborundum's customers; ownership stayed with Carborundum until delivery. Carborundum required a new bagging system costing $89,000. To amortize that investment and earn its anticipated twenty-percent profit, Lake River obtained a promise that Carborundum would ship at least 22,500 tons during the three-year term, with any deficiency invoiced at the prevailing bagging rates at the term's end. Full performance would produce roughly $533,000 in revenue.

The steel-market decline reduced demand, and by expiration in late 1982 only 12,000 tons had been shipped. Carborundum paid for all services actually performed. Lake River demanded approximately $241,000 more under the deficiency formula, and Carborundum refused. Lake River retained 500 tons of Carborundum's bagged product, then worth approximately $269,000, as leverage. It offered to sell the powder and escrow the proceeds, but Carborundum declined and supplied its customers from the East at an additional $31,000 expense. The opinion rounds these figures to the nearest thousand.
sections.Issue: Whether the contract's minimum-quantity deficiency formula was an enforceable liquidated damages clause or a penalty under Illinois law, and whether Lake River's claim for damages gave it a lien justifying its retention of Carborundum's bagged product.
sections.Holding: The Seventh Circuit, 1985, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Posner for Judges Eschbach and Gibson, with no separate opinion, held that the deficiency formula was an unenforceable penalty because it awarded unearned gross revenue without deducting avoided bagging costs. Lake River remained entitled to the unpaid price less the costs avoided on the remaining forty-five percent of the powder, to be fixed on remand. Lake River had no lien, so its retention of the powder was conversion, but Carborundum's conversion damages also had to be refigured. The judgment was affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded.
sections.Reasoning:
On the lien, an artisan's possessory lien ordinarily protects compensation for services already performed on the goods. Carborundum had fully paid for those services; Lake River withheld the product to compel payment for services never performed on powder never shipped. The specialized equipment gave no other basis, since Lake River had received almost $300,000 in service revenue and used the equipment on another contract.

Illinois required a reasonable formation-time estimate of likely damages and a need for estimation arising from difficulty of measuring the loss. Classification was a legal question, and Illinois resolved doubtful cases against enforceability. Posner discussed reasons competent commercial parties might want penalty clauses and questioned paternalistic refusal to enforce them, but those observations did not change the controlling Illinois rule, which a federal court could not replace with its preferred policy.

The formula was systematically excessive. On an immediate breach after the $89,000 purchase, Lake River could recover the full $533,000 while avoiding the remaining performance costs, a $444,000 gain against an expected $107,000 profit. At the roughly fifty-five-percent stage actually involved, the court's illustrative assumptions yielded about $260,000. These hypothetical computations tested the formula's design and were not findings fixing damages on remand. Mitigation would not cure the failure to deduct saved costs. The court distinguished natural-gas take-or-pay arrangements, where nearly all supplier costs are incurred before delivery.

On the counterclaim, Carborundum, awarded the product's full market value, could not simply add all costs of selling substitute product. It was not required to accept escrow to mitigate a converter's liability.

CT-NEXT-CM-0163.rule: A stipulated damages clause is enforceable if it is reasonable under the circumstances as a fair estimate of compensation; in commercial contracts between parties of comparable bargaining power it is presumptively reasonable, and the challenger bears the burden of showing it is unreasonable.

sections.Parties: Wasserman's Inc., the tenant under a thirty-year lease of Township land, and those claiming with it were the plaintiffs. They sought the two cancellation payments the lease promised if the Township cancelled: reimbursement of improvements and a payment based on gross receipts. The Township of Middletown, the landlord and defendant, attacked the validity of the lease and the gross-receipts provision; it initially disputed the improvement reimbursement but conceded that obligation on this appeal.
sections.Procedural History:
The plaintiffs sued for the contractual cancellation amounts. On cross-motions for summary judgment the Law Division upheld the lease and the cancellation provision and later awarded $346,058.44 plus ten-percent prejudgment interest, made up of $55,748.27 for renovations and $290,310.18 for gross receipts. The Appellate Division affirmed.

The New Jersey Supreme Court upheld the validity of the lease and the $55,748.27 improvement-cost award but remanded the enforceability of the gross-receipts cancellation payment. It affirmed in part, reversed in part, and returned the matter to the Law Division for the necessary damages proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Wasserman's operated a general store on Township land from 1948 to 1968. The Township advertised a new lease in 1969 and again in May 1970; Wasserman's was the sole bidder each time. A lease was signed May 21, 1971, running thirty years at a fixed monthly rent of $458.33. The bid specifications contemplated proportional reimbursement of improvements if the Township cancelled. The signed lease added a second cancellation payment not in the original solicitation: twenty-five percent of average annual gross receipts over the preceding three complete fiscal years.

Wasserman's spent $142,336.01 expanding and renovating the store in 1971. In 1973 it sold the business and sublet to Rocco Laurino, doing business as Jo-Ro, Inc., for $1,850 monthly, and the parties agreed to allocate any cancellation payment between them. The Township gave cancellation notice in December 1987, effective December 31, 1988, and in June 1989 sold the land at auction for $610,000.

Jo-Ro's receipts for 1985 to 1987 totaled $3,483,722.25, producing the claimed $290,310.18 payment. Its tax returns showed profits of $3,649 and $414 in the first two years and a $323 loss in the third.
sections.Issue: Whether the lease was invalid because the gross-receipts term was added after public bidding, and whether the cancellation payment of twenty-five percent of average annual gross receipts was an enforceable liquidated damages clause or an unenforceable penalty.
sections.Holding: The New Jersey Supreme Court, 1994, in an opinion by Justice Pollock for a unanimous seven-member court, held that the lease was valid under the statute in force when it was signed and upheld the $55,748.27 improvement award. The gross-receipts provision remained subject to the prohibition on penalties, judged by reasonableness under the circumstances, and the court lacked the factual basis to decide whether this twenty-five-percent amount reasonably approximated cancellation losses. It therefore remanded that question to the Law Division. The court did not finally declare the provision a penalty or finally enforce it.
sections.Reasoning:
On validity, the court applied N.J.S.A. 40:60-42, the statute in force at signing, which did not require public bidding for this private lease. Voluntarily advertising did not import the requirements of an inapplicable bidding statute. Wasserman's was the only bidder twice, and nothing showed bad faith, corruption, detriment to municipal interests or that the amended terms would have attracted another bidder. A replacement statute effective six weeks after signing was not retroactive.

On the clause, a valid agreed remedy fairly estimates compensation, while an excessive punishment cannot be enforced merely because the parties agreed to it. Difficulty of estimating loss is part of the reasonableness inquiry rather than an independent requirement; greater difficulty makes a stipulated figure more likely to be reasonable. Labels are not dispositive. The court invoked the UCC and Restatement formulations addressing anticipated or actual harm. Between commercial parties of comparable bargaining power, stipulated remedies are presumptively reasonable and the challenger bears the burdens of production and persuasion. The court reserved the enforceability of such clauses in consumer contracts.

Gross receipts ordinarily omit operating expenses and expenses specifically caused by termination, making them a risky proxy for loss, though the court did not hold that any percentage of gross receipts is automatically invalid. To the extent Jo-Ro's tax returns reflected economic results, they raised a substantial concern about a payment exceeding $290,000.

On remand the Law Division was to consider the appropriateness of using gross receipts regardless of cancellation date, the choice of one-quarter of one year's average, the parties' reasons for the formula, mitigation, market rent and available replacement space. The Township, as challenger, kept the burden of showing the clause unreasonable.

CT-NEXT-CM-0165.rule: A party who makes a positive, express promise must perform it despite unforeseen hindrance or hardship unless performance is prevented by an act of God, the law or the other party; difficulty short of absolute impossibility is no excuse.

sections.Parties: John A. and Washington M. Stees, owners of a lot in St. Paul, were the plaintiffs. They sued for $5,214.80 plus interest after the building they had hired the defendants to erect twice collapsed. Charles Leonard and Monroe and Romaine Sheire, the builders, were the defendants and the appellants. They maintained that their work complied with the specifications and that concealed quicksand caused both failures.
sections.Procedural History: A Ramsey County jury found for the owners. The builders moved for a new trial on a bill of exceptions and appealed from the denial of that motion. Their objections concerned the exclusion of evidence offered to support several related defenses. The Minnesota court affirmed the order denying a new trial, so the owners' jury result remained in place.
sections.Material Facts:
By an agreement under seal dated August 18, 1868, the builders undertook to erect and complete a three-story business building on the owners' St. Paul property for $6,735, payable in installments as construction progressed. Except for painting, completion was due January 1, 1869. The agreement incorporated detailed plans and specifications prepared by M. Sheire & Bro. These required foundation walls two feet thick with specified projecting footings but did not otherwise prescribe the foundation's character.

The first building reached three stories and collapsed on November 1, 1868. The builders tried again in 1869, and the second structure collapsed on August 1. They then abandoned construction. They maintained that their materials and workmanship complied with the specifications and that concealed quicksand, which could not support the structure when saturated, caused both failures. The owners alleged negligent construction and inferior materials. Their pleaded demand comprised $3,745.80 previously paid, $1,000 for loss of use and $469 for damage to an adjoining house and property inside it.
sections.Issue: Whether latent soil conditions excused the builders from their promise to erect and complete the building, and whether evidence of the owners' site selection and of their earlier and later promises to drain the land was properly excluded.
sections.Holding: The Minnesota court, 1874, in an opinion delivered by Justice Young, with no separate writing and no tally of participating justices reported, held that latent soil difficulties did not excuse an absolute promise to erect and complete an otherwise possible building. Compliance with the stated footings did not complete the broader obligation; stronger foundations or drainage, if necessary, remained the builders' responsibility. The prior oral drainage promise could not vary the later written contract, and the later offers of proof were properly rejected because the facts offered were not the defense pleaded. The order denying a new trial was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
The court's formulation required performance of a positive express undertaking despite unforeseen hindrance or hardship, subject only to prevention by an act of God, the law or the other contracting party. The contractor could have qualified the undertaking in the agreement. Using construction cases involving accidental fire, lightning, wind and concealed soft soil, the court distinguished destroying work already performed from rendering completion impossible. The parties had allocated the task of delivering a finished building to the builders, and unexpected expense or the need to redo work did not transfer it to the owners. The specifications identified features of the promised result without eliminating the duty to take other measures necessary for completion.

The site-selection argument failed on the pleadings: the complaint identified the owners' parcel, and the answer admitted that the builders contracted to build on that parcel and began performance there. Because drainage was necessary to complete construction, a prior oral promise allocating it to the owners was not collateral and could not vary the writing.

On the later promises, the court recognized an American exception allowing subsequent oral arrangements to modify a sealed contract if executed or acted upon, but did not decide whether it applied. The answer alleged that the owners promised to drain and wholly failed to do so, a naked promise that released nothing. At trial the builders offered a materially different account, that the owners began draining and later stopped. That theory might have been a defense if pleaded, but it contradicted the answer, and each offer, tendered as a whole, could be rejected as a whole.

The casebook abridges this subsequent-promise analysis, and the later design-specification doctrine in its Notes is editorial material, not this holding.

CT-NEXT-CM-0166.rule: A contract is voidable for mutual mistake about a basic assumption material enough to upset the exchange, but absent fraud or misrepresentation the rescinding party recovers only restitution of benefits conferred, not consequential damages for reliance expenditures.

sections.Parties: Roy Renner, Lawrence Colton and Kofa Farms, the buyers of agricultural-development leases, were the plaintiffs. They sued to rescind the purchase after test wells showed the land lacked adequate water. The Kehls and Moyles, the sellers, were the defendants; they counterclaimed for the unpaid contract balance. On review in the Supreme Court the sellers disputed both the buyers' entitlement to rescind and the award of consequential damages.
sections.Procedural History:
After an October 1983 bench trial, the trial court in January 1984 entered findings and an order allowing rescission for mutual mistake and failure of consideration. It ordered reassignment of the leases and awarded the buyers $309,849.84, representing the down payment and development expenditures, together with costs and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals affirmed by memorandum decision on December 17, 1985.

The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed the trial court in part and reversed in part, approved the appellate decision in part and vacated it in part, and remanded for proceedings consistent with its restitution formula. It upheld rescission but did not affirm the full award.
sections.Material Facts:
The Kehls and Moyles held state agricultural-development leases covering 2,262 acres of unimproved desert near Yuma and offered their interests for sale rather than developing the property. Roy Renner, Lawrence Colton and Kofa Farms wanted land for large-scale commercial jojoba cultivation and made adequate water a condition of their interest. Both sides believed the land had suitable soil and climate and enough accessible groundwater to support the venture.

On June 5, 1981 the buyers agreed to pay $222,200 for the leases, paid $80,200 down and undertook annual installments for the remainder. Beginning that November they developed the tract and drilled five test wells. None produced water of sufficient quantity or quality for commercial jojoba cultivation. After spending roughly $229,000, the buyers concluded the aquifer was inadequate and abandoned the project.

The trial court found there would have been no transaction unless both sides believed jojoba could be grown economically on the tract, and it expressly found no fraud or misrepresentation by the sellers or their agents. The sellers supplied no trial record on appeal.
sections.Issue: Whether a shared mistaken belief that the land had adequate water made the contract voidable for mutual mistake, and whether buyers who rescind on that ground may recover their development costs as consequential damages.
sections.Holding: The Arizona Supreme Court, 1986, en banc, in an opinion by Vice Chief Justice Gordon in which Chief Justice Holohan and Justices Hays, Cameron and Feldman concurred, unanimous among the five listed members, held that the shared belief in adequate water was a basic assumption material enough to upset the exchange, making the contract voidable under Restatement (Second) section 152. It rejected reimbursement of development costs as consequential damages. The buyers' recovery was the down payment plus the enhancement in the returned property's value attributable to their work, less the fair rental value of their occupancy, with the amounts to be determined on remand.
sections.Reasoning:
Water was essential to the agreed commercial project, so the mistake went to the basis of the bargain rather than an incidental preference. A footnote specified that failure to investigate thoroughly does not itself defeat rescission when the risk of mistake was not allocated and the mistake concerns a material basic assumption. Because the sellers challenged the evidence but supplied no trial record, the court presumed substantial evidentiary support for the findings.

The Court of Appeals had relied on Fousel, which allowed incidental or consequential damages alongside rescission. The Supreme Court rejected that analogy: Fousel concerned fraud and breach, whereas here the trial court expressly found no fraud or misrepresentation. Restoring all the buyers' losses on that reasoning would assign the whole risk of an innocent mutual mistake to the sellers. The opinion stated its damages rule in terms of the absence of proof of breach for fraud or misrepresentation.

Restitution remained available under section 376 even though the sellers acted honestly, its object being to prevent unjust enrichment. The buyers had to return the leasehold interests, with return conditioned on restitution, and account for their beneficial use of the property. The sellers, in turn, could not keep an increase in the returned property's value created by the buyers' development without paying for it. Section 371(b) measures that side of the accounting by the enhancement of the recipient's property, not by the developer's spending, so a costly or unsuccessful improvement does not necessarily generate restitution equal to its cost.

A footnote explained that the court used consequential or incidental damages to mean reliance expenses, including the development costs here.

CT-NEXT-CM-0169.rule: Where the nature of a contract makes the continued existence of a particular person or thing fundamental to performance, and its existence is not warranted, the law implies a condition excusing performance if that person or thing perishes without the contractor's default.

sections.Parties: Taylor and Lewis, promoters of a series of concerts, were the plaintiffs. They sued for the expenses they had incurred advertising and preparing the performances, alleging that the owners failed to supply the promised facilities. Caldwell and Bishop, who had agreed to give them the use of the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall, were the defendants. They obtained a rule seeking entry of a verdict in their favor.
sections.Procedural History: At trial before Blackburn a verdict went to the plaintiffs, with leave reserved to enter a verdict for the defendants on the second and third issues. The defendants obtained a rule seeking entry of a defense verdict, which counsel argued in January 1863 before Cockburn C.J. and Wightman, Crompton and Blackburn JJ. The court delivered judgment through Blackburn on May 6, 1863. It made the rule absolute to enter a verdict for the defendants, displacing the conditional verdict for the plaintiffs.
sections.Material Facts:
On May 27, 1861 Caldwell and Bishop agreed to give Taylor and Lewis the use of the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall for concerts and day-and-night fetes on June 17, July 15, August 5 and August 19. Taylor and Lewis would pay £100 at the close of each day and keep the entrance receipts. The owners were to supply an organized military and quadrille band, other amusements, fireworks and illuminations, while the promoters provided the concert artists and publicity. The agreement used the words 'let' and 'rent' and the phrase 'God's will permitting', but the owners retained possession.

The hall was destroyed by an accidental fire on June 11, before the first concert. The destruction was complete enough to prevent the contemplated concerts, and the court accepted that neither side was at fault. The agreement did not expressly address that event, and the court observed that the disaster was not in the parties' contemplation.
sections.Issue: Whether the contract, read according to its nature, carried an implied condition that the Music Hall would continue to exist, so that its accidental destruction excused performance even though the agreement contained no express clause about destruction.
sections.Holding: The Court of Queen's Bench, 1863, in a judgment of the court delivered by Blackburn, with no separate opinion and no numerical vote reported, held that the continued existence of the particular Music Hall was essential to this bargain and that its destruction without fault excused both sides: the promoters from taking the gardens and paying the price, and the owners from giving use of the hall and gardens and providing the related services. The promoters could not recover their preparation losses as damages for the owners' nonperformance. The rule was made absolute to enter a verdict for the defendants.
sections.Reasoning:
An absolute promise to do a lawful act ordinarily requires performance or damages despite unforeseen accidents that make performance burdensome or impossible. That rule does not eliminate express or implied conditions. Where the nature of the bargain makes the continued existence of a particular person or thing fundamental, and there is no express or implied warranty of its existence, the law implies a condition excusing performance when it perishes without the contractor's default before breach.

Blackburn first rejected the idea that the words 'let' and 'rent' necessarily created a lease; the owners kept possession and there was no demise, though he said nothing ultimately turned on that. The agreement as a whole showed that the performances could not take place as intended without the hall.

The court explained the implication as furthering the intentions of persons entering this kind of transaction: had the contingency been brought to their minds, they would ordinarily have provided such a condition. The holding did not rest on defense counsel's reading of 'God's will permitting'.

The court drew analogies from Roman law and Pothier on destruction of a specific subject without the debtor's act, neglect or default, while denying that civil law was itself authoritative in an English court. English examples extended the implication to personal performance, such as an author's death before completing a work and the death of an apprentice. The court also considered specific goods destroyed after property had passed, and the bailment discussion showed that innocent loss of a particular thing can excuse a promised return, provided the promisor did not assume the risk or cause the loss.

The casebook abridges the personal-service and specific-goods examples, and its lettered translation notes are editorial. Its caption says King's Bench, but the court was Queen's Bench.

CT-NEXT-CM-0170.rule: Performance is excused for impossibility or commercial impracticability only if an unexpected contingency occurred, the risk of it was not allocated by agreement or custom, and the contingency made performance commercially impracticable; added expense alone did not suffice on this record.

sections.Parties: Transatlantic Financing Corp., operator of the SS Christos, brought an admiralty libel against the United States, the other party to a voyage charter for a cargo of wheat, seeking the extra cost of sailing around the Cape of Good Hope after the Suez Canal closed. Transatlantic was the appellant. The United States, the appellee, disputed any entitlement to payment beyond the contract price.
sections.Procedural History: Transatlantic filed an admiralty libel seeking its diversion costs, and the District Court dismissed it. On appeal Transatlantic argued that admiralty's usual-route and deviation principles implied a charter specifically requiring passage through Suez, that the canal's closure made that contract impossible, and that performing the Cape voyage in response to the government's demand conferred a benefit recoverable in quantum meruit. The D.C. Circuit affirmed the dismissal.
sections.Material Facts:
Under an October 2, 1956 voyage charter, Transatlantic was to carry a full cargo of wheat on the SS Christos from a United States Gulf port to a safe Iranian port. The charter named endpoints but no route. Egypt had nationalized the Suez Canal Company in July, and international tension remained when the bargain was made.

The ship sailed from Galveston on October 27 for Bandar Shapur on the usual route through Gibraltar and Suez. Israel invaded Egypt on October 29, British and French forces entered the Canal Zone on October 31, and Egypt obstructed and closed the canal on November 2.

Around November 7 Transatlantic's representative sought instructions and additional compensation from an Agriculture Department employee who, Transatlantic conceded, lacked authority to bind the government. He said performance was expected according to the charter and disputed any right to added payment. The ship went around the Cape of Good Hope and delivered the wheat on December 30. The alleged extra expense was $43,972 beyond the $305,842.92 contract price, with roughly 3,000 miles added to an expected 10,000-mile voyage. Transatlantic had already collected the charter price.
sections.Issue: Whether the closing of the Suez Canal made performance of the voyage charter legally impossible or commercially impracticable, so that the carrier, having delivered the cargo by the longer Cape route, could recover its added expense from the government in quantum meruit.
sections.Holding: The D.C. Circuit, 1966, in an opinion by Judge J. Skelly Wright for a panel of Danaher, Wright and McGowan, with no separate writing or stated division, held that although the closure of Suez defeated the expected method of performance and the specific risk would not be deemed allocated solely from foreseeability, the Cape voyage was commercially practicable. Transatlantic was not entitled to recover the additional expense. The court also rejected the proposed remedy even assuming an excuse, because it sought to preserve Transatlantic's contract profit while shifting all the added expense to the government. The dismissal was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning:
