Justice Douglas thought the Board had chosen a general policy for all future elections and was bound to follow rulemaking procedures. Justice Harlan agreed and added that under Chenery I a court could not substitute its confidence that the agency would reach the same result once its stated ground was rejected.

The four-Justice plurality and the two dissenters shared the criticism of Excelsior's adoption but disagreed on its consequences.

LRS-ATLAS-O-YOUNGSTOWN.rule: Presidential authority to act must come from Congress or the Constitution, and neither the Commander in Chief power nor the Take Care duty authorizes the President to seize private businesses to avert a strike without statutory authorization.

sections.Parties: The steel companies sued Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer, who had taken possession of most steel mills under President Truman's Executive Order 10340. The companies sought declarations that the orders were invalid and preliminary and permanent injunctions, characterizing the seizure as lawmaking entrusted to Congress. The Government asserted inherent presidential authority, historical practice, and the combined executive, Take Care and Commander in Chief powers, and argued that a preliminary injunction was improper because the companies could obtain compensation.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court rejected the Government's arguments and issued a preliminary injunction on April 30, 1952. The D.C. Circuit stayed it the same day. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on May 3, on the companies' petition and Sawyer's cross-petition, and heard argument May 12 and 13. On June 2, 1952, the Court held the constitutional issue ripe at this preliminary stage, held the seizure unauthorized, and affirmed the District Court's judgment, sustaining the preliminary injunction.
sections.Material Facts:
During the Korean conflict, the steel companies and the United Steelworkers were negotiating new collective bargaining agreements; the existing ones expired December 31, 1951. The union announced a strike, federal mediation failed, and President Truman referred the dispute to the Wage Stabilization Board on December 22. The Board recommended a settlement, but the parties did not settle. The union then announced an industry-wide strike beginning at 12:01 a.m. on April 9, 1952.

Truman regarded uninterrupted steel production as indispensable to weapons, other defense materials and national security. On April 8 he issued Executive Order 10340, directing Secretary Sawyer to take possession of most steel mills and operate them. The order rested on the President's constitutional and statutory powers in the aggregate rather than a particular seizure statute. Sawyer ordered the companies' presidents to act as operating managers for the United States, and they complied under protest. Truman reported the seizure to Congress on April 9 and April 21; Congress had not acted on those reports when the Court decided the case. Existing statutes prescribed ways to address defense procurement and labor emergencies, and Congress had rejected a general plant-seizure proposal when adopting Taft-Hartley.
sections.Issue: Whether the President had authority, under any statute or under the Constitution's executive, Take Care and Commander in Chief provisions, to order the Secretary of Commerce to seize and operate the steel mills to avert a strike, and whether the question could be decided on a preliminary injunction.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1952, in an opinion by Justice Black, decided six to three, held that the seizure was unauthorized and affirmed the District Court's preliminary injunction. Justices Frankfurter, Douglas, Jackson and Burton joined the opinion while writing separately; Justice Clark concurred in the judgment alone; Chief Justice Vinson dissented, joined by Justices Reed and Minton. No statute expressly or impliedly authorized the seizure, and the Constitution did not give the President this power. The decision establishes the invalidity of this seizure; it does not decide every future emergency seizure or treat each separate Justice's reasoning as a holding.
sections.Reasoning:
Black first held that equity did not require postponing the question: it was doubtful the Court of Claims could compensate an unlawful taking, and seizure of ongoing businesses would cause injuries difficult to measure. Presidential authority had to come from Congress or the Constitution. The Selective Service Act and Defense Production Act permitted acquisition only under conditions admittedly unmet, and Congress had rejected seizure authority in Taft-Hartley. The Commander in Chief power did not reach domestic seizure of private property in a labor dispute, and the Take Care duty presupposed laws to execute; the order made policy rather than executing Congress's.

Frankfurter found an affirmative congressional choice against general seizure authority. A systematic, unbroken practice known to Congress could gloss executive power, but the comparable seizures were too isolated. Douglas reasoned that a seizure was a taking requiring compensation, which only Congress could authorize. Jackson described three situations: presidential power is strongest with congressional authorization, uncertain where Congress has neither granted nor denied authority, and at its lowest against Congress's expressed or implied will; this seizure fell in the third. Burton said Congress had prescribed mechanisms for this emergency and reserved seizure to itself. Clark accepted extensive independent presidential authority in grave emergencies but concluded that Congress's specified procedures controlled.

Vinson's dissent characterized the seizure as temporary execution of Congress's defense procurement and anti-inflation programs pending legislative action, supported by history, and read Taft-Hartley as not exclusive.

The assigned casebook passage is an editorial account; the brief notes that it groups Burton with Clark as receptive to independent emergency authority, though Burton only reserved catastrophic situations.

LRS-ATLAS-S-AMALGAMATED.rule: A broad delegation is constitutional when Congress determines the basic policy and the statute's text, purpose, history, duration and implied constraints supply standards by which Congress, courts and the public can assess compliance; breadth alone does not make it invalid.

sections.Parties: The Amalgamated Meat Cutters union and its affiliated locals sued Treasury Secretary Connally and other Cost of Living Council officials for a declaration that the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 and Executive Order 11615 were invalid and for an injunction against administering the stabilization program. A second count sought enforcement of the meat-packer employers' obligation to pay a scheduled wage increase. The government defended the statute and order; the employers contended that paying the increase would violate the order.
sections.Procedural History: The Union filed a two-count complaint. Count I sought a declaration of invalidity and an injunction against Council officials; Count II sought enforcement of the employers' wage obligations. A three-judge district court was convened on October 3, 1971 under the then-applicable statutes and heard argument on the preliminary-injunction motion on October 8. Because the parties' presentation contemplated no further evidentiary stage, the court treated the legal issues as calling for a determinative ruling. On October 22, 1971, it rejected the facial constitutional and statutory challenges and denied the Union's motion for injunctive relief. The reported order does not award unpaid wages or damages or separately announce dismissal of every claim.
sections.Material Facts:
In April 1970 the Union and its locals negotiated collective bargaining agreements with major meat packers. A general wage increase of twenty-five cents an hour was scheduled for September 6, 1971; the Union alleged this concession was decisive to accepting the agreements.

The Economic Stabilization Act of 1970, as amended, authorized the President in section 202 to stabilize prices, rents, wages and salaries at levels no lower than those prevailing on May 25, 1970, and permitted adjustments to prevent gross inequities. A 1971 amendment restricted controls aimed at a particular industry unless the President determined its prices or wages had increased disproportionately. Section 203 permitted delegation, sections 204 and 205 provided fines and injunctions, and the authority expired on April 30, 1972.

On August 15, 1971, President Nixon issued Executive Order 11615, imposing a ninety-day freeze on prices, rents, wages and salaries, generally at the highest rates applicable to a substantial volume of transactions during the thirty days ending August 14. The order created the Cost of Living Council, chaired by Secretary Connally, and delegated the President's statutory powers to it. The freeze intervened before the scheduled increase took effect. More than 150,000 employees were allegedly affected across numerous industries.
sections.Issue: Whether the Economic Stabilization Act of 1970 unconstitutionally delegated legislative power by giving the President discretion over whether, when and how broadly to stabilize prices and wages without adequate standards, and whether the freeze could lawfully reach wage increases promised in existing contracts and fringe benefits.
sections.Holding: A three-judge District Court for the District of Columbia, in 1971, in an opinion by Circuit Judge Leventhal for a panel with District Judges Robinson and Richey and no separate writing, held that Congress could delegate this stabilization authority because the Act's text, purpose, historical setting, duration, and implied procedural and substantive constraints supplied an ascertainable legislative policy. The court construed the Act to require broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity for controls following the initial freeze, ongoing administrative standards, and meaningful review under the APA, and sustained the delegation on that construction rather than accepting unlimited presidential discretion. It rejected the contract and fringe-benefit objections and denied injunctive relief.
sections.Reasoning:
The court first held it had equity jurisdiction: individual wage suits would multiply litigation, and later recovery was not the same as receiving scheduled increases on time.

On delegation, the question was accountability to legislative will, not breadth. Under Yakus and Hampton, Congress had to determine the basic policy and identify the field of action so that Congress, courts and the public could assess compliance, and standards could draw meaning from purpose, history and administrative experience. The statutory floor and the limits on sector-specific controls confined presidential choice; earlier wartime stabilization programs supplied a recognizable context; and the House committee report contemplated a short general freeze. Congress had reasons to leave timing to the President, since advance proceedings might encourage anticipatory increases. Limited duration mattered because expiration forced Congress to revisit the delegation, but the court rejected the government's suggestion that a sunset and open courthouse doors sufficed if judges lacked standards to apply.

The court therefore read section 202 and the Act's purpose to imply a duty of broad fairness and avoidance of gross inequity. A general freeze's arbitrariness could be tolerated for a short opening period, but follow-on controls required more refined standards, and subsidiary administrative policies, once developed, would limit executive latitude. APA sections 701 through 706 permitted review, including pre-enforcement review when requirements were met; the Council was subject to the APA, and the court did not decide whether the President could be sued by name.

Schechter was distinguished as involving comprehensive industrial codes and delegation to private groups, and Youngstown as a seizure without statutory authorization. The Contracts Clause applies to states; the order operated prospectively; and wages and salaries covered fringe benefits.

The casebook's discussion of later amendments and practical limits on review is editorial.

LRS-ATLAS-S-BOWSHER.rule: Congress may not reserve to itself the power to remove, other than by impeachment, an officer charged with executing the laws, because removal power gives it practical control over execution.

sections.Parties: Congressman Synar, joined by eleven other Members of Congress, and the National Treasury Employees Union, with an individual union member later added, challenged the automatic deficit-reduction mechanism of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985. The Comptroller General, the Senate and the House leadership were the appellants in the Supreme Court, defending the Act and proposing that any defect be cured by severing the older removal provision instead.
sections.Procedural History: Synar sued within hours of the Act's enactment, and the Union filed a substantially identical challenge. A three-judge district court composed of Judges Scalia, Johnson and Gasch found standing, rejected a nondelegation challenge because the Act supplied adequate standards, but held that executive functions could not be exercised by an officer subject to congressional removal. Direct appeals by the Comptroller General, the Senate and the House leadership followed under the Act. On July 7, 1986, the Supreme Court affirmed the district court's judgment and stayed its own judgment for no more than sixty days to allow Congress to implement the Act's fallback procedures.
sections.Material Facts:
The President signed the Act, commonly called Gramm-Rudman-Hollings, on December 12, 1985. It prescribed maximum deficits for fiscal years 1986 through 1991, declining to zero. A deficit exceeding the target by a specified amount triggered generally across-the-board reductions. The Directors of the Office of Management and Budget and the Congressional Budget Office estimated the deficit and calculated program-by-program reductions in a joint report to the Comptroller General under § 251. He reviewed it, exercised independent judgment, and reported his own conclusions to the President. Under § 252 the President had to issue a sequestration order consistent with that report and could not modify its estimates or reductions. Section 274(f) supplied a fallback if the reporting procedures were invalidated: the Directors' report would go to a joint committee and become a joint resolution for both Houses and the President.

The Comptroller General was nominated by the President from a list recommended by congressional leaders and confirmed by the Senate. By statute he could be removed by impeachment or by a congressional joint resolution, after notice and a hearing, for permanent disability, inefficiency, neglect of duty, malfeasance, or a felony or conduct involving moral turpitude. Congress could override a veto of such a resolution by two-thirds votes. The spending provisions suspended scheduled cost-of-living benefit increases for union members.
sections.Issue: Whether Congress violated the separation of powers by assigning the Comptroller General, an officer removable by congressional joint resolution, the function of determining the budget reductions the President must order under the Act, and, if so, whether the remedy was to invalidate that reporting mechanism or the removal provision.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1986, in an opinion by Chief Justice Burger joined by Justices Brennan, Powell, Rehnquist and O'Connor, held that Congress cannot reserve removal power, apart from impeachment, over an officer charged with executing the laws, and that the Comptroller General's reporting function was execution of the law. It affirmed the invalidation of the automatic mechanism and let the statutory fallback operate. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Marshall, concurred in the judgment on a different theory; Justices White and Blackmun dissented separately. The vote was seven to two for affirmance, with five for the removal rationale. The Court did not decide the validity of independent agencies whose members the President may remove for cause.
sections.Reasoning:
Standing existed because the individual union member would lose a scheduled benefit increase, so the Court did not decide whether the Union or the Members had standing, nor did it reach nondelegation.

Removal power is a practical means of controlling execution: an officer has reason to heed the authority that can terminate his service, and presidential appointment does not overcome that. The majority invoked the 1789 removal debate and Myers, and explained that Humphrey's Executor and Wiener concerned limits on presidential removal, not direct congressional participation in removing executive officers. The defect lay in the continuing relationship, whether or not Congress had ever used the power; the removal grounds were broad, and structural protections could not rest on a prediction that Congress would not act. Congress had also long treated the Comptroller General and his office as its agent.

The reporting task was execution, not ministerial calculation: he interpreted the statute, decided facts, specified reductions, and bound the President. Congress may change policy by legislation but may not retain control over execution, an arrangement the Court analogized to the legislative veto in Chadha. The Court declined to sever the 1921 removal provision because Congress had expressly supplied a fallback.

Justice Stevens thought limited removal authority did not make the officer subservient; rather, the Comptroller General was an agent of Congress, which can make binding national policy only through bicameral passage and presentment. Justice White favored a functional inquiry and found no real threat of congressional domination, since a removal resolution required bicameralism and presentment. Justice Blackmun would have refused to permit congressional removal if attempted, as the remedy least disruptive of Congress's objectives.

The casebook reproduces an editorial note with selected passages.

LRS-ATLAS-S-EDMOND.rule: Inferior officers are generally those whose work is directed and supervised at some level by officers appointed by presidential nomination with Senate consent; exercising significant federal authority separates officers from employees, not principal from inferior officers.

sections.Parties: Edmond and five other petitioners were persons whose courts-martial convictions and sentences had been affirmed, in whole or part, by the Coast Guard's intermediate military appellate court. They argued that two civilian judges of that court had not been validly appointed, because the Secretary of Transportation lacked statutory authority to appoint them and because they were principal officers. The United States defended the appointments and the affirmances.
sections.Procedural History: In the earlier Ryder case, the petitioner obtained relief from a conviction affirmed before the Secretary's memorandum by a panel including the improperly appointed civilians, in a decision that did not decide whether the Secretary's later appointments were valid. The six petitioners' convictions were affirmed by the Coast Guard appellate court after the Secretary's appointments; Chief Judge Baum participated in all six decisions and Judge Bridgman in two. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed, relying on its post-remand Ryder decision upholding the new appointments. On May 19, 1997, the Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the judgments as to all six petitioners.
sections.Material Facts:
The Coast Guard's intermediate military appellate court included two civilians, Chief Judge Joseph Baum and Judge Alfred Bridgman. The Department of Transportation's General Counsel, who served as the Coast Guard Judge Advocate General, originally assigned them to that court. Unlike commissioned military officers, the civilians could not rely on an existing military commission as their constitutional appointment. Anticipating challenges, the Secretary of Transportation issued a January 15, 1993 memorandum adopting their assignments as his own judicial appointments.

The judges reviewed serious criminal sentences, resolved constitutional questions, and independently weighed facts and witness credibility. The Judge Advocate General prescribed the court's procedural rules, helped formulate court-martial review policy, and could remove a judge from the judicial assignment without cause, but could not use removal threats to influence particular cases and could not reverse the court's decisions. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces reviewed death-sentence cases, cases certified by the Judge Advocate General, and cases accepted on an accused's petition, though it did not freely reweigh facts when competent record evidence supported every element.
sections.Issue: Whether 49 U.S.C. § 323(a) authorized the Secretary of Transportation to appoint the civilian judges notwithstanding UCMJ Article 66(a), and whether those judges were inferior officers who could constitutionally be appointed by a department head or principal officers requiring presidential nomination and Senate confirmation.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1997, in an opinion by Justice Scalia joined in full by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer, held that the Secretary's appointments were authorized by § 323(a) and were constitutional appointments of inferior officers by a department head. Justice Souter joined the statutory parts and concurred in the judgment, so all nine agreed the appointments were valid and eight joined the constitutional rationale. The Court affirmed each petitioner's judgment. The Court acknowledged that its cases had not supplied an exclusive criterion for inferior-officer status and examined the concrete combination of controls here.
sections.Reasoning:
On the statute, § 323(a) let the Secretary appoint officers and employees of his department, and the judges were department officers. Article 66(a) did not displace that authority because it described assignment, not appointment; as Weiss explained, selecting an already appointed officer for a judicial duty differs from the constitutional appointment itself. Constitutional avoidance supported this reading: a Judge Advocate General is not the President, a department head or a court of law, so reading Article 66 as an exclusive appointment provision would make it unconstitutional.

On the Constitution, the judges' powers were substantial, but significant authority separates officers from employees, not principal from inferior officers. Morrison's factors of limited duties, jurisdiction, tenure and removability were not an exclusive test. Generally, inferior officers are those whose work is directed and supervised at some level by officers appointed by presidential nomination with Senate consent; mere higher rank elsewhere is not enough. The concern is accountability: Congress may choose alternative appointment methods only for inferior officers.

Here supervision was divided. The Judge Advocate General exercised administrative oversight and could remove a judge from the assignment without cause, and the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces supplied decisional review. The judges' decisions could not become final for the United States without the permission, through that review arrangement, of other executive officers. Freytag did not require otherwise, since it classified special trial judges and regular Tax Court judges lacked analogous executive supervision.

Justice Souter thought a superior necessary but not sufficient for inferior status; he would weigh powers, duties, tenure, jurisdiction and removal together and defer to the political branches' rational determination.

The casebook's second occurrence is Arthrex's discussion of Edmond, not part of this decision.

LRS-ATLAS-S-FREYTAG.rule: Tax Court special trial judges are inferior officers because they hold a statutorily established office exercising significant authority, and the Tax Court, though an Article I court, is a court of law that may appoint them under the Appointments Clause.

sections.Parties: The taxpayers sought Tax Court review of federal income-tax deficiencies and, after losing, challenged the assignment of their case to a special trial judge. They argued that the statute did not authorize assigning a large, complex case and that the Chief Judge's appointment of special trial judges violated the Appointments Clause. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue defended the assignment, asserted waiver, characterized the special trial judge as an employee, and alternatively treated the Tax Court as an executive department.
sections.Procedural History: The taxpayers' cases were assigned to Tax Court Judge Wilbur in 1982 and trial began in 1984. After he became ill and later took senior status, the cases were reassigned, with the taxpayers' express consent, to Special Trial Judge Powell, whose opinion the Chief Judge adopted as the Tax Court's decision. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, sustaining the assignment and treating consent as waiver of the constitutional objection. The Supreme Court granted review of the statutory and structural constitutional questions and, on June 27, 1991, affirmed the Fifth Circuit.
sections.Material Facts:
The taxpayers had deducted approximately $1.5 billion in losses allegedly generated by a tax shelter. Their counsel described the litigation as potentially affecting 3,000 taxpayers and involving about fourteen weeks of evidence, 9,000 transcript pages and over 3,000 exhibits.

The Tax Court, established as an Article I court in 1969, had nineteen judges appointed by the President with Senate consent for fifteen-year terms. Congress authorized its Chief Judge to appoint special trial judges. Section 7443A(b) permitted assigning them declaratory-judgment proceedings, specified small-tax proceedings, cases within a $10,000 limit, and any other proceeding the Chief Judge designated. Under subsection (c) they could enter decisions in the first three categories, but in the fourth could only hear the case and prepare proposed findings and an opinion, with a regular judge rendering the decision.

When Judge Wilbur became ill in November 1985, Special Trial Judge Powell became evidentiary referee, with proceedings videotaped. After Wilbur retired and assumed senior status in April 1986, the taxpayers expressly consented to reassignment to Powell for written findings and an opinion. Powell found sham transactions and additional taxes due, and the Chief Judge adopted his opinion.
sections.Issue: Whether section 7443A(b)(4) authorized the Chief Judge to assign a large, complex case to a special trial judge; whether the taxpayers' consent barred their Appointments Clause objection; and whether special trial judges are inferior officers whom the Chief Judge of the Tax Court may constitutionally appoint.
sections.Holding: The Court, in 1991, in an opinion by Justice Blackmun, affirmed. All nine Justices held that section 7443A(b)(4) authorized assignment of any Tax Court proceeding, regardless of amount or complexity, for hearing and proposed findings while reserving the final decision to a regular judge. Five Justices, Blackmun with Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices White, Marshall and Stevens, reached the constitutional objection despite consent, held special trial judges to be inferior officers, and upheld their appointment because the Tax Court is a court of law within Article II. Justice Scalia, joined by Justices O'Connor, Kennedy and Souter, concurred in part and in the judgment.
sections.Reasoning:
On the statute, the phrase "any other proceeding" contained no amount, complexity or subject limit, and legislative history confirmed that Congress intended assignments regardless of amount so long as a regular judge entered the decision. The taxpayers confused authority to hear and recommend with authority to decide. The catchall did not make the earlier categories redundant, because those carried greater decisional authority.

The majority treated the appointment objection as nonjurisdictional but structural. Acknowledging the taxpayers' consent, it exercised discretion to hear what it called a rare case, a serious challenge to the validity of the very proceeding under review. The Commissioner's assurance that the Executive did not view its prerogatives as threatened was insufficient because the Clause protects the constitutional distribution of appointment power, which the branches cannot agree away.

Special trial judges were officers: the office was established by statute with specified duties, salary and appointment method, and its holders took testimony, ruled on evidence, enforced discovery orders and exercised substantial discretion. They could also enter final decisions in the smaller categories, and one office did not alternate between officer and employee status.

The Tax Court was not a department, which the majority read to mean executive divisions like Cabinet-level departments, reserving questions about principal independent agencies. But courts of law need not be Article III courts. The Tax Court performed exclusively judicial functions, and its decisions were reviewed by courts of appeals like district-court civil judgments.

Justice Scalia would have enforced forfeiture of the unpreserved objection. On the merits he read courts of law as Article III tribunals, regarded the Tax Court as an executive body, and would uphold the appointment because it was a freestanding executive department headed by the Chief Judge.

The casebook note excerpts the officer-status reasoning and summarizes the five-to-four disagreement.

LRS-ATLAS-S-LUCIA.rule: An official who holds a continuing position established by law and exercises significant authority under federal law, as SEC administrative law judges do in running adversarial hearings and issuing initial decisions, is an officer who must be appointed under the Appointments Clause.

sections.Parties: Raymond Lucia and his investment company were the respondents in an SEC administrative enforcement proceeding under the Investment Advisers Act. They challenged the proceeding on the ground that the administrative law judge who heard it, Cameron Elliot, was an officer of the United States who had not been appointed as the Appointments Clause requires. The SEC rejected that objection, treating its ALJs as employees. At the certiorari stage the federal government changed position and supported officer status, so the Court appointed an amicus to defend the judgment below.
sections.Procedural History: The Commission assigned the enforcement proceeding to ALJ Elliot, who issued an initial decision finding violations and imposing sanctions. The Commission remanded for further findings, and Elliot issued a revised initial decision with the same sanctions. Lucia raised the appointment objection before the Commission, which rejected it on the view that ALJs were employees exercising no significant authority independent of Commission supervision. A D.C. Circuit panel agreed. On rehearing, ten judges divided evenly, leaving a per curiam judgment rejecting Lucia's claim; that result conflicted with the Tenth Circuit's decision in Bandimere. The government also asked for a ruling on statutory removal protections, which no lower court had addressed; the Court declined that request both when granting review and on the merits. The Court reversed the D.C. Circuit and remanded for further proceedings.
sections.Material Facts:
Lucia and his company marketed a retirement strategy called 'Buckets of Money.' The SEC accused them of using misleading slideshow presentations and instituted an administrative proceeding, which the Commission assigned to ALJ Cameron Elliot. Elliot had been selected by agency staff rather than by the Commissioners; at the time all five SEC ALJs had been selected by staff. The Commission itself qualified as a department head able to appoint inferior officers but had not made Elliot's appointment.

After nine days of testimony and argument, Elliot found violations and imposed sanctions including $300,000 in civil penalties and a lifetime bar from the investment industry. His initial decision made findings on only one of four alleged ways the presentation deceived investors, and the Commission remanded for findings on the others, explaining that his experience with the witnesses put him in the best position to resolve evidentiary conflicts.

An SEC ALJ could supervise discovery, issue or modify subpoenas, decide motions, rule on evidence, administer oaths, examine witnesses, regulate the proceeding and sanction misconduct, and at the end issued an initial decision with findings, legal conclusions and a remedy. The Commission could review that decision; if it declined, it issued a finality order and the initial decision was deemed the Commission's action.
sections.Issue: Were the SEC's administrative law judges officers of the United States, who must be appointed in the manner the Appointments Clause prescribes, or mere employees who could be hired by agency staff? If they were officers, what relief was owed to a party who had timely challenged the appointment of the ALJ who heard and decided his case?
sections.Holding: The Court in 2018, in an opinion by Justice Kagan for six Justices (joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Kennedy, Thomas, Alito and Gorsuch), held that SEC ALJs were officers subject to the Appointments Clause. Elliot had not been properly appointed when he heard and decided Lucia's case, and Lucia had timely challenged the defect. Lucia was therefore entitled to a new hearing before a properly appointed different ALJ or the Commission itself. The Court did not erase the enforcement charges or decide whether the presentations violated the securities laws, did not decide the removal question, and declined to decide whether the SEC's November 2017 ratification of earlier ALJ appointments was valid.
sections.Reasoning:
Germaine required a continuing position established by law and Buckley required significant authority exercised pursuant to federal law. Everyone agreed SEC ALJs held continuing statutory offices. Rather than frame an exhaustive definition of significant authority, the majority applied Freytag, which had treated Tax Court special trial judges as officers. Both groups took testimony, conducted trials, ruled on evidence and enforced discovery compliance, exercising substantial discretion in shaping an adversarial proceeding, and both prepared findings, conclusions and proposed remedies. A special trial judge's proposed decision in a major case always needed a regular judge's adoption, whereas an SEC initial decision could itself become final when the Commission declined review, so the SEC arrangement gave at least as much independent effect.

The amicus's distinctions were not decisive: excluding a participant or suspending counsel was substantial enforcement power even without imprisonment or fines, and Freytag had not made review deference part of its analysis. Nor was final decisionmaking authority an indispensable prerequisite. The litigants treated the ALJs as inferior officers, so the principal and inferior line was not in dispute.

On remedy, Ryder entitles a timely challenger to a hearing before a properly appointed official. A different decisionmaker was required because Elliot had already heard the evidence and decided the merits; the Court did not require a replacement for every conceivable appointment violation.

Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Gorsuch, concurred, arguing that all federal civil officials continuously responsible for a statutory duty are officers. Justice Breyer would have decided the case under the APA and, joined on this point by Justices Ginsburg and Sotomayor, disputed excluding Elliot from the rehearing. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Ginsburg, dissented, requiring authority to make final binding decisions.

LRS-ATLAS-S-MISTRETTA.rule: Congress may obtain the assistance of another body when it supplies an intelligible principle, and it may place an independent rulemaking commission that includes judges within the Judicial Branch so long as that does not accumulate power, encroach on another branch, or impair judicial integrity.

sections.Parties: Mistretta was a federal criminal defendant indicted with another defendant on three counts arising from a cocaine sale. He sought a ruling that the Sentencing Guidelines were unconstitutional because Congress had delegated excessive legislative discretion to the Sentencing Commission and had created a Commission inconsistent with the separation of powers. The United States prosecuted him and defended the Sentencing Reform Act. Both sides asked the Court to review the case before the court of appeals ruled.
sections.Procedural History: Mistretta was indicted on December 10, 1987, and moved for a ruling that the Guidelines were unconstitutional. The District Court for the Western District of Missouri rejected his arguments, characterizing the Commission as executive despite its statutory placement in the Judicial Branch and analogizing the Guidelines to other agencies' substantive rules. He pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute cocaine, the other counts were dismissed on the Government's motion, and he was sentenced under the Guidelines. He appealed to the Eighth Circuit, and both sides then sought Supreme Court review before the appellate judgment. The Court granted certiorari before judgment because of imperative public importance and disagreement among lower courts about the new system. It affirmed the district court's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
Before the reform, Congress prescribed broad sentencing ranges, district judges chose sentences within them, and executive parole officials often determined actual time served. Congress became dissatisfied with large disparities among similarly situated offenders and uncertainty about time served. The 1984 Act replaced that arrangement with basically determinate sentences, prospectively abolished parole, and made the Commission's guidelines binding on sentencing courts, with departures permitted for aggravating or mitigating circumstances the Commission had not adequately considered.

Congress created the Commission as an independent body within the Judicial Branch, with seven voting members appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. At least three had to be federal judges, chosen after consideration of a six-judge list from the Judicial Conference; no more than four could belong to the same political party; and the Attorney General or a designee served without a vote. The President could remove members only for neglect of duty, malfeasance or other good cause.

Mistretta pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute cocaine under 21 U.S.C. §§ 846 and 841(b)(1)(B). His guideline sentence was eighteen months' imprisonment, three years' supervised release, a $1,000 fine and a $50 special assessment.
sections.Issue: Did the Sentencing Reform Act delegate excessive legislative power by letting the Commission determine the relative seriousness of crimes and the weight of offender characteristics? Did it violate the separation of powers by placing the Commission in the Judicial Branch, including federal judges among its members alongside nonjudges, and giving the President power to appoint and remove its members?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1989, in an opinion by Justice Blackmun for eight Justices (Justice Brennan did not join footnote 11), with Justice Scalia alone dissenting, affirmed and upheld the Sentencing Reform Act against the delegation and separation-of-powers challenges presented. The Act supplied an intelligible principle, and neither the Commission's placement in the Judicial Branch, its judicial membership, nor the President's appointment and good-cause removal power was unconstitutional. The Court did not decide that every judicial commission, compulsory judicial assignment, or delegation of equivalent rulemaking to an actual court would be permissible. In footnote 11 it assumed without deciding that the Commission could implement existing statutory death-penalty provisions.
sections.Reasoning:
On delegation, Congress may seek assistance from other bodies when it supplies a general policy, identifies the implementing institution and sets boundaries; the inquiry is whether the statute lets a reviewing court determine whether Congress's will has been followed. The Act did far more than direct the Commission to invent punishments. It stated objectives of certainty, fairness and reduced unwarranted disparity, specified the purposes of punishment, kept guidelines within statutory penalties, ordinarily limited each imprisonment range to a spread of twenty-five percent or six months, listed seven offense considerations and eleven offender characteristics, and prohibited considering race, sex, national origin, creed and socioeconomic status.

On separation of powers, the Court rejected airtight separation and asked about accumulation of power, encroachment and impairment of judicial integrity. Some nonadjudicatory work, such as procedural rulemaking, is compatible with the Judicial Branch, and sentencing had always involved all three branches. The Commission was not a court and did not exercise judicial power; Congress could revise or revoke the Guidelines, which defined no new crimes and only constrained discretion judges already exercised. Judges serving as commissioners exercised administrative authority under separate appointments, no judge was compelled to accept, and no incompatibility clause barred the service. Removal from the Commission could not affect a judge's Article III status or salary, so the President gained no control over adjudication.

Justice Scalia, dissenting, agreed the standards satisfied the Court's delegation precedents but argued that the Commission exercised no executive or judicial power to which rulemaking could be ancillary, so its binding sentencing policy was freestanding lawmaking by a body controlled by neither the President nor the courts.

LRS-ATLAS-S-MORRISON.rule: Congress may vest appointment of an inferior officer in a court of law and may limit removal of that officer to good cause, provided the restriction does not impede the President's ability to perform his constitutional duties.

sections.Parties: Alexia Morrison was the independent counsel appointed under the Ethics in Government Act to investigate Olson, who had been Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Counsel. Olson and the other witnesses were served with grand-jury subpoenas issued at Morrison's instance and moved to quash them, arguing that the independent-counsel provisions were unconstitutional. Morrison defended the statute and, after losing in the court of appeals, sought reversal in the Supreme Court. The case concerned subpoenas and contempt orders, not whether any witness had committed a crime.
sections.Procedural History: After the Attorney General's January 1987 refusal to refer related matters, Morrison caused grand-jury subpoenas for testimony and documents to be issued in May and June. The witnesses moved to quash on constitutional grounds. The district court rejected the challenge, denied the motions, and entered contempt orders when the witnesses continued to refuse compliance, staying those orders for appeal. A divided D.C. Circuit reversed, holding that counsel was a principal officer, that judicial appointment of an executive officer was improper, that the Special Division's duties violated Article III, and that the statute impermissibly impaired executive control. In the Supreme Court, Morrison's preliminary claim that Blair barred these objections in a contempt appeal was rejected because she had not raised it in district court and could waive it. The Court reversed the D.C. Circuit's judgment.
sections.Material Facts:
The Act provided for investigation and possible prosecution of specified high-ranking executive officials. On sufficient information the Attorney General conducted a preliminary investigation; unless he found no reasonable grounds for further investigation, he had to apply to the Special Division, three circuit judges or Justices selected by the Chief Justice, which appointed counsel and defined counsel's jurisdiction. Within that jurisdiction counsel exercised the Justice Department's investigative and prosecutorial powers and generally had to follow Department policy except where compliance was not possible. Apart from impeachment, only the Attorney General personally could remove counsel, and only for good cause, disability, incapacity or another condition substantially impairing performance, subject to judicial review. The Division could terminate the office when the work was completed or substantially completed.

The dispute grew from 1982 House subpoenas for EPA Superfund documents withheld under executive privilege. Olson testified on March 10, 1983, and a 1985 Judiciary Committee report alleged false or misleading testimony by him and improper withholding by Schmults and Dinkins. The Attorney General sought counsel only for Olson. The Special Division appointed James McKay on April 23, 1986, and, after he resigned, Morrison on May 29. In January 1987 the Attorney General refused her request to refer the allegations against the other two officials.
sections.Issue: Did the independent-counsel provisions violate the Appointments Clause by having a court appoint the counsel, on the theory that she was a principal officer or that interbranch appointment is forbidden? Did the Special Division's powers violate Article III? Did the good-cause removal restriction, or the Act as a whole, violate the separation of powers by impairing the President's control of executive functions?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1988, in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist joined by Justices Brennan, White, Marshall, Blackmun, Stevens and O'Connor, with Justice Scalia dissenting and Justice Kennedy not participating (7 to 1), upheld the independent-counsel provisions against the Appointments Clause, Article III and separation-of-powers challenges. The independent counsel was an inferior officer whom Congress could have a court appoint; the Special Division's powers, with its termination power construed narrowly, did not violate Article III; and the good-cause removal limit and the Act taken as a whole did not unduly interfere with the President's constitutional responsibilities. The Court did not announce an exhaustive line between principal and inferior officers.
sections.Reasoning:
Morrison was an inferior officer on several features taken together: a higher executive official could remove her; her duties were limited to investigation and prosecution without policymaking authority; her jurisdiction was defined through the statutory process; and her office existed for a particular task and ended with it. The Clause's text lets Congress choose among the listed appointing authorities, and Ex parte Siebold supported interbranch appointment, subject to the qualification that an arrangement not impair a branch's functions or be incongruous with courts' ordinary work. Appointment authority came from the Appointments Clause independently of Article III, and defining jurisdiction was incidental to appointing, so long as it was demonstrably related to the Attorney General's request. The Division's other duties gave it no supervisory power over prosecution, and its termination power was read narrowly to reach only an office whose work was truly finished.

On removal, Bowsher and Myers were distinguished because Congress kept no role in removal. Applying Humphrey's Executor and Wiener, the Court declined to make validity turn rigidly on whether duties were purely executive; the question was whether the restriction impeded the President's constitutional responsibilities. Counsel's functions were executive, but her inferior status, limited mission and lack of policymaking authority meant good-cause protection did not unduly restrict presidential authority. Viewed as a whole the Act involved neither congressional aggrandizement nor judicial usurpation, and the Attorney General kept sufficient control.

Justice Scalia, dissenting, argued that Article II vests all executive power in the President, that prosecution is quintessentially executive, and that the statute deliberately displaced presidential control. He considered counsel a principal officer because she was not subordinate, and warned that a prosecutor assigned to one person risks unaccountable, selective prosecution.

LRS-ATLAS-S-SHOEMAKER.rule: Congress may enlarge the powers and duties of an existing office with duties germane to it without requiring the incumbent, already appointed through the constitutional process, to be nominated, confirmed and appointed again.

sections.Parties: The United States, acting through a five-member Rock Creek Park commission, petitioned to condemn land in the District of Columbia for a public park. Pierce Shoemaker owned land within the selected area; he died after the petition was filed, his heirs and devisees were substituted, and his executors challenged the proceedings. The owners were plaintiffs in error in the Supreme Court. They objected to the commissioners' appointments, the President's role, the appropriation ceiling, condemnation for a park, the valuations, the exclusion of alleged gold deposits, and the later omission of some mapped tracts.
sections.Procedural History: The commission petitioned the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia on May 20, 1891. That court rejected the owners' initial constitutional challenge, and attempts at immediate review failed because the ruling was interlocutory. Appraisers were appointed, heard evidence and reported in December 1891; the court overruled the owners' exceptions and confirmed the valuations. The President approved the appraised prices for a reduced selection in April 1892. The owners refused the sums and demanded interest from the first map; in May the court ordered the awards paid into its registry without that interest. On July 16, 1892, it entered a final decree vesting fee-simple title in the United States and directing delivery of possession. The owners obtained a writ of error bringing the final judgment and their preserved objections to the Supreme Court, which affirmed. The full brief notes that the closing affirmance was read from an archived reproduction because the report copy on hand stopped before it.
sections.Material Facts:
A statute of September 27, 1890, authorized a public park along Rock Creek in the District of Columbia of no more than 2,000 acres and appropriated $1,200,000 for acquisition and expenses, half charged to District revenues. A five-member commission selected and surveyed the land: three civilians appointed by the President with Senate consent, plus the Army Chief of Engineers and the District's Engineer Commissioner. The two latter members already held presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed offices. A majority could act.

The commission was first to seek voluntary purchases at prices approved by the President. Failing agreement, the District's Supreme Court appointed three appraisers, and the President then decided whether the appraised prices were reasonable for the government's acquisition. Payment to owners, or deposit in court if they declined, completed the transfer.

The initial map was recorded April 16, 1891. Only five of eighty-four selected tracts were acquired by agreement. To stay within the appropriation the commission later reduced the acquisition area. The owners also claimed value for supposed gold deposits in tract 39 and interest from the filing of the map.
sections.Issue: Did the statute violate the Constitution's appointment rules by placing the Chief of Engineers and the Engineer Commissioner on the park commission without a fresh nomination and confirmation? Was a public park a public use supporting condemnation in the District, and did the President's price approval, the appropriation ceiling, the valuation method, the exclusion of mineral value, or the denial of interest invalidate the taking?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1893, in an opinion by Justice Shiras with no separate opinion reported, rejected the asserted constitutional and legal defects and affirmed the District court's judgment. No second appointment was required for the two officer members, because they had already been appointed through the constitutional process and Congress had only added duties germane to their existing offices. A public park was a public use; the President's approval of prices was not a judicial determination of compensation; the appropriation capped total spending without fixing any tract's value; any gold deposits belonged to the United States; and the owners were not entitled to interest from the filing of the map.
sections.Reasoning:
The owners argued that Congress may create an office but not appoint its occupant, so the two engineer officers needed fresh appointments like the three civilians. The Court accepted the importance of the appointment rules but rejected the premise. Congress may enlarge an existing office's powers and duties without requiring the incumbent to be nominated, confirmed and appointed again. The line between military and civil duties might sometimes be difficult, but the park duties were not dissimilar to or outside the sphere of these officers' existing responsibilities. The statute was thus an enlargement of duties, not congressional selection of new officers. The full brief adds that this reasoning does not let Congress put a preferred individual in a new office by assigning an unrelated job, and that the Court rested on germaneness, not on the lower court's alternative that the three civilians could act as a majority.

On the taking, a park for recreation and health is a public use, and the amount of land needed rests in legislative discretion subject to just compensation; Congress's exclusive power over the District supplied the authority, and the Maryland cession proviso did not surrender eminent domain. The President decided only whether the United States would buy at a price already fixed by agreement or appraisers. The appropriation limited aggregate expenditure, and the government could shrink the acquisition. Appraisers could use inspection and judgment along with evidence. Adopting the lower court's chain-of-title reasoning, the Court held any gold belonged to the United States under royal-mine reservations, Maryland's confiscation and the cession. Interest was denied because the owners kept possession, rents and profits until payment into court.

LRS-ATLAS-S-WEISS.rule: A commissioned military officer already appointed by the President with Senate consent needs no second appointment under the Appointments Clause to serve as a military judge, and due process does not require that military judges have a fixed term of office.

sections.Parties: Weiss and Hernandez were Marines convicted by courts-martial on guilty pleas. As petitioners in the Supreme Court they argued that the military trial and appellate judges in their cases lacked constitutional authority because Judge Advocates General had selected them without a new appointment under the Appointments Clause, and that the judges' lack of fixed terms denied due process. The United States was the opposing party in both cases.
sections.Procedural History: Weiss pleaded guilty at a special court-martial and Hernandez pleaded guilty at his court-martial. The Navy-Marine Corps Court of Military Review separately affirmed their convictions. The Court of Military Appeals rejected both of Weiss's claims: on appointments, two judges considered the existing military commissions sufficient, one regarded the Clause as inapplicable to the military, and two dissented separately. Relying on that decision, the court also affirmed Hernandez's conviction. The petitioners sought joint Supreme Court review. The Court affirmed both judgments.
sections.Material Facts:
Weiss pleaded guilty to larceny; his sentence included three months' confinement, partial forfeiture of pay and a bad-conduct discharge. Hernandez pleaded guilty to cocaine possession, importation and distribution, and conspiracy; his sentence included twenty-five years' confinement, reduced to twenty by the convening authority, forfeiture of all pay, reduction in rank and a dishonorable discharge.

Military trial judges had to be commissioned officers and members of a state or federal bar. The relevant Judge Advocate General selected and certified them, and they acted as judges when detailed to courts-martial. Appellate judges, who could be commissioned officers or civilians, were assigned to the service Courts of Military Review. All the judges in these two cases were already commissioned military officers appointed by the President with Senate consent; the question of civilian appellate judges was outside the case. Military judges had no fixed term of office. The petitioners alleged no actual or apparent bias by the judges in their cases, and they sought some fixed term, not Article III life tenure.
sections.Issue: Did the Appointments Clause require military officers who had already been appointed by the President with Senate consent to receive a second appointment before serving as military trial or appellate judges? Did the absence of a fixed term of office for military judges deny the accused due process?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1994, in an opinion by Chief Justice Rehnquist joined in full by Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg, with all nine Justices agreeing in the result, affirmed both judgments. The judges had satisfied the Appointments Clause through their existing commissions, and neither the statute nor the Clause required another appointment for judicial duties. The Due Process Clause did not require a fixed term for military judges. Justices Scalia and Thomas joined the appointments part and the history of military judicial tenure and concurred in the judgment. The decision rejected structural challenges only; it did not retry the pleas or revise the sentences.
sections.Reasoning:
The parties agreed that military judges were officers and that the Clause applied to the military, so the question was whether already appointed officers needed a second appointment. Special qualifications such as bar membership did not create a separate office. Congress expressly required additional presidential appointment and Senate confirmation for several senior military positions but used the words assignment and detail for military judges. Shoemaker allowed Congress to add duties germane to an existing office; the Court distinguished it because Congress here had not selected particular individuals, then, assuming without deciding that germaneness applied, found it satisfied. Officers traditionally maintained discipline, served on courts-martial and reviewed sentences, and military judges had no judicial authority apart from the court to which they were assigned.

On due process the Court deferred to Congress's authority over the armed forces and asked, following Middendorf, whether the factors favoring a fixed term were so extraordinarily weighty as to overcome Congress's balance. Military courts had historically operated without tenured judges, and the Code protected independence: command authorities could not evaluate or censure judicial work, judges could be challenged for cause, and the civilian Court of Military Appeals, whose judges had fifteen-year terms, enforced these safeguards.

Justice Souter concurred on the understanding that military judges were inferior officers. Justice Ginsburg stressed that servicemembers retain constitutional protections. Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, treated germaneness as necessary whenever someone outside the Clause's appointing authorities assigns duties amounting to a new office, and found settled military tradition sufficient for due process.

LRS-ATLAS-S-WIENER.rule: When Congress creates a body to adjudicate claims on evidence and law free from executive influence, the President has no power under the Constitution or the statute's silence to remove a member merely to install someone of his own choosing.

sections.Parties: Wiener was a former member of the War Claims Commission whom President Eisenhower had removed. He sued the United States in the Court of Claims for the salary he would have earned from his removal through June 30, 1954, the last day of the Commission's existence. The Government asserted a presidential power of removal that depended on commissioners serving at the President's pleasure, since no cause was identified beyond his preference for a different membership.
sections.Procedural History: An earlier quo warranto proceeding had been dismissed, and its appeal was dismissed as moot by agreement. Wiener then sued for back pay in the Court of Claims, which, by a divided court, dismissed the suit. In the salary litigation the Government asserted that the earlier judgment barred relitigation of certain issues; the Court did not decide that contention, saying the Government should have presented it under the Court's rules as a reason not to review the case, and it withheld any endorsement of the estoppel claim. On June 30, 1958, the Court reversed, without specifying a monetary award.
sections.Material Facts:
The War Claims Act of 1948 established a three-member commission to receive and adjudicate claims arising from enemy-inflicted personal injury or property damage during World War II, covering internees, prisoners of war and religious organizations. At least two commissioners had to be members of the bar. The President appointed them with Senate advice and consent. Their tenure was defined by the Commission's limited life: it was to finish its work within three years after the claims-filing period expired, and successive legislation extended that filing deadline to March 31, 1952. Its determinations were final and not reviewable by another official or a court. Congress did not expressly provide for removal.

President Truman nominated Wiener, the Senate confirmed him on June 2, 1950, and he took office on June 8. He refused a request to resign. On December 10, 1953, President Eisenhower removed him, explaining that completing administration of the Act with personnel of his own selection served the national interest; he identified no misconduct. The President made recess appointments the next day, including to Wiener's seat, and submitted the nominees to the Senate on February 15, 1954. They remained unconfirmed when a reorganization plan abolished the Commission on July 1, 1954.
sections.Issue: Where the statute creating an adjudicatory commission said nothing about removal, could the President remove a commissioner, without any claim of cause, simply because he wanted the Commission staffed with personnel of his own selection?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1958, in an opinion by Justice Frankfurter with no separate opinion or dissent, held that the President could not remove this member of an adjudicatory commission merely to replace him with someone of his own choosing. Neither the Constitution nor the statute's silence supplied that power. The Court reversed the Court of Claims' dismissal. It did not address removal for cause concerning a member's rectitude or a temporary suspension while the Senate considered a replacement, so the holding is not an absolute immunity from every kind of removal.
sections.Reasoning:
The question was what to infer from Congress's failure to write a removal provision. The Commission had neither the FTC's express for-cause language nor an indefinite existence. The Court explained that Myers concerned an executive postmaster though its discussion reached officials with quasi-judicial duties, and that Humphrey's Executor later confined Myers to purely executive officers and rejected its broader statements. That distinction rested on function: an official who must exercise independent judgment cannot reliably do so while serving at another's pleasure. The nature of the assigned duties was therefore the most reliable indicator of congressional intent. Congress knew of the removal controversy and of Humphrey's Executor when it created the Commission, so its silence had to be read in that setting.

The legislative history reinforced the inference. The House would have put a narrow class of claims under an executive official, the Federal Security Administrator; the Senate substituted a commission empowered to adjudicate three classes of claims according to law, with final determinations paid from a War Claims Fund, and that design became law. Congress could have used direct appropriations, the Executive, or the courts, and it chose an adjudicatory body. Calling it a commission did not change the judicial character of its task: it had to decide each claim on evidence and governing law, free from coercive influence by the Executive or Congress.

If the President could not influence the adjudication of a particular claim, Congress could not plausibly have meant him to hold over members a threat of removal simply because he preferred his own appointees. Eisenhower's reason closely matched Roosevelt's unsuccessful attempt to remove Humphrey.

LRS-ATLAS-S-YAKUS.rule: A delegation is valid when Congress states the policy, chooses the means and sets standards definite enough for a court to tell whether its will was obeyed, and Congress may confine challenges to a regulation's validity to an exclusive, adequate review route.

sections.Parties: Yakus and the petitioners in the companion Rottenberg case were wholesale beef sellers prosecuted by the United States in the District of Massachusetts for willfully selling beef above maximum prices fixed under the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942. Convicted and unsuccessful in the First Circuit, they were petitioners in the Supreme Court, attacking the Act's delegation to the Price Administrator and its bar on challenging the price regulation in their criminal trials. The Government defended the standards and the exclusive review system as necessary to uniform wartime controls.
sections.Procedural History: The petitioners never filed an administrative protest or sought review in the Emergency Court of Appeals, and the sixty-day protest period had expired when they were indicted. At trial they offered proof that the ceilings failed the statutory standards and deprived them of property without due process because efficient wholesalers could sell only at a loss. The district court excluded the proof as irrelevant, rejected their constitutional and statutory objections, and entered convictions on guilty verdicts. The First Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari. The Court affirmed the convictions.
sections.Material Facts:
Congress enacted the Emergency Price Control Act as a temporary wartime measure to stabilize prices and prevent inflation, profiteering, hoarding and speculation. It authorized a Price Administrator to set ceilings when prices had risen or threatened to rise inconsistently with the Act's purposes, required the prices to be generally fair and equitable and to effectuate those purposes, and directed him, so far as practicable, to consider prices in an October 1941 base period and adjust for relevant factors.

Sections 203 and 204 created a special review system. A person subject to a regulation generally had sixty days to file a protest with the Administrator; a protestant denied relief could complain within thirty days to the Emergency Court of Appeals, which could set aside a regulation but could not grant interim relief, with Supreme Court review by certiorari. Section 204(d) made that route exclusive and withheld regulation-validity jurisdiction from other courts.

Revised Maximum Price Regulation No. 169, issued December 10, 1942, fixed prices for beef and veal with a statement of supporting considerations. The jury found the petitioners knowingly violated it within eight days after issuance. They did not claim lack of notice.
sections.Issue: Did the Act unconstitutionally delegate legislative power to the Price Administrator? Did section 204(d) bar a defendant in a criminal prosecution from defending on the ground that the price regulation was invalid, and if so, did that bar, together with the limits of the separate review process, violate due process, the Sixth Amendment or the judicial power?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1944, in an opinion by Chief Justice Stone, with Justice Roberts dissenting and Justice Rutledge dissenting joined by Justice Murphy, affirmed the convictions. It sustained the delegation, held that the statutory review route excluded a regulation-validity defense in these criminal prosecutions, and rejected the due-process and jury-trial objections on this record. The Court did not itself decide whether the price regulation complied with the Act or was confiscatory. It reserved the cases of a regulation unconstitutional on its face and of a defendant convicted while diligently pursuing statutory review.
sections.Reasoning:
Congress kept the essential legislative function by stating a policy, choosing maximum-price regulation as the means, and defining the conditions and standards for its use. The Administrator could find complex facts and form subsidiary policy within that framework; Congress need not choose the means involving the least discretion. The test was whether the field was marked clearly enough for a court to determine whether the legislative will had been obeyed. Schechter was distinguished: its broad rehabilitation purpose lacked adequate standards and left formulation to private groups, whereas here the anti-inflation objective, the fair-and-equitable constraint, the base-period considerations and the required statement of considerations gave definite guidance.

Section 204(d)'s text was broad enough to exclude validity challenges as criminal defenses, while enforcement courts could still consider the constitutionality of the statute itself. Due process required a reasonable opportunity to be heard, but the petitioners had never used the protest process and had not shown it incapable of providing one; sixty days was not unreasonably short given wartime urgency. Barring interim relief was permissible because stays could cause regional disparities defeating nationwide policy, and an injunction is not an absolute entitlement. A constitutional objection may be forfeited by failure to raise it timely before a competent tribunal, so Congress could assign validity and violation to different tribunals.

Justice Roberts, dissenting, thought the Act's multiple broad purposes set no real boundary and the review was ineffective. Justice Rutledge, joined by Justice Murphy, agreed with the delegation holding and exclusive review but would not let Congress give courts criminal jurisdiction while forbidding them to consider the regulation's validity; he would have reversed.

LRS-CB-0045.rule: Congress may exercise its legislative discretion to revive an earlier law either expressly or conditionally, making its operation depend on a future event that the President is to declare by proclamation.

sections.Parties: The United States sought forfeiture of merchandise imported aboard the brig Aurora; the proceeding was directed against the cargo itself. Robert Burnside, described as a citizen of Orleans, claimed the goods as his property and appealed their condemnation to the Supreme Court. He challenged the revival and effective date of the import restrictions, invoked a statutory exemption for American-owned goods, and objected to the government's pleading.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the District of Orleans condemned the cargo on a forfeiture libel, the pleading that begins a proceeding against goods. Burnside appealed to the Supreme Court. He argued that the restrictions had not validly revived or were not yet in effect, that the cargo fell within the American-ownership exemption, and that the libel was defective for not alleging the absence of American ownership. His counsel contended that making revival depend on a presidential proclamation transferred legislative power; the government answered that Congress had prescribed evidence of a fact on which its law would operate. The Court affirmed the sentence of condemnation.
sections.Material Facts:
The Nonintercourse Act of March 1, 1809, prohibited specified imports from Great Britain and France after May 20, 1809, on pain of forfeiture. After extensions it expired on May 1, 1810. A statute enacted that day provided that if either country revoked or modified its restrictions so that they ceased to violate American neutral commerce, the President was to proclaim that fact, and if the other country did not follow within three months, designated provisions of the earlier act would revive against it.

On November 2, 1810, the President proclaimed that France had made the required change. The Aurora cleared Liverpool on December 11, sailed on December 16, and arrived in New Orleans between February 2 and February 20, 1811. The cargo was seized on February 20 under restrictions said to have revived against Great Britain on February 2.

On March 2, 1811, Congress exempted qualifying wholly American-owned merchandise imported in American-owned vessels that had left a British port before February 2. The bill of lading said the goods were shipped on account of a United States citizen and consigned to Burnside but did not name that owner, and testimony identified a Liverpool shipper without establishing on whose account he acted.
sections.Issue: Could Congress make revival of the expired import restrictions depend on a future event declared by presidential proclamation? If so, did the restrictions resume on February 2, 1811, or only after a renewed May 20 starting date? Had Burnside proved the American-ownership exemption, and was the libel defective for not negating it?
sections.Holding: The Court in 1813, in an opinion by Justice Johnson with all the Justices except Justice Todd present and no separate opinion reported, affirmed the condemnation. Congress could exercise its legislative discretion to revive the earlier law expressly or conditionally. The revived restrictions operated against Great Britain from February 2, 1811. Burnside failed to prove American ownership, and the libel did not have to plead the absence of a fact that was his defense or an exception to the statute. The report's printed date entries conflict, so the full brief does not certify an exact decision day.
sections.Reasoning:
Justice Johnson located the decision to revive the law in Congress. A legislature could have restored the restrictions directly, and it could equally specify the circumstances on which restoration would occur. The expiration clause in the original act limited that enactment's duration but did not exhaust Congress's later power over the subject. The 1810 statute supplied the new legislative authorization, and the President's proclamation operated within it; the holding does not recognize an independent presidential power to revive expired legislation.

On timing, revival with full force and effect restored the act as it stood when it expired. By then the original May 20 waiting period had already passed, so what was restored was an immediately operative prohibition. Carrying the old calendar date forward into a new year would postpone the restrictions despite the later statute's express three-month mechanism, which was inconsistent with the words Congress used.

The exemption failed for want of readily obtainable proof. Burnside could have produced correspondence or testimony identifying the owner on whose account the goods were shipped; an unnamed citizen in a bill of lading and a consignment to Burnside left the question unanswered, and the Court treated the absence of accessible proof as supporting the conclusion that the property was not American. On pleading, American ownership was a defense or exception for the claimant to establish, so the libel could state the prohibited importation without anticipating and negating it.

The full brief notes that the ownership and pleading discussion comes from the full report, which the casebook excerpt compresses, and that the opinion does not use the later intelligible-principle terminology.

LRS-CB-0047.rule: Congress does not delegate legislative power when it prescribes a contingency and the legal consequence that follows and leaves the President only to ascertain and proclaim that the contingency exists; and a duly authenticated enrolled act cannot be impeached by legislative journals.

sections.Parties: Marshall Field & Co. was an importer challenging customs duties paid to John M. Clark, the collector at Chicago, on woolen goods and silk embroideries. The cases heard with it involved Boyd, Sutton & Co.'s duties on silk and cotton laces and Herrman, Sternbach & Co.'s duties on colored cotton cloths, with the United States and, in the Boyd matter, the New York collector as parties. The importers sought relief from assessments under the Tariff Act of October 1, 1890, by arguing that defects elsewhere in the act invalidated the statute under which their goods were taxed.
sections.Procedural History: The importers protested their assessments to the Board of General Appraisers, which sustained the collectors. The respective federal circuit courts affirmed. The Supreme Court considered the resulting cases together and separately addressed the enrollment objection, the reciprocity delegation and the sugar-bounty challenge. It affirmed each of the judgments sustaining the assessments. The casebook excerpts mainly the delegation question and Justice Lamar's separate opinion; the enrolled-bill and severability discussion comes from the full opinion.
sections.Material Facts:
The 1890 act imposed the duties in question. Its reciprocity section generally let specified sugar, molasses, coffee, tea and hides enter free of duty. Beginning January 1, 1892, the President was to suspend that treatment as to a producing country if he found its exactions on American products reciprocally unequal and unreasonable. During suspension the statute itself prescribed the duties to be collected on the listed goods, and the President could determine how long suspension should last.

The act also authorized Treasury bounties for specified domestic sugar production. The importers argued that Congress lacked power to pay them and that the bounty provisions were so connected with the tariff system that their invalidity would invalidate the duties.

A further objection concerned enactment. The enrolled act, signed by the presiding officers of both houses, approved by President Harrison and deposited with the Secretary of State, lacked a tobacco-rebate provision that the importers said had passed both chambers. They proposed to prove the discrepancy through legislative journals, committee materials and other congressional documents. This was an allegation; the Court did not find that the omission actually occurred.
